Keep the route review tied to current hazard information; several saved map lines may all share the same closure. After the exercise, change one weak assumption rather than buying a larger bag. A missing pet acceptance check needs a destination correction. An overloaded helper needs a role or transport correction. A phone-only plan needs accessible written information. Repeat the relevant part once the correction is made, and leave the complete plan usable for another adult. Manageable go-bag Get-home planning Time a calm departure rehearsal with the actual people, bags and transport. Record the slowest step and fix it. No universal bug-out destination or timetable suits every disaster. Avoid flooded roads and do not enter an active danger area for supplies. Work from confirmed reachable options and supplies already accessible. Help may be delayed, so keep your own contacts, route notes and essential care information available without internet. Assign an adult to each dependent and identify who can drive or arrange accessible transport. Check shelter rules for pets, service animals and support equipment before an event. Bug out & bug in bug out bugout Build an evacuation plan with a real destination Choose triggers you can recognize Develop two destinations and check their assumptions Connect routes, vehicles, and carrying capacity Prepare roles, bags, and change messages Rehearse one failed assumption at a time Put the plan on a one-page departure card Test the decision before rehearsing the departure Choose departure triggers Write hazard-specific triggers: evacuation instructions, unsafe building conditions, approaching wildfire, flood access loss or inability to sustain essential care. Leave before routes become unsafe where possible. Confirm destinations Arrange a nearby and an outside-area destination. Check acceptance, accessibility, pets, parking and essential care. An unconfirmed shelter or public campground is not a guaranteed destination. Plan transport and alternatives Map at least two practical routes where available. Consider no-car travel, fuel, road closures, bridges, water hazards and travel time with dependents. Make a short grab list Prioritize medicines, identification, contacts, mobility aids, keys, phone power, water and weather protection. Assign bags and dependent care; never delay an urgent departure to complete packing.

title: Burns & scalds
summary: Stop contact with the heat source safely. Cool a thermal burn promptly with clean running water for 5-20 minutes while preventing whole-body chilling, then loosely cover it with a clean nonadherent dressing. Seek urgent help for deep, large, sensitive-area burns or breathing trouble.
text: No running water Use clean available water and seek clinical guidance; do not use floodwater or contaminated water. Avoid improvised creams while awaiting assessment. Smoke inhalation Breathing trouble, facial burns or soot around nose or mouth needs urgent medical help, even if the skin burn seems limited. Should I wrap it tightly? No. Use a loose clean nonadherent covering after cooling; swelling can make a tight wrap dangerous.  Seek professional assessment for serious burns and worsening pain, redness or fever. Chemical and electrical injuries need their own assessment even when skin damage looks small. Do not apply ice directly, butter or toothpaste. Do not break blisters. This cooling sequence is for thermal burns, not every chemical exposure. Use clean available water to cool the thermal burn while seeking assessment; keep the unburned body warm. Breathing difficulty or smoke around the mouth or nose requires urgent help. Do not turn lack of specialist access into a reason to apply household remedies. A child can cool too quickly during whole-body showers. One caregiver should watch temperature and breathing while another manages water and contact with care. Keep labels or exposure details when chemicals or electricity were involved, without carrying contaminated items into a clean area.  Stop the exposure Move away from the heat safely. Do not touch an electrically injured person until the power source is safely isolated. Cool the burned area Use clean running water promptly for 5-20 minutes. Keep the rest of the person warm, especially children; stop whole-body chilling. Remove tight items Remove jewelry and tight items before swelling if they are not stuck. Do not pull away material adhering to the skin. Cover and seek assessment After cooling, loosely cover with a clean nonadherent dressing. Get prompt care for deep burns, burns larger than the person’s palm or those involving face, hands, feet or genitals.

title: Bushcraft: a practical beginner’s foundation
summary: Learn shelter, navigation, water planning and equipment care on short, supported trips. Bring reliable essentials first; practice should not depend on catching food, making fire or improvising every item.
text: The practice site or conditions are unsuitable? Use a permitted easier setting or postpone the session. A skill depends on removing essential equipment? Keep the real equipment available and practice the skill separately. A supply or route assumption fails? Use the known return or checked alternative before increasing the consequence. Must bushcraft involve making everything from natural materials? No. Reliable equipment, useful field organization and supported practice have immediate value. Follow site rules and avoid damaging the area for a demonstration. Should I rely on foraging for a practice trip? Bring suitable familiar food. Identification and local permission require specialized knowledge; an introductory trip should not depend on finding food. Choose skills with immediate value Start with tasks that improve ordinary trips: keeping sleeping equipment dry, organizing a manageable pack, reading the area map, describing your location, using suitable water equipment and carrying out the site’s waste requirements. These tasks connect directly to a comfortable return and a workable delay plan. An original introductory skill sequence Session Useful result Equipment access Find weather layers, light, care items and signal without emptying the bag. Shelter system Use the actual supported configuration and keep ground/sleep layers organized. Navigation Explain the start, intended route and known return on a familiar map. Water planning Describe carried volume, verified source and the actual treatment instructions. Repair and packing Complete one known non-critical task, then account for tools and waste. Choose one session at a time and keep all real essentials available. A good session ends with a clear observation and one correction, not a claim of wilderness mastery. If the whole group will use the equipment, involve the least experienced person so the plan does not depend entirely on the strongest adult. Food, water and fire boundaries Carry food that suits the people and can be eaten as packed. A supported beginner trip should not depend on hunting, trapping or identifying wild plants. Keep planned meals and spare food distinct so a late return has a visible reserve rather than a vague promise to find something. For natural water, the source, likely contamination and treatment method matter. NPS describes treatment as a process requiring suitable equipment and the product’s instructions. Clear appearance does not prove safe drinking water. If contamination cannot be addressed by your method, use a different suitable source or change the trip. Build the session so it remains workable without a campfire. Current rules, conditions and site protection may prevent fire use. Carry lighting, weather protection and food directly rather than assuming flame will solve missing equipment. If an activity requires combustion, resolve a suitable permitted system separately; it is not an automatic addition to every practice trip. Pick a supported site and a modest objective Use a permitted location with an easy known return and suitable support. Check the current rules, weather and access before packing. Name the session’s objective in one sentence, such as “set up and repack our shelter system” or “explain the familiar route from paper.” Write the stop conditions: changing weather, uncertainty about the route, discomfort, unsuitable equipment or insufficient time to finish and return. Keep a trusted contact informed about the actual plan. The practice site should let you stop without creating a second problem, especially with children or people needing assistance. Practice-plan fields Field Example of a useful entry Objective One ordinary task with a recognizable result. Site Permitted location and known access/return. Time Session length and a clear return/check-in arrangement. Support Appropriate instructor/helper and essential equipment kept available. Stop A condition that ends the exercise without an endurance test. Organize the camp by what must remain usable Keep critical items accessible and separate wet equipment from protected sleeping layers. Decide where the group enters, where bags rest and where food, water, care items and lights are kept. Keep the arrangement simple enough that another adult can find the necessary item. Use named pouches or a short location list if it helps. A person assisting someone else may need a lighter load and an accessible care pouch. Avoid spreading small items over the whole site, where they can be lost or become a trip problem. Give each person an appropriate personal light and signal rather than relying on one shared bag for every need. During supported practice, ask someone else to retrieve a specific item. Record the exact problem if they cannot: unclear label, awkward opening, deep packing or a missing part. Fix that organization at home. Good field competence includes being able to repack equipment correctly while tired, without leaving fittings or rubbish behind. Learn materials through the actual equipment Read the maker’s care instructions for the tarp, pad, bedding, pack and water equipment you own. Record compatible repair supplies and which tasks the owner can reasonably perform. A collection of generic materials is less useful than one patch or spare part whose purpose is known. Inspect seams, closures, fittings and guards before the trip. A visible issue should become a decision: correct it as permitted, arrange service, select an alternative or postpone the session. Do not pack damaged equipment on the assumption that improvisation will make the trip more educational. For hand tools, choose the material and ordinary task first, then obtain instruction in the specific tool. Keep the tool guarded when not in use. Do not harvest branches or alter a site simply to produce a demonstration object. Existing compatible equipment and permitted materials can teach the useful organization skill with less impact. Hand-tool selection and care Run a one-skill session with a visible finish Begin with the objective and the instructions for the actual equipment. Arrange the suitable practice area, keep essential supplies available and assign roles. The person learning should explain what they intend to do before the task begins. A supported skill session Prepare Choose one task, read the relevant instructions and confirm the site and stop conditions. Demonstrate Use the actual equipment and permitted material with suitable instruction. Explain Have the learner describe the task, its limits and how to stop. Reset Account for parts, pack the equipment and leave the site clean. Improve Record one correction and the person responsible for it. Osprey Zero planning aid. These are conditional choices; current conditions and individual needs control the decision. Examples include repacking a dry sleeping system, locating a map junction or finding the personal light with gloves. Do not remove the real backup or wait until dark to create a problem. If the exercise reveals missing equipment or understanding, treat that as useful information and end the session while the return remains easy. Evaluate the result and plan the next ordinary trip Keep a short log: date, task, equipment, conditions, result and correction. Replace broad judgments such as “worked well” with a fact: the supplied cords reached the approved supports, the care pouch opened with gloves, or the map print was too small for one person to read. Compare the result with the one-sentence objective. Ask each person what was difficult to find or understand. Inspect and care for equipment according to its instructions. Account for waste and small fittings. Make one correction before repeating the task. Increase only one ordinary complication at a time, with support still available. A next trip can add a slightly different permitted site or a longer supported session without removing essentials. Keep route, weather and household limits in the planning. Practical bushcraft is a continuing collection of reliable habits; no single weekend establishes the ability to manage every wilderness emergency. NPS · Ten essentials Use the equipment systems framework to check what the session still needs. NPS · Leave no trace Review site-impact principles and the specific land manager’s rules. NPS · Water treatment methods Read the treatment-method distinctions before practicing with your selected equipment. Trip accountability Complete tarp/sleep system Run a daylight shelter-and-packing session close to home. Finish with a gear check and a written lesson learned. No eating unidentified plants, unsafe knife experiments, destructive shelters or unsupervised fire practice. Outdoor skills require hands-on training and judgment. Use the equipment and safe route you brought. Turn back early if conditions exceed your ability, your group is tiring or essential equipment fails. If lost, stop and use the lost-outdoors plan rather than experimenting with shortcuts. Choose distance and terrain for the least mobile person. Include individual medicines, warm layers and snacks. Give every person a light, whistle and simple instructions for separation. Bushcraft bushcraft bushcrafting Choose skills with immediate value Food, water and fire boundaries Pick a supported site and a modest objective Organize the camp by what must remain usable Learn materials through the actual equipment Run a one-skill session with a visible finish Evaluate the result and plan the next ordinary trip Choose a low-consequence practice site Use a permitted location near an easy return route. Check weather, land rules and water availability; tell someone your itinerary and return time. Pack dependable essentials Bring navigation, a headlamp, insulation, weather protection, water, food, first aid and a shelter appropriate to conditions. Tools complement these supplies. Practice one skill at a time Pitch a shelter, organize a dry sleeping system or locate yourself on a map before adding complications. Practice before dark with enough time to stop. Leave a clean site Use existing durable sites where permitted. Carry out waste and follow local rules for fires, wood collection and wildlife protection.

title: Carbon monoxide
summary: If a CO alarm sounds or carbon monoxide exposure is suspected, get everyone into fresh air immediately and call emergency services. Do not stay inside to find the source. Headache, dizziness, nausea or confusion can be warning signs.
text: Can I turn off the appliance first? Move everyone to fresh air before investigating. A fuel-burning appliance may continue exposing people while it is being inspected. Call from outside and do not reenter until the hazard has been assessed by appropriate qualified personnel. Can the household sleep elsewhere inside? Changing rooms is not a reliable answer to a suspected CO exposure. Get outside to fresh air and seek medical evaluation for symptoms. Keep people together so confusion, faintness or worsening breathing is noticed.  Install CO alarms and service heating equipment. Keep generators and grills outdoors, far from openings. CO is invisible and odorless. A silent smoke alarm is not proof that air is safe. Leave the building even if responders cannot be reached. Gather outside away from exhaust, keep everyone out and seek reachable medical care for symptoms. Do not send someone back inside to ventilate or switch equipment off. Children, sleeping people and people with limited mobility may not recognize symptoms or reach fresh air independently. Assign evacuation help in advance and keep functioning CO alarms near sleeping areas. Do not make a symptomatic person drive. Air & gas Leave the building Move people and pets into fresh air, without delaying to ventilate or troubleshoot. Call from outside Report the alarm, symptoms and possible fuel-burning source to emergency services. Get medical help Tell responders about suspected exposure even if symptoms improve outdoors. Wait for clearance Do not reenter until responders say it is safe.

title: Caregiver handover: a plan for missed visits
summary: Write down essential tasks, confirm who can perform them safely, and define when a missed visit becomes urgent. A name on a contact list is not a confirmed backup caregiver.
text: What if my usual helper also needs to evacuate? Agree a second helper or destination before the emergency. Ask both helpers about the conditions that would make them unavailable so the backups do not all fail together. Keep the summary short and current Editorial format: one page for the immediate routine, with detailed instructions and specialist plans stored separately. Date the summary and name who updates it. Have a backup helper explain the plan back to you; confusing wording discovered in a calm practice run is easier to fix than during an outage. Test the access problem A helper may know the routine but be unable to enter the building or reach supplies. Discuss keys, building rules and any safe access arrangement without publishing codes. Include what happens when lifts stop or transport is disrupted. Do not make the entire backup depend on a single phone, driver or person. Run a calm handover exercise with the backup helper. Record one task they cannot perform and arrange a qualified alternative. Generic emergency advice does not replace an individual clinical or equipment plan. Do not improvise lifting, feeding, medication changes or medical-device work. If no helper can attend, use the individual plan to prioritize safe independent tasks and seek reachable assistance early. A situation involving essential care that cannot be delivered may require moving to a setting that can support it. Include the person receiving care in decisions. Protect their privacy and ask about language, hearing, vision and communication needs. Ensure helpers know who can authorize changes to the plan. care handover missed caregiver support network List the next essential tasks Record what must happen during the next day: meals, personal care, medicines, equipment checks and mobility assistance. Separate everyday help from tasks requiring training. Confirm responsibility Ask a primary and backup helper what they can actually do, when they can arrive and what supplies or access they need. Do not assign clinical work to an untrained volunteer. Write a short handover Record the usual routine, communication preferences, relevant contacts, supply locations and limits. Share with consent through a private method. Set escalation points Agree what happens if the person cannot be reached, a critical task is missed or the environment no longer supports care. Identify a realistic accessible destination before that point.

title: Cartridges and calibers: a practical comparison
summary: Read the complete cartridge or shotshell designation, then compare manufacturer compatibility, sporting context, local availability, package cost and carried mass. Similar names and nominal bullet diameters do not establish interchangeability.
text: Caliber, cartridge and bullet: three different things Anatomy of a cartridge Conceptual centerfire cartridge: a bullet sits at the front of a case; the case contains propellant, with a primer at its base. Not to scale; rimfire priming is in the case rim. Caliber often refers to an approximate bore or bullet diameter. Cartridge is the complete ammunition designation: it describes a particular family with its own case and chamber requirements. Bullet is the projectile, not the entire round. A .22 LR cartridge and a .223 Remington cartridge have roughly similar diameter projectiles, yet belong to very different systems. Shared digits do not establish compatibility. Rimfire ammunition places priming compound in the case rim; centerfire ammunition uses a primer in the center of the base. Both include a case and propellant. A grain is a unit of mass, not a type of powder: bullet weight printed as “124 gr” is not the propellant charge. Box velocity is a result from a stated test setup and may differ in another firearm. .22 LR and .22 WMR: inexpensive practice and small game Two rimfire families, not interchangeable versions Cartridge Common civilian uses Practical tradeoffs .22 Long Rifle (.22 LR) Target practice, introductory sporting instruction and small-game hunting where permitted. Usually modest recoil, compact ammunition and a broad selection of target and hunting loads. .22 Winchester Magnum Rimfire (.22 WMR / .22 Magnum) Small-game and varmint hunting, plus recreational shooting. A different, larger case; generally more report and higher ammunition cost than .22 LR. For a household that already owns a lawful sporting firearm, .22 LR can make regular range practice relatively affordable. The cartridge is used in rifles and handguns; the action and specific ammunition still affect reliability and the experience. .22 WMR is a distinct chambering, not a “magnum setting” on a .22 LR firearm. Some revolvers have manufacturer-supplied interchangeable cylinders, but that is a model-specific arrangement rather than permission to mix ammunition. Small-game hunting is a skill and a regulated activity, not an automatic food plan. Species identification, access to permitted land, seasons, humane harvest and food handling all matter. In Florida, for example, rimfire rifles are not a legal method of taking deer. Lightweight ammunition does not remove those limits or make large-game use appropriate. Handgun cartridges: names, platforms and real tradeoffs Common centerfire handgun cartridges Cartridge Typical sporting platforms What to understand 9mm Luger / 9×19mm Semiautomatic pistols and some sporting carbines. Widely encountered; its common name does not include every cartridge beginning with “9mm.” .380 Auto / .380 ACP / 9mm Browning Short Often compact semiautomatic pistols. Distinct from 9mm Luger. A lighter firearm can feel sharper or be harder to handle than the smaller cartridge suggests. .38 Special Commonly revolvers; also some sporting rifles. A rimmed cartridge. It is not .38 Super or .380 Auto. .45 Auto / .45 ACP Semiautomatic pistols and some sporting carbines. Larger cartridge and typically heavier projectiles than common 9mm loads; not .45 Colt. A comfortable range firearm depends on grip fit, overall mass, controls and the particular load. A compact pistol is easy to store but may have a less forgiving grip and sight picture than a larger sporting model. It is therefore misleading to promise that a cartridge is “easy for everyone” or rank the whole experience by bullet diameter alone. Suffixes matter. +P denotes a higher-pressure designation for certain standardized cartridges; it is not an upgrade for any firearm bearing the base name. +P+ is not a single universal SAAMI pressure standard. The firearm manufacturer must authorize the exact ammunition category. Keep ordinary and special-pressure products distinctly labelled rather than combining loose rounds because the headstamps look similar. .223, 5.56 and the three very different “7.62” names Centerfire rifle families Designation Common sporting context Important distinction .223 Remington Target, varmint and other hunting uses where permitted. Closely related to 5.56×45 NATO, but chamber specifications and ammunition requirements are not identical. 5.56×45 NATO Common in rifles also used for organized recreational shooting. Do not assume a .223-marked chamber accepts 5.56 ammunition. .308 Winchester Target shooting and game hunting with a suitable load and lawful method. Closely related to 7.62×51 NATO; verify the exact firearm’s authorization. 7.62×51 NATO Some rifles used in sporting and target activities. The “51” distinguishes this family from 7.62×39. 7.62×39 Sporting rifles used for recreational shooting and permitted hunting. A different case and chamber from .308 Winchester / 7.62×51. SAAMI explains that .223 Remington ammunition can generally be used in a manufacturer-confirmed military-specification 5.56 chamber, while 5.56 ammunition should not be assumed safe in a .223 Remington chamber. A .223 Wylde marking refers to a chamber design, not a separate cartridge on the shelf; consult that firearm’s manual. The useful lesson is specific compatibility, not an improvised fit test. A number such as “7.62” gives too little information to choose ammunition. Case length, shape, chamber standards and intended loading differ. Likewise, “.308 and NATO are the same” is too broad for every firearm, including older examples. Rifle cartridges also tend to add ammunition bulk and report compared with rimfire. Hunting suitability depends on the species, projectile, firearm and law; there is no universal caliber that solves every outdoor task. 12 and 20 gauge: read the whole shotshell label Gauge is a historical bore-size system, not a caliber in millimeters. Within this system 12 gauge is a larger bore than 20 gauge; .410 bore is an exception named by bore diameter. A shotgun may use shot, a group of pellets, or a slug, a single projectile. Those are different load types within the shotgun family, not different names for the firearm. What a shotshell box tells you Label Meaning Gauge The shell family must match the firearm. Do not mix 12 and 20 gauge in one container. Shell length The designated length refers to the fired/opened shell, not simply the unfired length in your hand. Match chamber authorization. Shot size For common numbered birdshot, a higher number generally means smaller pellets. Buckshot uses another naming scale. Payload The quantity of shot, often in ounces; separate from pellet diameter. Material Lead, steel and other materials have different properties; hunting and firearm restrictions can apply. Clay sports and bird hunting often use shotshells selected for the rules of that activity. Bigger gauge, heavier payload or “magnum” branding does not automatically mean better results. Firearm fit, total weight and the particular load affect recoil. Check both firearm and ammunition instructions; a shell slipping into an opening does not prove it belongs there. Build a comparison that answers your actual question For a sporting purchase, write down the activity first: affordable paper-target practice, a particular licensed hunting activity or an established club discipline. Compare the cost of routine ammunition, range fees, instruction, secure storage and maintenance as well as the firearm. Availability in your area matters more than an attractive specification from a product you cannot regularly obtain. Record the full chamber designation, exact model and manufacturer-approved ammunition categories. Compare prices per round within the same cartridge and intended sporting load type. Keep product codes and lot numbers when you buy; they make recall checks possible. Reject simple “bigger is better” claims. Cartridge names alone do not describe reliability, accuracy or suitability. Use the cartridge guide alongside the ammunition-storage guide; identification and condition are separate checks. For preparedness, preserve the sporting equipment you already understand before adding unfamiliar systems. A labeled, modest inventory that remains secure, dry and identifiable is easier to manage than assorted loose ammunition. Skills, lawful access and realistic expectations give the equipment a purpose; the cartridge label alone does not provide one. Read an ammunition label as separate fields Treat the package as several descriptions rather than one caliber number. The recognized cartridge designation identifies the cartridge family. The bullet or shot description, stated projectile weight, package count and product/lot identification describe that particular product. These fields answer different questions. A weight printed in grains describes mass; it is not a powder-loading instruction. Illustrative label-reading worksheet Example field What it tells you What remains to check 9mm Luger A complete cartridge designation, rather than the broad phrase “9mm.” The exact firearm manual and any additional product restrictions. 124 grain The stated projectile mass for this example product. Its manufacturer-described intended use; this number alone is not a compatibility decision. 50 cartridges The quantity sold in this example box. Cost per cartridge and whether several listings use the same package size. 12 gauge / shell length Two distinct shotshell identity fields. The complete chamber and ammunition specifications in the shotgun manual. These are invented worksheet entries, not a recommendation for a particular firearm. Copy a real package’s full wording before comparing products. Product names can sound nearly identical while identifying different offerings. Keep the original label and lot reference with stored ammunition; a handwritten caliber abbreviation drops information you may need for a recall or manufacturer question. Compare cost and carried mass without a performance ranking Separate compatibility from preference. First confirm that a product is appropriate for the exact firearm and permitted for the sporting activity and location. Then compare the things that affect ownership: availability, packaging, recurring purchase cost, storage space and actual transport mass. A cartridge family does not have one fixed price or one universal legal sporting use. An original comparison example; prices are invented Offer Calculation Planning result Box A: 50 for 25 currency units 25 ÷ 50 0.50 per cartridge before taxes or delivery. Box B: 100 for 46 currency units 46 ÷ 100 0.46 per cartridge; compare the same product type and applicable costs. Stored case: 8 kg, container: 1 kg 8 + 1 9 kg total to lift and transport; projectile weight is not complete-cartridge weight. Annual planning Expected purchases + venue fees + consumables + service Use your own routine rather than an advertised one-time equipment price. For a sporting comparison, write the relevant discipline or species, land-manager rules, ammunition restrictions, likely availability near the destination and your qualified instructor’s or outfitter’s requirements. Do not turn “larger,” “magnum” or a numerical energy listing into a universal recommendation. For hunting, verify current rules for that jurisdiction and species; the linked Florida example applies to Florida and cannot establish rules elsewhere. Florida FWC · Taking game A jurisdiction-specific example of hunting method and ammunition rules; check the regulator for your actual location. List the chambering of each sporting firearm you own and link the corresponding manufacturer manual. Use that list for purchases rather than memory. Ammunition remains hazardous regardless of its size. Keep it secured and correctly identified; never force a cartridge into a firearm or use damaged, recalled or disaster-exposed ammunition without the manufacturer’s clearance. Set unidentified or mixed ammunition aside in secured, clearly marked packaging. Do not try it in a firearm to discover whether it fits. A photograph of markings and the original box can help the manufacturer identify the product. Use full names on storage labels, including gauge and shell length where relevant. Anyone authorized to manage the inventory should understand that similar numbers and similar appearance do not establish compatibility. calibers calibres 22 LR 9mm 5.56 7.62 223 308 rifle ammunition Read an ammunition label as separate fields Compare cost and carried mass without a performance ranking Read the complete designation Match the firearm’s chamber marking and manual to the box, including suffixes such as LR, WMR, Luger, NATO and Magnum. Separate cartridge from load A cartridge identifies the ammunition family. Bullet weight, construction and manufacturer product code identify the particular load within it. Compare the actual platform Recoil, weight and ammunition availability are properties of the firearm-and-ammunition combination, not caliber alone. Check sporting rules Hunting rules specify species, seasons, permitted methods and sometimes projectile materials. An emergency does not automatically suspend them.

title: Checkpoints & interrupted travel
summary: Avoid unnecessary travel through active fighting or uncertain checkpoints. Check the route and requirements as recently as possible, keep identification and essential medical information accessible, and avoid confrontation. A uniform, posted order or claimed safe corridor does not guarantee safe passage. Rules and protection risks differ by place.
text: Avoid unnecessary travel through active fighting or uncertain checkpoints. Check the route and requirements as recently as possible, keep identification and essential medical information accessible, and avoid confrontation. A uniform, posted order or claimed safe corridor does not guarantee safe passage. Rules and protection risks differ by place.    Where you face detention or abuse risk, seek trusted local legal or humanitarian protection advice before travel when possible. Keep a private record of events only when doing so is safe. This is civilian safety planning, not advice to evade checkpoints or legal restrictions. Never assume passage based on a map, an insignia or an unverified promise. If nobody can verify a route and travel is not immediately necessary, remain in the safer available place while reassessing. Do not assume a public convoy or unofficial driver has secured protection. Assign a trusted adult to each person who needs assistance. Keep medicines, essential contacts and a workable reunion plan with the group. Make decisions around the least mobile person, not the fastest; avoid splitting the family without a clear, safe way to reconnect. For this situation, brief every person on the first action: decide whether travel is necessary. Agree who will manage children, pets or mobility needs while that action happens. This is civilian safety planning, not advice to evade checkpoints or legal restrictions. Never assume passage based on a map, an insignia or an unverified promise. checkpoint roadblock curfew travel road closed conflict Decide whether travel is necessary Compare the danger of staying with the risks of the route. Do not travel only to investigate a closure. Have a known destination and another option. Verify current conditions Compare recent trusted local information with independently verified humanitarian information. Check dates and exact locations; old route advice may be unsafe. Keep essential documents accessible Carry identification and medical information securely. Know where they are so you do not need a hurried search. Do not display sensitive details unnecessarily. Avoid escalating an encounter Remain calm, avoid sudden gestures and do not film an encounter when doing so increases danger. There is no universal script that guarantees safe treatment. Keep the household together Have an agreed check-in and separation plan. Do not send a child or vulnerable person ahead alone to test a route.

title: Chemical release
summary: Move away from a chemical release and follow official instructions about evacuation or sheltering indoors. If exposed, get the chemical off and seek help. For severe symptoms, call emergency services; in the U.S., Poison Control is 1-800-222-1222.
text: Wait for official clearance before returning. Keep contaminated items isolated as responders direct. A dust mask or N95 does not protect against toxic gases. If no reliable instruction arrives, move away from the visible release or affected area without passing through it. If leaving would put you into contaminated outdoor air, use an intact indoor space, shut openings and turn off outdoor-air intake while seeking trustworthy information. Do not identify a gas by sniffing it. Keep the family together in the correct shelter for the hazard and separate potentially contaminated items from the living area. Use covered food and safe water. Prepare a bag for relocation, but do not send someone outside for it during an active release. For this situation, brief every person on the first action: leave the release area. Agree who will manage children, pets or mobility needs while that action happens. A dust mask or N95 does not protect against toxic gases. Chemical Leave the release area Do not approach a spill or plume to identify it. Follow shelter or evacuation orders The right action depends on the substance and where the release is; use location-specific instructions. Get clean Follow Poison Control or responder instructions for removing contaminated clothing and washing; avoid spreading contamination to others. Get medical help Tell responders what was involved if known, your location and symptoms.

title: Chest pain & suspected heart attack
summary: New chest pressure, squeezing or unexplained discomfort with shortness of breath, sweating, nausea or pain in the jaw, back or arm can be a heart attack. Stop activity, call the local emergency number and rest. Do not drive yourself.
text: Unresponsive but breathing Continue watching breathing. Use a recovery position if appropriate and safe; do not give oral medication. No AED nearby Do not leave CPR to search for distant equipment. Send another person when possible. Can the person wait until morning? Suspected heart attack needs urgent medical evaluation. Improvement is not proof that the risk has passed.  Arrange urgent evaluation even if pain eases. Record symptom onset and any medicine taken, including dose and time. Chest discomfort is not always a heart attack, and absence of chest pain does not exclude one. Do not diagnose it using an online checklist or exertion test. Keep contacting reachable medical care and a trusted local helper while the person rests. Confirm whether assistance is actually coming and ask a clinician about transport when ambulance access fails. The affected person must not drive; household planning cannot replace urgent treatment. Choose one person to remain with the patient and one to communicate. Prepare a concise medication and allergy list, leave room for first aid and keep dependents supervised. If alone, put the call on speaker and share the location before giving a long history.  Stop and seek urgent care Help the person rest in a comfortable position. Request emergency medical assistance and an AED if someone can bring one. Stay nearby Monitor breathing and responsiveness. Symptoms can be subtle or come and go; do not wait for a textbook pattern. Use medicines carefully Assist with the person’s own prescribed medication as directed. Ask a dispatcher or clinician about aspirin; avoid it if contraindicated, allergic, unable to swallow, or uncertain. If they collapse If unresponsive and not breathing normally, begin CPR and use an AED promptly. A heart attack can lead to cardiac arrest.

title: Child & infant CPR
summary: If a child or infant is unresponsive and not breathing normally, call the local emergency number, begin CPR and get an AED. Compressions plus breaths are important for children and infants. Follow dispatcher coaching and current hands-on training.
text: Breathing normally Do not give compressions to a normally breathing child. Monitor closely and request urgent assessment for unresponsiveness. No pediatric AED pads Follow the AED instructions for available pads. Do not delay all resuscitation while looking for specialist equipment. Is adult hands-only CPR enough? Breaths are especially important in pediatric arrest. Give compressions if breaths are not possible, and seek dispatcher coaching.  Arrange urgent medical care after resuscitation. Enroll caregivers in current pediatric CPR training before an emergency. This is a single-rescuer summary, not neonatal resuscitation. Two trained rescuers may use a different compression-to-breath ratio. Follow the dispatcher and current course guidance. Continue CPR while another person seeks help if possible. If breathing returns, watch continuously; be ready to restart if normal breathing stops. Do not stop simply because the expected ambulance time has passed. Rescuer safety and exhaustion can limit what is possible. Plan for two roles: caller/AED finder and rescuer. Rotate compressions with minimal interruption if another capable person is present. Keep the child’s age, collapse circumstances and known medical needs ready for handover; new birth resuscitation needs a different protocol.  Check quickly Check responsiveness and normal breathing for no more than 10 seconds. Gasping is not normal breathing. Place on a firm, flat surface. Call and get an AED Use speakerphone or send someone. If alone without a reachable phone after an unwitnessed pediatric collapse, give about 2 minutes of CPR before leaving to call and get an AED; follow dispatcher guidance. Give compressions For a single rescuer, give 30 compressions at 100-120 per minute, about one-third chest depth: about 2 inches in a child and 1.5 inches in an infant. Use one or two hands for a child; current AHA infant CPR uses one hand or two-thumb encircling hands. Add 2 breaths and repeat Open the airway and give 2 breaths, each about 1 second with visible chest rise. Use a neutral head position for infants. If unable or unwilling to give breaths, provide compressions rather than no CPR. Use the AED Follow device prompts and pediatric pad instructions. Pads must not touch; use front-and-back placement when needed. Continue until normal signs of life, takeover, exhaustion or an unsafe scene.

title: Civil unrest
summary: Move away from violence or dangerous crowd movement by a safe route, or shelter in a secure place if movement is riskier. Avoid confrontation, keep family members together and check the actual conditions on your route. Do not assume official presence makes an area safe. If authorities are involved in threats, seek independently verified local or humanitarian help when safe.
text: Move away from active violence and keep your route decisions grounded in current information.    Before going out, check whether your route crosses a closure and identify an alternative. Carry basic identification, necessary medication, and phone power. Do not assume a protest is violent or that a citywide alert applies equally to every neighborhood. If an order applies, read its location, hours, and exceptions. Use what you can see safely from your location to judge immediate danger; do not approach a crowd to investigate. Agree on a place to regroup away from the disturbance. If officials or armed personnel are involved in threats, use trusted private contacts or independently verified humanitarian help when safe. Choose two reunion places and an out-of-area contact. Keep children with a trusted caregiver and carry a written contact card. Share sensitive addresses and travel details only with people who need them; avoid posting live locations or images of other families without consent. For this situation, brief every person on the first action: separate the event from your location. Agree who will manage children, pets or mobility needs while that action happens. Do not assume a protest is violent or that a citywide alert applies equally to every neighborhood. If an order applies, read its location, hours, and exceptions. Civil disruption Separate the event from your location Check what is happening on your route, not just citywide headlines. Peaceful assembly and a nearby dangerous incident are different conditions. Choose a safe path Move away from active violence and blocked roads. If there is no safe exit, shelter inside, away from windows, and update a trusted contact. Stay informed Use official local notices for curfews, transport changes, and emergency services, and verify unconfirmed social posts before acting. Regroup deliberately Arrange a meeting point and a backup contact if mobile networks are strained. Wait for reliable updates before returning to a disrupted area.

title: Civilian distress signaling and location information
summary: Be easy to locate without creating a new hazard. Carry a whistle, light and suitable communications equipment, know your position, and keep signals distinct from routine activity.
text: You can send a message? Send location and situation first, then confirm the intended action and follow-up. Only local visual/audible signaling is available? Use it from a suitable safe position without assuming anyone is within range. A beacon acknowledgment appears? Interpret the exact feature correctly; receipt is not a rescue-arrival promise. Does a return-link acknowledgment mean rescue has launched? No. NOAA explains that RLS confirms the alert was received, located and routed; it does not confirm that a rescue has been organized or launched. Can I practice the SOS function? Use only the manufacturer’s designated test or routine functions. Never create a real distress alert as a practice exercise. Is a location pin enough? Include readable coordinates with their format when available, a useful landmark and access information; a pin is useful only if the recipient can receive and interpret it. Build a usable distress message A help message should reduce uncertainty. Give the current location or last confirmed landmark, what happened, number of people, urgent needs, immediate hazards and a way to contact you. Say whether the position is confirmed or estimated and whether the group can remain there. An editorial message template Field Practice wording Location “At [confirmed trail/junction or coordinates with format]; position [confirmed/estimated].” People “[Number] people; [brief urgent needs or condition].” Event “[Lost, injured or delayed]; [what changed].” Hazards “[Relevant weather, water, terrain or exposure].” Intention “We intend to [remain here / move only for immediate safety to stated place].” Contact “Reply through [available device/channel]; battery [relevant condition].” Read numbers slowly and ask the recipient to repeat the location back when possible. Do not silently mix decimal degrees with degrees-and-minutes notation. Use the format shown by the device and state it. A dropped pin can supplement the message but may not open on the receiving system. Keep the message accurate rather than filling every field with an assumption. Equipment has limits Distinguish a phone, a satellite messaging product and a 406 MHz personal locator beacon. A phone depends on its available service. A selected messenger’s routine messages, emergency service, subscription and reply functions depend on the product and active service. NOAA describes PLBs as portable 406 MHz distress beacons; they are not ordinary two-way texting devices. Device-selection questions Device Question to resolve before departure Phone Can the area be contacted, and can the map/location information be accessed without reception? Satellite messenger What active service, sky view, power, message and SOS procedures does this exact model require? 406 MHz PLB Is it correctly registered, within its battery/service requirements and accessible to the user? Whistle / light / visible material Can the person reach and use it, and is anyone likely to be close enough to notice? Learn the selected device while support is readily available. Record the exact instructions and ordinary test method. Do not assume every product permits replies, tracking or user-replaceable batteries. A single shared device may be unavailable to another person if the group separates; plan personal lights and simple signals accordingly. Make location information easy to interpret Before the trip, find the location display and note its coordinate format. Check the units and map information required for the area with appropriate instruction. Keep the local trail names, access point and intended route on a written card. During an actual request, state the coordinates as displayed and identify whether the location is current or the last reliable position. A good location description adds context without pretending to be more precise than the evidence. “Near the signed junction last seen at [time]” is different from “at the junction now.” A saved screenshot may be old. A map dot may need checking against visible landmarks. If uncertainty remains, communicate it explicitly and keep the device available for follow-up. Practice the read-back with another person indoors: one reads a non-emergency example and the other writes it down, including format and hemisphere or sign. Compare the result. Do not send practice coordinates to an emergency service or imply that an invented example is a live request. Use signals without creating another hazard Use a suitable position and equipment you can operate from it. A whistle can reduce the need for sustained shouting; a personal light or visible material can help someone notice the group. Their usefulness depends on distance, conditions and whether someone is actually looking or listening. Plan visibility with the rescue task in mind. Bright clothing or a visible signal can be helpful when a person needs locating, even if their ordinary travel preference is discreet clothing. Do not climb unstable terrain, approach a hazardous road edge or wander for a better angle merely to improve a signal. Keep the group and essential equipment together. Use the device’s instructions and any responder instructions received. Avoid uncontrolled fire, smoke or aircraft interference; never point a laser at an aircraft. Local signaling customs and equipment differ, so learn the guidance relevant to the activity before the trip. No repeated pattern guarantees that a nearby person recognizes a distress request. Understand registration and acknowledgments For U.S.-coded 406 MHz beacons, NOAA requires registration and current owner/contact information. It also describes a two-year registration renewal cycle. Confirm the beacon identity against the registration confirmation and update changes. A non-U.S.-coded beacon uses its applicable registration authority; NOAA’s database is not the destination for every country code. For a beacon with Return Link Service, NOAA says the indication confirms the distress alert was received and localized by the system and forwarded for action. It does not mean a rescue has been organized or launched. Continue the practical weather, care and location plan rather than using the acknowledgment as an arrival estimate. Keep registration administration separate from the emergency procedure. At home, check contacts, service dates and the authorized self-test. In a real emergency, use the exact activation instructions and any appropriate follow-up received. If an alert is accidentally activated, follow the manufacturer and relevant authority’s cancellation/reporting instructions rather than assuming silence resolves it. NOAA · Beacon registration Check the applicable U.S.-coded beacon registration and renewal requirements. NOAA · 406 MHz distress beacons Compare distress-beacon types and read the exact meaning of a Return Link Service indication. Keep a follow-up and waiting record Write down the time, position, channel used, message sent and response received. Separate “attempted,” “sent” and “acknowledged” according to what the device actually reports. A spinning icon or saved draft does not establish that someone has the message. If the group must move because of an immediate hazard, record and communicate the new position where possible. Keep the reason for moving clear. Do not update a message with an uncertain destination and then travel elsewhere without explanation. Make the device accessible to the responsible person instead of burying it in a packed shelter bag. Prepare for delay while keeping contact possible: weather protection, essential care, drinking water, food and personal lights. Review the people and the site as conditions change. Avoid exhausting batteries through unplanned repeated attempts, and follow the selected device’s power and use instructions. If communication remains unavailable, the trip contact’s overdue plan and suitable local signaling still matter. Practice routine functions, never a false emergency Run a supported check before traveling. Each user should locate the signal equipment, read the device instructions and explain the ordinary test boundary. Use a designated self-test or routine message only where the maker permits it. Find the location screen and identify the format. Read a practice location aloud and check the read-back. Locate the whistle, light and visible material without emptying the bag. Review beacon registration or messenger service and battery requirements. Send only an ordinary permitted message to a consenting trusted contact. Record the result and correct any access or understanding gap. Include the person with the least familiarity and any sensory or dexterity needs. An emergency-only device can remain useful without routine messaging, but everyone should understand that distinction. Keep the trip plan with the trusted contact and revise it when the route or timing changes. Trip accountability Lost outdoors Practice reading your location aloud and checking a device battery. Test routine functions rather than triggering an emergency alert. No signal guarantees timely rescue. Avoid unsafe climbs, roadside exposure, uncontrolled smoke or interference with aircraft. Use the trip plan and remain at a safe known location if lost. Continue safe signaling without exhausting yourself or starting a fire that could escape control. Give every person their own whistle and light when appropriate. Teach children what the agreed signal means and how to respond without walking toward unknown voices. Survival priorities distress signal rescue signal Build a usable distress message Equipment has limits Make location information easy to interpret Use signals without creating another hazard Understand registration and acknowledgments Keep a follow-up and waiting record Practice routine functions, never a false emergency Prepare location information Know how your map or device displays coordinates and the location format. Include trail, landmark, access point and number of people in a request for help. Use a safe visible position Stay away from floodwater, unstable edges and overhead hazards. Move only as needed to reach immediate safety; do not roam simply to find a better signal. Use equipment deliberately A whistle and light can attract attention without sustained shouting. Follow any signaling device’s instructions and local response guidance. Never point lasers at aircraft. Conserve and communicate Keep messages brief and specific. Preserve enough battery for follow-up and state whether you can remain at the reported position.

title: Cleaner air room: a household wildfire-smoke plan
summary: If it is safe to remain home, choose a room that fits your household, close doors and windows without blocking escape, keep it cool and use a suitable air cleaner. Avoid producing smoke or particles indoors. Filtration does not make a home safe during a fire, dangerous heat or a chemical release.
text: The room becomes too hot? Use the safer temperature and relocation plan. A fire threatens the building? Use the evacuation plan rather than relying on filtration. Is a cleaner air room a shelter for every hazard? No. This plan addresses wildfire smoke while staying home is otherwise safe. Fire, excessive heat and chemical releases require different decisions. An equipment plan before shopping Editorial checklist: measure the room, check available outlets, record the cleaner model and filter type, find replacement filters and choose where people will sit and sleep. Photograph the filter label for later shopping. Avoid relying on a device nobody has learned to operate. Prepare for a power interruption Write down a checked alternate location where cleaner air and a tolerable temperature may be available. Determine the transport and care needs before smoke arrives. A closed room without working cooling may become unsuitable; review both heat and smoke rather than treating one as the only risk. Practice setting up the room and replacing the filter. Reassess when outside conditions improve; the linked EPA guidance explains when to air out the room. Do not seal anyone inside or block emergency escape. Ordinary particle filtration does not remove every harmful gas. Follow evacuation instructions for nearby fire. When filtration or cooling is unavailable, avoid adding indoor particles and check whether a safer alternate location can be reached. Do not remain in dangerous heat simply to keep windows closed. Plan around people with heart or lung conditions, children, older adults and pregnant people. Keep their usual care instructions and medicines accessible. Ask their clinician about a personal smoke plan before the season. clean air room smoke air purifier wildfire air filter Pick a workable room Use a room everyone can occupy comfortably. Keep exits usable and plan access to a bathroom. Limit smoke entry Close exterior openings. If the air conditioner has an outside-air option, use recirculation as its instructions allow. Use appropriate filtration Choose a CARB-certified portable cleaner with a tobacco-smoke CADR at least two-thirds of the room area in square feet. Follow its instructions and operate continuously during smoke. Reduce indoor pollution Avoid smoking, candles, sprays and high-heat cooking. Clean settled dust with a damp cloth.

title: Communications outage
summary: Conserve phone battery, try short texts for nonurgent check-ins and use a battery radio for official information. For immediate danger, try calling local emergency services; text-to-911 availability varies. Do not travel into danger just to find signal.
text: Can a weather radio send my location? A normal weather receiver supplies broadcasts; it does not report your location or send a request for help. Use a separately verified communication method and keep a paper movement plan. Does sent mean someone received the message? No. Record whether the recipient acknowledged it and which facts remain unconfirmed. Use the agreed fallback without assuming silence proves an injury. Work out what failed without delaying protection A phone showing no signal, an unavailable messaging app, and a home router without power are different failures. From a safe place, check the simplest explanation once: whether other devices work, whether the phone has charge, and whether a known connection is available. Do not spend the first minutes restarting every device while a fire, flood, or medical emergency needs action. Carry out the protective step and try the appropriate emergency channel. A quick connection check What you observe What to try safely What it does not establish One app fails A short ordinary text or another familiar service. That the whole cellular network is unavailable. Home internet fails Cellular service, if available. That a powered router has a working upstream connection. Cellular calls fail A short nonurgent text; a known working connection. That a message was delivered or someone is responding. Every usual channel fails The written household fallback and a working broadcast receiver. That roads, destinations or help are available. Keep this check brief. A familiar landline may also depend on electricity or internet equipment. Treat every alternative as a method to verify, not a guaranteed rescue route. If equipment is damaged, wet, or unsafe to reach, leave it alone. Separate urgent help from household check-ins For a true emergency in the United States, call 911 if you can; text if you cannot and the local service supports it. The National 911 Program notes that unsupported text-to-911 should generate a bounce-back. A message in a family chat, a social-media post, or a text marked sent is not a request confirmed by an emergency dispatcher. Elsewhere, use the applicable local emergency system. Give the location in plain language When connected, state the address, apartment or room, what is happening, and the assistance needed. Do not assume a device automatically supplies a complete usable location. Follow the call-taker’s instructions. Routine family updates have a different purpose: accounting for people and avoiding unnecessary travel. Keep those messages short and direct. Do not use emergency lines for outage estimates or a practice call. If a test of emergency access is needed for an individual accessibility plan, arrange it in advance through the local service’s nonemergency process. Use one message format and one outside coordinator An agreed format helps a tired reader understand an update quickly. Use names or an agreed identifier, present location, condition, who is together, and the next intended check-in. Include the time and distinguish a current fact from a proposed move. Do not report a destination as reached until someone has actually arrived. Keep exact locations and care details within the trusted contact group. Household message and confirmation Send Report who is with you, current location, condition and next check-in. Confirm Ask the receiver to acknowledge when practical; record which updates remain unconfirmed. Coordinate The agreed outside contact relays confirmed information instead of everyone repeating calls. Editorial planning aid. Actual hazards, individual needs and current instructions control the response. Editorial example: “Alex and Sam together at our agreed host, 4:20 pm, no injuries, phone low, next check 6 pm.” This is more useful than “we’re fine” followed by a long silence. Choose realistic check-in windows before a crisis; a missed window is a reason to use the agreed fallback, not evidence by itself that someone is injured. Keep power for the tasks that matter Prioritize warning access, urgent help, essential care communication, and agreed check-ins. Use the phone’s documented power-saving settings, reduce unnecessary screen time, and stop repeatedly refreshing unavailable apps. Store a known compatible charging cable with an appropriate charged power bank. Test the full combination in normal conditions so that an incompatible connector is not discovered during the outage. Keep paper contact and destination details so a dead phone does not erase the plan. Avoid assuming a displayed power-bank capacity equals a fixed number of phone charges; device use, conversion and battery condition differ. If limiting radios or using airplane mode between checks, understand that calls and cellular alerts will not arrive while the relevant connection is disabled. Use another working warning route when available rather than silencing the only source of urgent information. Charge equipment only through safe, compatible supplies. Do not run a vehicle in an enclosed place to charge a phone. Choose priorities around the actual user. A communication aid may be more important than a general-purpose phone, while a lone person may need continuous access to incoming messages. The goal is a usable communication plan, not the lowest possible battery consumption. Use a movement plan that does not depend on a new message Write where each person should remain or go if contact fails, subject to the actual hazard and safe access. Different plans may be needed for home, work, school, and travel. A nearby fire meeting place is not automatically the destination for a neighborhood evacuation. Never set a rule that requires crossing floodwater, entering a closed area, or returning to an unsafe building just because nobody replied. Before networks fail, agree these details Question Write an explicit answer Who coordinates? A named out-of-area contact and a backup. What if the usual location closes? A checked alternative and the conditions for using it. Who collects a child? Authorized collectors and the school’s own release arrangements. What if travel is unsafe? The safest available location and how updates will be attempted. If the family is together, avoid splitting up to search for signal. If already separated, keep your own location as predictable as safety allows. A working broadcast radio supplies information but normally cannot tell another person where you are; reception and two-way communication are separate capabilities. Practice the fallback without disconnecting essential care Use a tabletop scenario: one adult is away, home internet fails, and a short text is not acknowledged. Have each person explain the next action using the paper plan. Then test an ordinary message, the known charger, and the broadcast receiver safely. Do not intentionally cut off a medical device, disable emergency access, or create a surprise separation to make the exercise realistic. Find the contact list without internet or a device unlock. Send a normal test check-in to the consenting outside contact and ask for confirmation. Identify what is unknown if no confirmation arrives. Describe the safe stay-put or movement fallback for each person. Review battery use, accessible message formats and missing equipment. Fix the single most consequential failure and date the corrected plan. After a real outage, record which methods worked rather than assuming the most expensive option performed best. Review the plan when a phone, carrier, school, caregiver, or destination changes. Satellite messaging and other specialist services need their own documented compatibility, coverage and setup checks; do not count an advertised feature as already tested. Household contact plan Warning systems Keep paper contact lists, offline maps and a radio. Arrange check-in times before a crisis. A message sent is not necessarily delivered. Do not assume emergency texting is supported everywhere. Write a short message with your status, location and next check-in time; try it periodically rather than draining the battery with constant retries. Use your agreed meeting plan only when the route is safe. Do not split up to hunt for signal. Give every person a usable paper fallback and an agreed check-in method. Plan who assists a child or someone who cannot use the usual message format. Keep private locations and care information within the trusted group. Connectivity Work out what failed without delaying protection Separate urgent help from household check-ins Use one message format and one outside coordinator Keep power for the tasks that matter Use a movement plan that does not depend on a new message Practice the fallback without disconnecting essential care Check alternatives Try a safe available landline, another carrier or Wi-Fi calling if configured and functioning. Keep messages short Send your location, status and next check-in time to your out-of-area contact. Protect battery Lower brightness, enable low-power mode and limit unnecessary use. Use the meeting plan If networks fail completely, follow the agreed safe meeting and contact arrangements.

title: Damaging winds
summary: Shelter inside a sturdy building away from windows when damaging winds threaten. Avoid trees, power lines and lightweight structures. Follow tornado warnings separately; straight-line winds can also cause severe damage.
text: Inspect damage without entering unstable buildings. Arrange help for trees touching wires. Do not attempt to clear a tree from a power line. Wait for winds to ease in the best shelter you can reach without exposure. Keep a torch and shoes nearby for broken glass. If the building is failing, move to a safer reachable space without going beneath trees, loose roofing or wires. Account for children, older people, pets and anyone who needs assistance before moving. Keep shoes, medicines and a torch in the shelter area. Decide who helps whom and who carries the essential supplies; do not send a lone child to retrieve items. For this situation, brief every person on the first action: secure items beforehand. Agree who will manage children, pets or mobility needs while that action happens. Do not attempt to clear a tree from a power line. Severe storms Secure items beforehand Bring loose items inside while conditions are calm; do not go out once winds are dangerous. Use an interior room Stay away from glass and large exterior openings. Limit driving High-profile vehicles are vulnerable; avoid routes lined with falling trees or debris. Keep clear afterward Assume downed lines are live and report them from a safe distance.

title: Disaster scams & false aid offers
summary: Pause before paying, sharing identification or following an urgent aid message. Verify the organisation using a contact you find independently, ask for written terms and avoid pressure to pay immediately. Keep emergency funds for verified essentials. A logo, uniform or forwarded link does not establish trust.
text: Pause before paying, sharing identification or following an urgent aid message. Verify the organisation using a contact you find independently, ask for written terms and avoid pressure to pay immediately. Keep emergency funds for verified essentials. A logo, uniform or forwarded link does not establish trust.    Warn trusted people privately about confirmed scams without circulating sensitive victim information. If payment or credentials were compromised, contact the relevant bank or provider through a known channel. An offer of transport or shelter may also carry exploitation risk. Do not surrender documents or separate from family because a stranger promises priority assistance. If reporting channels are unavailable, stop contact, protect remaining money and accounts, and retain the records for later. A promised refund is not a reason to make another payment. Assign a trusted adult to each person who needs assistance. Keep medicines, essential contacts and a workable reunion plan with the group. Make decisions around the least mobile person, not the fastest; avoid splitting the family without a clear, safe way to reconnect. For this situation, brief every person on the first action: find an independent contact. Agree who will manage children, pets or mobility needs while that action happens. An offer of transport or shelter may also carry exploitation risk. Do not surrender documents or separate from family because a stranger promises priority assistance. fake aid disaster fraud scam relief fake contractor Find an independent contact Use the organisation’s known website or an existing trusted number rather than the contact in an unsolicited message. Confirm the specific programme or provider. Protect personal information Share only what the verified process needs. Never give account passwords, one-time codes or a full identity document to an unverified caller. Check payment demands Unexpected upfront fees, gift cards, cryptocurrency or pressure to pay immediately are warning signs. Ask for written terms and time to review. Check repair offers Verify relevant credentials, references and a written scope before hiring. Do not let a door-to-door offer rush you into unsafe entry or a large advance payment. Preserve evidence safely Keep receipts and message details without engaging further. Use verified consumer-protection or legal support when safe and available.

title: Displacement & temporary shelter
summary: Choose a reachable place away from the immediate hazard, keep the family together and retain medicines, identification and contacts. Confirm shelter and transport directly before moving. Ask who operates the shelter, what is required and whether it meets access needs. Aid may be delayed or unavailable; have a second destination.
text: Choose a reachable place away from the immediate hazard, keep the family together and retain medicines, identification and contacts. Confirm shelter and transport directly before moving. Ask who operates the shelter, what is required and whether it meets access needs. Aid may be delayed or unavailable; have a second destination.    Keep a short record of where the household stayed, contacts and assistance received. Use UNHCR or Red Cross channels relevant to the country for protection and family tracing; availability varies. Pressure to surrender documents, pay unexpected fees, separate from children or keep a journey secret is a warning sign. A logo or social post is not verification. If official shelter is unavailable, contact trusted relatives or community members and agree on water, sleeping, hygiene and check-in arrangements. Avoid an unverified ride or address simply because it promises immediate help. Assign a trusted adult to each person who needs assistance. Keep medicines, essential contacts and a workable reunion plan with the group. Make decisions around the least mobile person, not the fastest; avoid splitting the family without a clear, safe way to reconnect. For this situation, brief every person on the first action: confirm the destination. Agree who will manage children, pets or mobility needs while that action happens. Pressure to surrender documents, pay unexpected fees, separate from children or keep a journey secret is a warning sign. A logo or social post is not verification. displaced refugee shelter lost home temporary housing fleeing war Confirm the destination Check that the address exists, is accepting people and can provide accessible shelter. Ask about water, sanitation, medication storage, pets and transport. Keep documents with you Carry originals securely where possible and a separate copy or digital backup. Do not hand documents to an unverified person offering transport or accommodation. Travel with a clear plan Agree who stays with each child and how to reconnect if separated. Use a destination and route checked as recently as possible. Check shelter conditions Identify exits, drinking water, toilets and the people responsible for the site. Keep sleeping and food areas separate from waste. Raise safety concerns through a trusted channel. Protect personal information Give only necessary information to verified providers. Avoid public posts showing children, exact sleeping locations or live routes without consent.

title: Do-not-drink advisory
summary: Use commercially bottled or officially approved water for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth, ice, formula and pets. Do not try to make chemically contaminated water safe by boiling. Read the notice for which other uses are allowed.
text: Why not simply boil it? Chemical contamination can remain after boiling and some substances can become more concentrated. Follow the restriction exactly and obtain a verified alternate drinking source. A home treatment claim must match the identified contaminant; an ordinary filter is not a universal solution. Can I use it for other tasks? Use only the purposes explicitly allowed by the notice. Do not infer that cooking, brushing teeth, making ice or medicine preparation is safe because bathing is mentioned. Check the exact instruction before each household use.  Save the utility notice and alternative-water distribution location offline. Clear appearance and normal taste cannot confirm safety. Set aside sealed water for drinking, food and medicines, including pet needs. Mark the unsafe taps so nobody uses them by habit. If you have no trusted update, keep using the safer supply; restored pressure or clear appearance does not establish safety. Prevent accidental drinking by children, visitors or people with memory difficulties. Label restricted taps and safe containers. Arrange an alternative for medicine, oral care, pets and any medical use rather than treating those as exceptions. Water Read restrictions Check what contaminant is involved and which uses are prohibited. Replace drinking water Use the approved alternative for anything swallowed or used to prepare food. Check household uses Bathing, laundry and cleaning depend on the exact local notice. Wait for clearance Follow any flushing or filter replacement instructions before resuming use.

title: Do-not-use advisory
summary: Do not drink or use tap water for any purpose while a do-not-use advisory is in effect. Avoid contact with skin, eyes and lungs. Use commercially bottled or officially approved alternatives and follow local instructions for sanitation.
text: What does a complete use restriction mean? Avoid the restricted water for drinking, cooking, washing and other uses covered by the notice. Some hazards involve contact or vapor as well as ingestion. Use an alternate source and do not test the water yourself by smell, taste or a home filter. What if I cannot wash or flush normally? Keep clean drinking water separate from dirty-water handling. Follow the restriction and the sanitation fallback in Emergency hygiene and Sewer failure. A bucket or cleaning product cannot override a chemical exposure restriction.  Plan temporary access to safe washing and sanitation if restrictions continue. Boiling does not override a do-not-use order. Make the unsafe supply physically obvious with signs and tell every person in the household. Use a separate clean-water container for essential washing. Avoid flushing or other contact unless the advisory specifically permits it; find another sanitation arrangement. Make the restriction visible at every affected tap and brief every caregiver. Plan safe hygiene for infants, wounds, mobility needs and pets. Avoid carrying restricted water through clean food-preparation areas. Water Stop tap-water use Do not bathe, wash dishes or use connected water and ice appliances. Get safe alternatives Check official water distribution and hygiene arrangements. Prevent accidental exposure Tell everyone in the household and keep children and pets from using taps. Follow restoration steps Wait for the official all-clear and complete any required flushing or appliance instructions.

title: Downed wires & electrical hazards
summary: Keep away from fallen wires, damaged electrical equipment and anything touching them, including water, fences and vehicles. Assume wires are live even when they are quiet or the neighbourhood has no power. Do not attempt a rescue by touching a person or object in contact with electricity. Contact the utility or emergency services from a safe place.
text: Keep away from fallen wires, damaged electrical equipment and anything touching them, including water, fences and vehicles. Assume wires are live even when they are quiet or the neighbourhood has no power. Do not attempt a rescue by touching a person or object in contact with electricity. Contact the utility or emergency services from a safe place.    If a wire falls onto a vehicle you occupy, generally stay inside and call for help; fire or another immediate threat changes the decision. Follow qualified emergency instructions rather than touching the vehicle and ground together. Do not assume a fixed visible distance proves safety. Lines may reenergise without warning; no spark or hum is not an all-clear. Keep the hazard avoided if the utility cannot be reached.
