Do not move a wire to open a road or restore access; arrange a different safe route. Assign a trusted adult to each person who needs assistance. Keep medicines, essential contacts and a workable reunion plan with the group. Make decisions around the least mobile person, not the fastest; avoid splitting the family without a clear, safe way to reconnect. For this situation, brief every person on the first action: stay back. Agree who will manage children, pets or mobility needs while that action happens. Do not assume a fixed visible distance proves safety. Lines may reenergise without warning; no spark or hum is not an all-clear. fallen wire power line down electrical flood live cable Stay back Do not approach to determine whether a wire is live. Current can travel through wet ground and conductive objects. Keep others and animals away. Avoid connected objects Do not touch fences, trees, vehicles or debris that may contact a wire. Do not use a stick or tool to move it. Stay out of flooded electrical areas Never enter water to reach a breaker, appliance or person near damaged electrical systems. Use qualified help. Warn from safety Tell people to avoid the area from your safe location. Report a clear location without approaching for a photograph. Do not restore damaged systems Leave flooded, scorched or broken equipment off until qualified personnel assess it. A restored grid does not make damaged wiring safe.

title: Driving near a dust storm
summary: Avoid entering blowing dust. Find a visible, safe place completely clear of traffic. Only after stopping fully off the traveled roadway, turn off all lights, set the parking brake, and release the brake pedal. Stay buckled. Fire, flooding, or immediate collision danger can change the waiting plan.
text: Dust is ahead and a safe stopping option is available Stop before entering it. You are still moving or remain in an active lane Do not apply the parked-off-road lights-off instruction. The only pull-off leads into unseen terrain Do not blindly leave the pavement; keep looking for a safe option. You are fully stopped in a safe place clear of traffic Use the dust-storm lights-off sequence and remain buckled. Should I switch off hazard lights? Yes, after completing the safe dust-storm pull-off and stopping completely clear of the traveled roadway. ADOT includes emergency flashers in the lights-off advice. This does not apply while driving or sitting in a live lane. Can I just follow the car ahead? No. Its lights do not prove it is moving, in a lane, or on safe ground. Following lights is one reason parked vehicles can be struck. How many minutes should I wait? There is no reliable countdown. Wait for restored visibility, a safe re-entry, and any official all-clear or route instructions. Should I get out to film or check the road? Stay buckled during the wait. Leave only for immediate danger or responder instructions. Recognize the decision before visibility disappears Dust can be a large approaching wall or a narrow plume crossing one part of a road. Either can hide stopped traffic. Do not use another driver’s willingness to continue as your test of safety. A warning is a reason to change the trip; visible dust is a reason to act even if your phone has not alerted. Avoid first; go dark only after the safe stop Dust ahead Use a safe exit or established stop before reaching it. Already encountering dust Slow carefully and look for visible, safe ground completely clear of traffic. Safely stopped off the traveled roadway Set the parking brake; switch off all lights and release the brake pedal. Waiting Remain buckled. Reassess any new danger; resume only after visibility and safe access return. If no safe pull-off exists, the lights-off stage does not apply. Never turn lights off while moving or treat an active lane as a safe waiting place. Planning example: a passenger handles navigation while the driver concentrates on traffic. Alone, change navigation only after stopping safely. Choose a safe pull-off without creating a second emergency Look around before slowing or moving sideways. ADOT recommends leaving the highway completely when possible and avoiding travel lanes and emergency lanes as waiting places. The goal is separation from moving traffic, not merely reaching the pavement edge. Use an exit or established parking area you can still see. Beyond pavement, check for a ditch, wash, soft ground, slope, or barrier before moving onto it. Never blindly leave the pavement. Do not reverse on the highway, cross a median, or get out to scout an unseen route. If no safe pull-off is visible Keep your lights on while moving, reduce speed to match what you can see, and keep looking for a safe way out of traffic. Do not intentionally choose an active lane as a waiting place. If traffic stops or the vehicle becomes disabled, treat that as an emergency; the parked-off-road lights rule does not make your position safe. Once stopped clear of traffic, manage lights and restraints Other drivers may follow visible vehicle lights through dust and strike a parked car. After reaching a safe location fully clear of the traveled roadway and coming to a complete stop, select the appropriate parked gear, apply the parking brake, and take your foot off the brake pedal. Switch off headlights, taillights, emergency flashers, and interior lights. Keep everyone buckled in their seat or correctly fitted child restraint. Wait inside rather than opening doors to watch the storm. Do not step into the dust to check whether rear lights are off. Learn the controls while safely parked before a trip. This is a narrowly defined lights-off instruction It applies to the dust-storm pull-off described here. It does not mean driving without lights, going dark in a traffic lane, or ignoring a responder’s direct instructions. Keep the wait organized and make your location usable Once secure, one adult can watch people and conditions while another handles necessary communication. Avoid competing calls and instructions. Note road, direction, marker or exit, side of road, and vehicle description. Add a map location if available. Update a contact and ask them not to drive into the storm to meet you. Keep essentials in the cabin so no one needs to unload luggage. Original message template “Stopped off [road/direction], near [marker], in [vehicle]. [Number] people. We are waiting for visibility and will update when conditions change.” In an emergency, give dispatch your location, callback number, and the danger. Explain any live-lane position or urgent medical need, then follow instructions. Know when waiting in the vehicle is no longer the right plan Staying buckled is the normal waiting plan. Smoke, fire, nearby impacts, rising water, or urgent illness may change it. Report the specific new danger. Exceptions that need a new decision Threat Response Vehicle fire or growing smoke Stop if moving, shut off the vehicle, get everyone out, and move away from it and traffic. Call 911. Do not open the hood or return for belongings. Water rising around a low stopping place Call 911 and seek higher ground if it can be reached safely. Do not drive or walk into floodwater. Immediate collision threat or a crash Call 911 and describe the road position. Follow scene-specific instructions; do not blindly step into moving traffic. Serious breathing difficulty, collapse, or other urgent illness Request emergency help immediately and follow the call-taker’s instructions. A vehicle fire requires substantial separation: U.S. Fire Administration advises at least 100 feet and well away from traffic. Do not expose yourself to another hazard just to retrieve supplies. Leave the pull-off only after checking the whole route A brief view of the lane is not an all-clear. Dust may be followed by rain, damage, or flooding. Check visibility, the re-entry route, and official road information. From the protected position, look for debris, disabled vehicles, emergency crews, water, and renewed dust. Check the next usable destination rather than assuming your original route is still sensible. An established safe stop may be the better goal. Restore normal driving lights and use normal signals before moving. Rejoin only when you can see that it is safe. If the vehicle is damaged, warning lights appear, or you cannot assess the pull-off surface, arrange assistance instead of forcing a restart. Once safely parked elsewhere, update your contact, document damage, and replace supplies. Do not inspect the car from an exposed shoulder. Prepare the people and the decision, not just the bag Before leaving, identify reasonable stopping places and check the full route’s forecast and road reports. Save the relevant official services below. Agree on who will navigate, contact family, and support a child or person who becomes distressed. Keep a written location/contact card if phones or communication aids fail. Ask each passenger what help they would need to leave the vehicle in an actual emergency; do not assume everyone can walk on rough ground. Keep pets secured so opening a door during an emergency does not release them into traffic. Common mistakes to avoid Do not race the dust, copy another driver’s route, wait until you are blind to consider stopping, or turn lights off while still moving. Avoid treating “off the road” as permission to drive onto ground you cannot judge. While safely parked at home, practice parking-brake and light controls, including automatic lights and brake hold. Check the manual; do not experiment beside a highway. NWS local forecasts and warnings United States: enter a location and check alerts for the route. Weather information does not confirm a road is open. FHWA state road-condition directory United States: choose the state for its road-information service. Coverage and updates vary; obey local closures. AZ511 road conditions Arizona: road closures, incidents, cameras, and weather layers. This is state-specific and is not a rescue request service. Revise your arrival plan and check road conditions. Arrange assessment or assistance for a damaged vehicle. Watch for renewed dust, approaching vehicles, smoke, rising water, excessive cabin heat, or worsening health. Without calls or road updates, wait in the safe pull-off while visibility remains poor, unless immediate danger requires moving. Do not walk out to find reception. Preserve phone power and retry. An unsent message or map pin does not establish rescue. Plan for the least mobile passenger. Keep restraints fitted, medicines and communication aids reachable, and pets secured. Tell responders about transfer, mobility, hearing, language, or medical needs. dust storm haboob visibility highway pull aside roadside monsoon pileup Avoid entering dust Take a safe exit or established stop while the route is still visible. Pull clear carefully Check traffic, slow progressively, and use ground you can actually see and safely reach. Go dark only after the safe stop Completely clear of traffic and stopped: parking brake on, all lights off, foot off brake. Wait and reassess Stay buckled; watch changing threats and confirm a safe route before continuing.

title: Earthquake
summary: During shaking, Drop, Cover and Hold On. Protect your head and neck beneath a sturdy table if nearby; stay indoors rather than running outside. If near the coast, strong or long shaking may mean tsunami danger: move inland and uphill once shaking stops.
text: Should I run outside during shaking? Use Drop, Cover and Hold On where you are when the shaking starts, adapting to mobility needs. Moving through falling objects, glass or stairs can add risk. Once shaking stops, assess the safe route rather than rushing automatically. What if I am near the coast? Strong or prolonged shaking or sudden unusual sea behavior can be a natural tsunami warning. After shaking, follow the tsunami route to higher ground or inland when safe, without waiting for an electronic alert. Check the separate Tsunami guide.  Check injuries and use texts to communicate. Leave a damaged building by stairs when safe and follow official reentry instructions. Doorways are not generally the safest shelter. Do not use elevators after damaging shaking. After shaking, account for people, put on shoes and check from a safe position for fire, gas smell, damaged wiring and instability. Do not reenter a seriously damaged building while waiting for inspection. Expect aftershocks and keep clear of masonry and power lines. Practice how each person protects their head and body with their actual mobility device or sleeping location. Keep shoes and a light accessible for broken glass afterward. Establish a reunion point without depending on elevators or a working mobile network. Geological Protect yourself now Drop onto hands and knees and cover your head and neck. With a mobility device, lock wheels and protect your head. Hold on Stay under sturdy cover until shaking ends. Keep away from windows and objects that can fall. If outdoors or driving Move away from buildings and lines. Pull over safely clear of bridges, wires and trees and remain in the vehicle during shaking. Check secondary hazards Expect aftershocks; avoid damaged structures and check for fire, gas leaks and tsunami warnings.

title: Emergency alerts
summary: Check an official alert for your exact location, hazard, timing and required action. Enable emergency alerts on your phone and add local emergency management notifications. Keep a battery radio as backup rather than relying on one app.
text: Do I need an app for U.S. Wireless Emergency Alerts? NWS describes WEA delivery through compatible participating mobile service without an app subscription. Check current phone and carrier support; a separate app or local signup may cover other information. Does no alert mean no danger? No. A channel can fail or not cover a particular event. Act on obvious immediate danger and use the relevant protective plan and another working information route. Read an alert for place, time, hazard and action An alert is useful when you can tell whether it applies to you and what to do next. Read the affected location, issue time, hazard, required action, and issuing organization. An old screenshot, a warning for the next county, or a storm headline without an action can cause the wrong response. Do not let searching for extra detail delay a clear instruction to protect yourself. Turn an alert into an action Locate Does the named area include where you are now, not only your home address? Identify What hazard, timing and protective action does the message describe? Act Carry out the applicable instruction and use a working source for subsequent updates. Editorial planning aid. Actual hazards, individual needs and current instructions control the response. Editorial example: a family visiting another town needs information for that town as well as the home they left. Keep names of counties, local places, and accommodation addresses available. If an alert uses an unfamiliar zone, verify the location against the local system in advance; do not assume a flood zone, evacuation zone, and warning area are interchangeable. Build several warning routes with different weaknesses A phone, a broadcast receiver, and a local notification service can complement one another. Multiple apps on one uncharged phone still share the same device and power failure. List what each route covers, how it is powered, and who can perceive it. Include warning arrangements at work, school, a campground, or another regular location, rather than limiting the plan to the living room. A household warning map Route Useful role Check its limit Phone emergency alerts Area-based urgent messages on compatible participating service. Device settings, coverage, charge and accessible presentation. Local subscribed notices Area-specific evacuation, utility or community updates. Registration, chosen areas, delivery channels and actual operation. Weather radio Weather broadcasts and supported automatic alerts. Coverage, setup, backup power and receiver features. Building or workplace alarms Immediate site-specific warning. Meaning, audibility or visibility, and the site response plan. No single channel covers every kind of incident. A weather receiver is not a household smoke alarm, and an email utility notice may not arrive quickly enough for an immediate hazard. Record a backup that serves the particular need instead of collecting notification services without checking their function. Configure the device and local service deliberately Use the phone and carrier’s current instructions to check supported emergency alert settings. Separate those settings from an app’s notifications and a city’s subscription list. The NWS describes U.S. Wireless Emergency Alerts as messages delivered through participating mobile service without needing an app subscription. That does not establish that every phone, location, or hazard will generate an alert. Find the local emergency management subscription from an independently obtained official address, rather than a forwarded signup link. Select the relevant places and delivery methods. Review saved addresses after moving or changing work locations. Check that a telephone number or email address was entered correctly and complete any legitimate confirmation process. Review language and accessibility options, and teach another adult where the settings are. Check current device behavior for mute, focus, notifications and power settings using its instructions; do not assume every alarm bypasses every mode. A successful signup is only the beginning. If the service offers a documented test or sample message, use that procedure. Do not contact emergency dispatch to ask whether an app notification works. Match each warning to the correct protective plan The same loud sound may introduce very different hazards. Keep a short response card with the household’s relevant shelter spaces, departure arrangements, and care tasks. Use the current message and hazard-specific guide. A generic instruction to “go downstairs” can be unsuitable for some flooding or chemical incidents; a generic instruction to “go outside” can also place people in danger. A response card is more useful than a list of alert names When the message requires… The household must already know… Immediate building escape Usable exits, dependent assistance and a safe outside accounting point. Tornado protection The appropriate sturdy shelter and how to reach it safely. Regional evacuation The affected location, transport, checked destination and route. Hazard-specific sheltering The correct space and any ventilation instructions for that incident. Define tasks that can happen together: one adult reads the action aloud while another supports a child or dependent person. If alone, put the essential instruction and reachable equipment in one familiar place. Do not make verification of a message a lengthy voting process when direct danger is already apparent. Hazard-specific sheltering Evacuation guide Make warning access work during sleep and impairment A warning nobody notices cannot support the plan. Check the actual sleeping arrangement, normal door positions, hearing and vision needs, and whether someone uses headphones or assistive communication. For supported weather receivers, compatible visual or vibration equipment may help. Verify the full system, including power to any attachment, through its manufacturer’s documented procedure. Volume alone is not an accessibility plan Ask the person what presentation they can reliably perceive and understand. An adult assigned to wake them also needs a backup if away, asleep elsewhere, or unable to help. Write a plain-language interpretation for household members who may not understand the alert language or technical terms. Use agreed words such as the named room or destination instead of vague calls to “get ready.” Do not promise that any device guarantees waking everyone, and do not test alarms in a way that creates injury, panic, or unnecessary distress. Keep the plan usable when alerts are absent or conflicting A missing alert does not establish safety. Act on obvious immediate danger and the relevant natural warning signs. If two reports appear to conflict, compare issue times, locations, hazards, and source identity from a safe place. The later report may apply elsewhere, or one may be an old repost. Keep observations, verified instructions, and rumors separate in a short note. Record the exact location and time of the message you are using. Carry out any applicable immediate protective instruction. Use another available warning route for updates without abandoning necessary protection. Tell the household what has changed and what remains unknown. Change the plan when credible new information or actual conditions require it. Afterward, review missed alerts, configuration and assistance needs. Do not treat silence from a receiver or a phone as an all-clear. A dead battery, weak signal, or transmitter problem can look like a quiet day. Once conditions allow, inspect the failed channel and repair the cause. Keep the written response card current so a technical fault does not also erase the household’s knowledge of what to do. Write down local frequencies and contact information. Test devices and accessibility features with your household. Alerts can be delayed or missed. Act on obvious immediate danger and natural warning signs. Treat direct signs of danger as a reason to act even if an alert has not arrived. Compare a battery-radio bulletin with another independently obtained source when possible. Record the place and time; an old screenshot can be dangerously misleading. Check how each person notices and understands warnings, including while sleeping. Assign assistance and a backup, and use suitable visual, vibration, language or communication support where needed. Warnings & information Read an alert for place, time, hazard and action Build several warning routes with different weaknesses Configure the device and local service deliberately Match each warning to the correct protective plan Make warning access work during sleep and impairment Keep the plan usable when alerts are absent or conflicting Enable phone alerts Review emergency notification settings and keep the phone charged. Add local channels Sign up with your county or city emergency management office and utility. Use weather backup For weather hazards, use NOAA Weather Radio or your local official warning service. Read the action Distinguish preparation notices from instructions to shelter or evacuate.

title: Emergency contacts, meeting points and household cards
summary: Keep a small, current contact plan that works without your phone. Include trusted people, meeting points and essential support contacts, while protecting private information.
text: A card should stay small Record name, trusted contact, meeting point and a few essential support details. Avoid putting full identity documents, access codes, firearm storage locations or detailed medical histories on a card that can be lost. Keep sensitive supporting documents separately with controlled access. Practice a status message Use a simple format: safe or needing help, current location, who is present, planned destination and next check-in. An outside contact can relay a consistent message so several household members do not spend battery repeating long calls. Avoid posting private locations publicly. Call or message your chosen contact during ordinary conditions, confirm their role, and replace one outdated number. A listed contact may be unavailable. Verify destination and care arrangements in advance and keep alternatives. Use the agreed meeting plan and written numbers. If calls fail, short texts may be more practical when service becomes available; neither is guaranteed. Do not enter danger to retrieve a phone or make a call. Provide large print, relevant languages or accessible formats. Children need age-appropriate instructions and an adult helper; a card does not replace supervision. Documents & support phone numbers contact cards emergency contacts Choose an outside-area contact Ask a trusted person to help relay status if local calls fail. Confirm what information they should collect and share. Record reachable support Include household members, caregivers, schools where relevant, veterinary support and essential service contacts. Use current local numbers rather than assuming one number works everywhere. Choose two meeting arrangements Name a nearby location for an ordinary separation and an outside-area destination for a wider event. Confirm access and acceptance. Make usable copies Keep a paper card with each person and a protected home copy. Update numbers and care details after a change.

title: Emergency cooking: meals without adding a new hazard
summary: Keep meals you can eat without heat as your first backup. Outdoor-only cooking equipment stays outdoors; if you cannot use it safely, change the menu rather than bringing it inside.
text: Can I just heat food in the garage? Not with charcoal grills or camp stoves. An open garage door does not make that safe. Use an appropriate outdoor location under product instructions or choose food that needs no heating. Build a menu around actual meals Editorial no-cook examples: ready-to-eat beans with crackers and shelf-stable fruit; a suitable nut or seed spread with bread; canned fish or an alternative ready-to-eat protein with vegetables. Check allergens, label instructions and household preferences. These examples are meal ideas, not a prescribed nutritional or medical diet. Count the dependencies For each meal, write down water, utensils, opening tools, heat and leftover storage. Dry rice may be inexpensive, but it is a poor first fallback when fuel and safe water are scarce. Choose ready-to-eat portions where cooking access is uncertain; use foods your household already eats so rotation does not become an unwanted expense. Write a one-day no-cook menu for the actual household and check that every ingredient and opening tool is present. Do not use a gas oven for heating. Do not assume a window, fan or CO alarm makes outdoor-only equipment safe indoors. Follow food safety rules for opened and perishable foods. If safe outdoor cooking is unavailable, use the no-cook menu. Do not trade a warm meal for carbon monoxide or fire exposure. If safe food and water cannot be maintained, reassess the location and seek a workable alternative. Account for infants, swallowing needs, allergies and medical diets. Use individual clinical guidance for special feeding requirements; a general pantry list may not be appropriate. camp stove safety no power meals emergency menu Start with no-cook meals Choose familiar ready-to-eat foods that suit your household. Include a manual opener and portions you can finish without depending on refrigeration. Check your cooking option Read the exact equipment and fuel instructions. Never use charcoal grills or camp stoves indoors or in a garage, even with the door open. Plan water and cleanup Include safe water for drinking, preparation and hand hygiene. Avoid a menu that assumes unlimited washing water or a working sink. Practice a simple menu Prepare one normal meal using the backup arrangement in safe conditions. Check opening packages, lighting, portion sizes and waste handling.

title: Emergency documents: a private, usable recovery folder
summary: Organize the information needed to identify yourself, contact providers and recover after disruption. Keep protected copies in separate places and check that you can actually open them.
text: Should everything go in my go bag? Carry what you realistically need and protect it. A bag can be lost or stolen, so keep a separate backup and avoid carrying a single unprotected collection of all your sensitive records. Separate three levels of information Editorial organization: an everyday card with limited contacts; a travel folder with relevant copies; and a protected archive with fuller financial and identity records. This reduces the need to carry every sensitive document everywhere. Label folders plainly so a tired household can find housing, care and insurance details quickly. Treat passwords differently Avoid putting account passwords beside a complete identity and financial file that could be lost. Use a secure access arrangement suited to your household, and document recovery steps without exposing secrets. A password-protected file is not useful if its only unlock information is on the phone you just lost. Choose five records you would miss most after losing access to home. Check their dates, make protected copies and test retrieval. Do not post identity documents, account numbers or recovery credentials in public help requests. Storage and legal requirements vary; consult relevant providers about acceptable copies. If online services fail, use the paper contact index and protected copies for available in-person or phone services. Do not give documents to an unverified person claiming to arrange aid. Include each household member’s relevant records and discuss permission to share them. Plan language support, accessibility and how a caregiver can locate necessary care information. documents binder identity copies recovery folder Gather the essentials Identify relevant identity papers, insurance details, housing records, medical information and financial contacts. Prioritize what your household would need away from home. Make a contact index Record provider names, official phone numbers and enough account information to locate the service. Keep full sensitive records separate from an everyday contact card. Protect copies Store copies separately from originals and protect digital access. Consider fire, water, loss and unauthorized viewing when choosing storage. Test retrieval Check that a trusted authorized person can find the information if you are unavailable. Test access without your usual phone and note any account recovery dependence.

title: Emergency restrictions & martial law
summary: Check what restriction actually applies to your location and time, and plan essential travel cautiously. Keep identification and medical information accessible. Avoid confrontation at checkpoints; an official order does not guarantee safe treatment or passage. Where authorities are a source of threat, use trusted local legal or humanitarian support if contacting them is safe. Rules and rights vary by jurisdiction.
text: Find the actual order. Work from its words, place, and time.    A declaration of emergency, a curfew, and martial law are distinct legal actions. Their meaning and lawful scope depend on the jurisdiction and the actual instrument issued; this guide cannot determine the law for a specific place. Do not infer blanket rules from the phrase “martial law” in a headline. Follow live safety instructions, and verify any claim about suspended rights or universal powers against the actual order and local legal advice. Avoid confrontation and plan essential travel conservatively. An order does not guarantee that a checkpoint or transport corridor is safe. Where authorities are implicated in abuse, seek trusted local legal or humanitarian support when doing so will not increase your exposure. Do not broadcast sensitive travel plans. Choose two reunion places and an out-of-area contact. Keep children with a trusted caregiver and carry a written contact card. Share sensitive addresses and travel details only with people who need them; avoid posting live locations or images of other families without consent. For this situation, brief every person on the first action: verify the announcement. Agree who will manage children, pets or mobility needs while that action happens. Do not infer blanket rules from the phrase “martial law” in a headline. Follow live safety instructions, and verify any claim about suspended rights or universal powers against the actual order and local legal advice. Civil disruption Verify the announcement Read the original order or official alert rather than a repost. Confirm the issuing authority, jurisdiction, and effective time. Map the practical effect Note what movement or services are restricted, who is exempt, and where to obtain food, medication, medical care, and shelter. Plan essential movement Carry identification and relevant documentation, tell a contact your route, and use current official information about closures and checkpoints. Avoid unnecessary travel into a restricted area. Keep records and reassess Save the order, updates, and emergency contacts offline if possible. If you are detained or need advice about your rights, contact a qualified attorney or local legal aid.

title: Emergency tarp shelter and dry sleeping systems
summary: A shelter needs a safe site, wind and rain protection, and insulation from the ground. Test your tarp and sleeping equipment before a trip; a tarp alone does not make cold or severe weather safe.
text: The site has a hazard? Choose a nearby suitable position before arranging shelter. The complete system is inadequate for forecast conditions? Use a suitable alternative or return early; a roof alone is not sufficient. The pitch needs unfamiliar improvised supports? Use the tested manufacturer-supported configuration or change the plan. Does a tarp keep a person warm by itself? It can provide a weather barrier, but ground insulation, sleeping insulation, clothing and conditions determine whether the complete system is suitable. Can I use a stove under the shelter to compensate? Do not use fuel-burning cooking or heating equipment inside a tent or improvised shelter. It creates carbon-monoxide and fire risks rather than fixing inadequate insulation. A complete shelter system Think in separate layers: overhead weather barrier, ground protection, ground insulation, sleeping insulation and dry clothing. Each has a different job. A tarp can reduce wind or rain exposure in an appropriate configuration; it does not provide the ground insulation of a pad or the sleeping insulation of suitable bedding. An original system inventory Layer Practical check Roof / wind barrier Coverage, compatible supports, entry/exit and manufacturer-supported configuration. Ground barrier Fit beneath the occupied area and a placement that avoids collecting runoff. Insulating pad Condition, size and suitability for the expected ground conditions. Sleeping insulation Manufacturer-described use conditions, fit and protection from wetting. Dry clothing Accessible protected layers matched to the actual person. Test the complete arrangement at home or a permitted supported site before a trip. Include the bags, shoes, personal light and space needed to assist another person. A shelter that technically fits two sleeping bodies may not provide the usable space the household needs for care or an orderly exit. Know when to leave A tarp is an equipment choice with limits, not a substitute for every building or tent. Set the early-return or alternative-shelter decision before the trip. Check weather, daylight, the group’s condition and the manufacturer’s stated limits for the complete equipment. An apparently sheltered hollow can collect water; overhead damaged branches and exposed edges introduce other hazards. Do not settle on an unsuitable site merely because it is easier to pitch there. If the conditions exceed the system or the group’s ability, change the plan while the known return remains practical. Conditional shelter choice Suitable site and complete system Use the tested configuration and inspect how people, equipment and exits fit. Site unsuitable Move to a nearby suitable position before arranging the shelter. System or conditions unsuitable Use the confirmed alternative or early return rather than promising that extra improvisation solves the gap. Osprey Zero planning aid. These are conditional choices; current conditions and individual needs control the decision. These are alternatives. A tarp does not make severe wind, flooding or a thunderstorm safe. If immediate danger develops, protect the people first and seek appropriate help; do not stay to finish a tidy pitch or retrieve nonessential equipment. Select the site before unpacking the system Review the occupied area and surrounding hazards in daylight when possible. Identify drainage, water changes, overhead condition, slope, access and the route back to a known place. Choose permitted durable ground and follow the site’s current rules. A visually flat patch is not the entire assessment. Think about the whole group: a dependent person may need room for assistance, and a mobility aid may require a suitable approach. Plan an entry that can be found in darkness and keep the path clear of loose equipment. Do not dig trenches, cut branches or create new structural anchors as a default way to force the site to fit the equipment. Site review worksheet Question Useful check Water Could runoff, a drainage channel or rising water affect this position? Overhead Are damaged branches or other overhead hazards present? Access Can each person enter, exit and reach the known return route? Permission Is camping allowed here and what site protections apply? Weather Can the complete equipment serve the expected conditions here? Use a tested configuration and inspect it Follow the selected shelter’s instructions and compatible supplied or manufacturer-approved supports. Practice the actual configuration before departure, including cord access and the tools needed for it. Do not assume every tarp, attachment point or support can accept the same arrangement. During ordinary setup, keep the occupied area and exits clear, arrange the ground and sleep layers, then check the overhead coverage and ventilation appropriate to the product. Look for sagging areas where water may collect and cord or stake positions that create a trip problem. Use the maker’s instructions for any adjustment; this guide does not provide structural loads or a universal knot/anchor recipe. Check the pitch again after a meaningful weather change and before sleeping. Account for everyone’s access and the location of lights, shoes and care equipment. If the setup cannot remain usable without continual improvised fixes, reassess the configuration or site rather than treating persistence as proof of adequacy. Protect the dry sleeping area Organize the shelter so the dry system remains protected during entry and packing. Keep wet outer equipment separate from bedding where practical, and leave enough room to handle the care tasks the group actually needs. Mark which bag contains the protected sleeping layers so another person can find them. Use the pad and bedding according to their instructions. Compare the manufacturer’s conditions and rating method rather than assuming one printed temperature has the same meaning across every product. Include the person’s fit and care needs in the decision. If a system has not been tested in ordinary supported use, do not discover its limits on an isolated severe-weather trip. A foil emergency blanket can be one contingency item, but it is not equivalent to a complete sleeping system. Do not pack it as the sole solution to an expected cold overnight stay. Keep the return or suitable-shelter plan available instead of depending on an improvised heat source. Keep cooking and combustion outside the shelter Plan food that can be eaten as carried when the trip must work without fire. Fuel-burning appliances can generate carbon monoxide; CDC warns against indoor use of portable fuel-burning appliances. Never use a stove, charcoal, lantern or improvised heater inside a tent or tarp enclosure to replace missing insulation. For any permitted outdoor cooking, use the exact appliance’s siting and operation instructions and current local restrictions. An open entrance or a cracked edge does not certify a safe combustion arrangement. Keep hot equipment and incompatible chemicals away from sleeping and care materials. The simplest shelter meal is one that introduces no setup problem: suitable ready-to-eat food, a workable container and the needed utensils. Check the package while planning and keep water needs visible. If warm food is important to the trip, resolve a suitable permitted cooking system separately; do not conceal it inside the shelter plan. Rehearse the full system and leave the site usable Practice at a permitted supported location with an easy stop and all real help available. Test entry, exit, dry-layer access, personal lighting and how equipment is packed again. A photograph of an empty pitch cannot show whether the people can use it. Inventory the complete shelter and sleep layers. Choose a suitable permitted practice site and read the instructions. Use the intended compatible configuration. Place the actual bedding, bags and care equipment. Check access and lighting without creating a real cold or wet exposure test. Pack and inspect the system, carry out waste and record one correction. After ordinary use, follow the manufacturer’s cleaning and drying instructions before storage. Account for stakes, cords and small fittings. Leave the site without trenches, cut vegetation or scraps. Correct missing parts at home so the next trip does not begin with an untested substitute. NPS · Ten essentials Review the shelter, insulation and lighting systems in the essentials framework. NPS · Leave no trace Read site-use and impact principles, then follow the specific land manager’s current rules. No-fire camp planning Outdoor trip plan Pitch your actual shelter before dark, simulate rain with a hose at home, and check pooling, runoff and exit access. Improvised anchors are not climbing protection. Do not cut structural branches, sleep beneath unstable trees or rely on a campfire for overnight warmth. Use the safest reachable shelter and keep the group together. Reduce wind exposure and ground heat loss with available equipment; do not undertake a risky climb or river crossing to find a prettier campsite. Fit shelter and sleeping systems to actual body sizes, mobility needs and weather. A person who cannot help pitch the tarp still needs a dry, insulated place and an accessible exit. Navigation & shelter tarp survival shelter A complete shelter system Know when to leave Select the site before unpacking the system Use a tested configuration and inspect it Protect the dry sleeping area Keep cooking and combustion outside the shelter Rehearse the full system and leave the site usable Choose the site first Avoid drainage channels, rising water, unstable slopes, cliff edges and dead or damaged overhead branches. Move to a safer location before arranging equipment. Protect from ground moisture Use a ground barrier and insulation suited to conditions. Keep your sleep area above local runoff; do not dig unauthorized drainage trenches. Pitch and check Use the shelter’s instructions and existing suitable anchors. Keep fabric tensioned so rain does not pool. Check that stakes and cord do not create trip hazards. Keep warmth and airflow Protect dry layers and your sleeping insulation. Maintain ventilation appropriate to the shelter. Never use fuel-burning heaters or cooking equipment inside an improvised shelter.

title: Emergency water storage
aliases: how much water should i store
summary: Store at least one gallon of water per person per day for three days; aim for two weeks if practical. Allow more for heat, illness, pregnancy and pets. Use commercially bottled water or clean food-grade containers, and keep it cool and away from chemicals.
text: The stored water cannot be reached safely? Treat it as unavailable in your plan and change the storage arrangement. A notice warns of chemicals? Do not assume boiling or an ordinary filter makes the supply usable; open the matching advisory guide.  Work out the household quantity Start with a written count of people and days. CDC’s baseline is at least one U.S. gallon per person per day for three days, with a two-week supply if possible. Extra needs can include pets, hot weather, pregnancy, illness, and particular care requirements. A U.S. gallon is about 3.8 litres; do not confuse it with an imperial gallon. Baseline arithmetic before extra needs People 3 days 7 days 14 days 1 3 gal / 11.4 L 7 gal / 26.5 L 14 gal / 53 L 2 6 gal / 22.7 L 14 gal / 53 L 28 gal / 106 L 4 12 gal / 45.4 L 28 gal / 106 L 56 gal / 212 L The table is multiplication of the CDC baseline, rounded for planning. It is not a complete allowance for all household washing, laundry, or toilet flushing. Add those needs separately and identify which uses require drinking-quality water. Record the actual amount stored, not the capacity of empty containers. Build in stages if space or money is limited Start with a usable three-day reserve and improve it gradually. A small supply you can access, label, and maintain is more useful than an ambitious target that remains empty containers. Choose containers you can actually handle Unopened commercially bottled water is a straightforward emergency option. For refilled supplies, use suitable food-grade water containers, with tight lids and a design you can clean and dispense from. Never reuse a container that held toxic chemicals. Check the manufacturer if you are unsure whether a container is suitable for drinking water. Match storage format to the household Format Practical advantage Check before choosing Small sealed bottles Easy to distribute and carry Enough total volume, packaging condition, and storage space. Small refillable water containers Manageable portions and flexible placement Food-grade suitability, cleaning access, tight lid, and rotation. Larger water containers Less packaging for a larger reserve Filled weight, safe support, accessible tap, and ability to clean. For planning, a five-gallon water load weighs about 42 pounds before the container. That may be too heavy for a child, an older adult, or someone with limited mobility. Choose several smaller containers if necessary. Test the empty container’s placement and dispensing position before filling it; do not plan to lift a heavy container overhead during an outage. A container must also fit the task. A sealed bottle for a go-bag, a jug for a household dispenser, and water for a pet may need different arrangements. Do not make everyone depend on a single heavy container that only one person can move. Clean, fill, and label without confusion Follow the CDC container-cleaning procedure in the reference below and the container’s instructions before filling a reusable vessel. Use a clean, suitable water source and close the lid tightly. Keep container sanitation separate from drinking-water disinfection: they have different purposes and instructions. A maintainable storage routine Prepare Check suitability and condition; wash and sanitize following the linked container procedure. Fill and identify Use safe water; mark drinking water, fill date, volume, and the next rotation date. Store and review Keep cool, away from sunlight and chemicals; check access, leaks, and the review schedule. Editorial process map. Use the CDC reference for the exact cleaning method and bleach concentration; do not improvise a drinking-water dose from it. Use durable labels that remain readable in dim light. A simple record might say: “Drinking water; filled 3 October; 2 gallons; replace by 3 April.” Keep the source and any container instructions in the household notebook. If a different container holds water for an allowed non-drinking use, make the distinction unmistakable. Store for access as well as capacity Choose a cool storage place away from direct sunlight, fuel, pesticides, and other chemicals. CDC suggests 50–70°F for stored home-filled water. If your only available space becomes very hot, improve the location rather than assuming any cupboard is suitable. Follow the storage directions and date information for bottled water. Spread manageable containers across appropriate locations so one blocked cupboard or a single leak does not remove all access. Keep frequently used drinking water where household members can reach it without climbing, moving furniture, or relying on power. Use sound support and avoid creating a falling or trip hazard. Consider the combined weight before loading shelves. Keep a small ready-to-carry portion with evacuation essentials; the whole household reserve is not automatically portable. In an apartment or trailer, sketch the actual spaces you have and label what will go in each. Record both stored gallons and reachable gallons for a person who cannot lift or use stairs. Accessibility is part of the reserve, not an optional refinement after the quantity target is met. Make rotation a simple routine CDC recommends replacing home-filled stored water every six months. Observe the dates on commercially bottled water. Use a calendar reminder and a written shelf label so the routine does not depend on the founder of the household plan remembering everything. Check containers for damage, leakage, readable labels, and a secure lid. Use the oldest appropriate supply first in normal household use when suitable, then replace it. For a refill, repeat the proper cleaning and sanitation process; do not keep topping up an uncertain old supply. Update the fill date and the inventory with the real volume. Check whether household numbers, care needs, pet needs, or storage conditions have changed. Keep the system easy enough that another person can maintain it. A paper inventory needs only container, location, amount, fill or purchase date, and review date. If a container’s history is unclear or it may be contaminated, do not count it as confirmed drinking water. Plan meals and dispensing around the reserve Water use includes what meals require. Write a sample day of familiar food and note every step needing water: preparation, drinking, cleanup, and care. An emergency pantry full of foods that need long boiling can be a poor match for limited water and fuel. Include options that need little or no preparation water. Keep a clean dispensing method with the container. Avoid repeatedly dipping hands or a used cup into the supply. Agree which containers are for everyday use during the disruption and which remain closed as reserve. Allocate suitable water for pets and any provider-directed care requirement. Keep drinking-quality water available for brushing teeth and food preparation during a water advisory, as directed by that notice. Do a tabletop exercise: list tomorrow’s meals, estimate the water used, then compare it with a day of actual routine use. The exercise reveals omitted tasks without deliberately depriving anyone of water. Use the result to improve storage and reduce unnecessary water-heavy tasks. Storage is only one layer of the water plan A reserve buys time; it does not establish an unlimited source. Identify how you would obtain suitable water if the disruption exceeds your stock: a confirmed retailer, distribution point, trusted person, or other verified supply. Record access, carrying capacity, and the possibility that the location is closed. Do not count swimming-pool water, floodwater, an unknown stream, or chemically contaminated water as drinking supply. Boiling and ordinary filters do not solve every contamination problem. If tap service fails or an advisory is issued, use the water-outage guide to determine the allowed uses and the next safe source. Water outage and advisories Long-duration blackout planning Learn the local advisory system. Plan how to transport water if distribution sites open. Do not reuse containers that held toxic substances, even after washing. Calculate the household quantity on paper and store smaller containers if lifting a large container is difficult. Keep one portable supply ready. Divide storage between safe places so damage to one container does not lose all the household water. Choose container sizes and dispensing positions that the least mobile household member can use. Include pets, guests, hot-weather needs, pregnancy, illness, and provider-directed care needs in the quantity plan. Ask another capable person to locate and explain the reserve. Keep drinking and non-drinking containers clearly distinct. Water & food Work out the household quantity Choose containers you can actually handle Clean, fill, and label without confusion Store for access as well as capacity Make rotation a simple routine Plan meals and dispensing around the reserve Storage is only one layer of the water plan Calculate needs Count people and days and add water for pets and extra needs. Choose containers Use commercially bottled water or food-grade containers intended for water. Label and store Mark fill dates and store away from sunlight, fuel and cleaning products. Rotate supplies Follow bottled-water dates and replace self-filled stored water every six months.

title: Evacuating with pets
summary: Take pets when you can evacuate safely, using a carrier or lead and a destination that accepts them. Keep food, water, medicines, identification and veterinary information together. Do not delay escape into immediate danger or reenter a hazardous building for an animal.
text: Take pets when you can evacuate safely, using a carrier or lead and a destination that accepts them. Keep food, water, medicines, identification and veterinary information together. Do not delay escape into immediate danger or reenter a hazardous building for an animal.  Are pets accepted wherever people shelter? Do not assume so. Verify the particular site’s current admission, containment and care arrangements, including any separate housing. Keep an alternative suitable destination. What if a pet is still inside a dangerous building? Do not reenter active danger. Give reachable responders accurate information from safety and use verified animal-assistance channels when available. Make a separate departure task for every animal Name who collects each animal, which carrier or restraint is used, and where the animal will travel. Include pets that hide, cannot be handled by every adult, or need special care. Start containment early in a developing evacuation when it is safe; searching for a frightened cat after doors open can consume the departure time. Keep the human immediate-escape plan separate from planned packing. Plan the animal’s whole journey Contain Use suitable familiar restraint or a secure carrier before loading. Move Fit people, animals and essential care equipment into the actual transport. Receive Confirm an animal-compatible destination and care arrangement. Editorial planning aid. Actual hazards, individual needs and current instructions control the response. Editorial example: two dogs have bags of food ready but only one adult can safely handle both leads while helping a child. The gap is responsibility and transport, not food. Practice a calm loading sequence in normal conditions and adjust the plan before warning time is short. Do not delay escape from a fire or reenter danger to collect equipment or an animal. Confirm admission rather than assuming a shelter accepts pets Check the destination directly before relying on it. Ask whether it accepts the animal’s species, size and number, what containment and records are required, whether animals stay with owners, and what care remains the owner’s responsibility. A hotel, host, boarding facility or evacuation center may have different rules and limited space. Keep a realistic alternative that is not exposed to exactly the same hazard. A useful destination confirmation Question Record the actual answer Acceptance Species, number and any relevant restrictions. Admission Opening, availability, reservation or registration requirements. Equipment Carrier, lead, records, food and other supplies required. Care Who feeds, handles and gives prescribed medicines. Separation Where animals stay, visiting arrangements and how ownership is verified. Do not conflate pets and service animals. They may have different accommodation rules. Red Cross guidance describes possible separate animal housing depending on circumstances and welcomes service animals that assist people with disabilities. Use the specific facility’s current arrangements; do not present an old shelter list or general policy as a confirmed space for tonight. Pack usable care, identification and a concise instruction card Use the normal suitable food, safe water, appropriate bowls, prescribed medicines and needed waste supplies. Count pet water and food separately so human reserves are not silently assigned twice. Include the equipment needed to open or serve the actual food. Ask the veterinarian about special diets, medicine storage and emergency care needs; do not improvise a dose or sedate an animal from a generic evacuation tip. Keep a suitable carrier, harness or lead with an accessible loading location. Use a current identification tag and review microchip contact details where applicable. Keep a recent photograph and veterinary information privately with the responsible adult. Write the feeding routine, prescribed instructions, veterinarian contact and important handling needs. Include appropriate waste containment and clean-up supplies without packing chemicals beside food. Add a familiar item if manageable, while keeping essential human and animal care accessible. Label by animal where needs differ. A generic bag saying pets can conceal a missing medicine or the wrong food. Keep a grab list for daily-use care items and review it after treatment changes. Store records so they can be found even if a phone fails, while protecting information that is unnecessary for admission or care. Test transport space and controlled loading Check the actual vehicle with people, mobility equipment, bags and suitable animal restraint. Carrier dimensions and access matter as much as total cargo space. Use the restraint and transport equipment as intended and maintain appropriate ventilation and temperature. Never leave an animal in a hot vehicle while negotiating admission or checking a room. Travel conditions and the animal’s health may require veterinary advice. A calm loading rehearsal Check Problem it reveals Carrier access An animal cannot enter calmly or the door does not secure. Responsible handler The assigned adult is also needed for another dependent person. Vehicle layout People or essential equipment lose necessary space. Transfer at arrival Opening a door creates an escape opportunity. Backup driver The alternative vehicle cannot fit the same arrangement. Keep doors and animals controlled during transfers. Do not let children manage a distressed animal beyond their ability. If the usual adult is away, identify a trusted helper with appropriate access and knowledge before the emergency, rather than counting on an unfamiliar volunteer. A helper must also have a safe route; do not ask them to enter active fire, floodwater or another dangerous area. Maintain care in temporary accommodation On arrival, count animals and confirm that each is secured in the intended arrangement. Place food, medicines and clean equipment where the responsible person can find them. Keep animals under appropriate control around unfamiliar people and other animals. Distress can change behavior, so do not assume a normally friendly animal is comfortable with crowding, noise or strangers handling it. Keep a daily care record if responsibility changes Record feeding, prescribed care, waste needs and any concern for the next trusted handler. Note what was actually done rather than leaving two adults to guess whether medicine was already given. Check temperature, available water and suitable rest without relying only on the weather outdoors. Seek veterinary help for worrying changes or injury. Maintain hygiene between animal waste, meal tasks and child care. If separate boarding is necessary, verify who holds the animal, how updates are obtained, and how collection will work. Keep the information with the household coordinator so onward movement does not leave the animal unaccounted for. Plan lost-pet checks and safe return If an animal is missing, record its last confirmed place and time, description, identification and photograph. Contact verified animal services, veterinary contacts or the relevant facility through independently obtained channels when available. Do not enter a dangerous area or pay an unknown caller solely on a claim of finding the animal. Keep public appeals limited to useful information and protect private identity and location details. Account for each animal before every move and after arrival. Tell the trusted handler or household coordinator of any missing animal. Record sightings separately from confirmed identification. Verify found-animal reports through a known service or safe trusted contact. Confirm collection and update outdated notices when reunited. Return home only when the setting is suitable for people and animals. Keep animals controlled around damage and debris. After an evacuation, review the part that actually failed: capture, loading, admission, care or communication. Replace used supplies and adjust responsibility before the next event. Livestock, large numbers of animals and specialist species need their own transport and welfare plan; this household guide does not make a small pet carrier plan sufficient for them. Household evacuation Returning home Check animals regularly for overheating, cold and distress in transport. Keep them restrained in crowded temporary accommodation and maintain hygiene. A service animal and a pet may have different accommodation rules. Never leave animals in a hot vehicle while arranging shelter. Use a confirmed trusted host or animal-care arrangement and keep a viable alternative. Ask the actual evacuation site about current animal housing rather than assuming every site accepts pets or keeps them beside their owners. Assign a capable handler to each animal while another adult manages children or access needs. Test transport with the actual people and equipment, and verify pet and service-animal arrangements separately. pets evacuation dog evacuation cat emergency Make a separate departure task for every animal Confirm admission rather than assuming a shelter accepts pets Pack usable care, identification and a concise instruction card Test transport space and controlled loading Maintain care in temporary accommodation Plan lost-pet checks and safe return Contain animals early Use a secure carrier or lead before loading or opening doors. Distress and noise can cause animals to run. Confirm the destination Ask whether pets are accepted and what documents or carriers are needed. Make a backup arrangement with a trusted person. Pack basic care Take normal food, safe water, medicines, waste supplies and a familiar blanket if readily available. Include pet water in the household total. Keep identification current Use a tag and a recent photo, and check microchip contact details before emergencies. Keep veterinary records privately. Avoid unsafe rescue Tell reachable responders where an animal may be, but do not return to fire, floodwater or active danger yourself.

title: Evacuation
summary: Leave a threatened location while a safer route and destination are still available. Take people, pets, essential medicines, identification, shoes, water and phone power; do not delay for belongings. Confirm the route and a place to stay, tell a trusted contact, and avoid flooded, closed or actively dangerous roads. Do not wait for an order when immediate danger is evident. Radiation or airborne hazards may make sheltering safer than travel.
text: A departure is easier when the destination and route are already decided. Your first destination is closed? Use the checked alternate and tell the outside contact when safe. A vehicle is unavailable? Use the early transport arrangement; see evacuation without a car. Do not wait until travel conditions deteriorate to investigate capacity. Should I finish packing before escaping a fire? No. Leave immediate danger and do not return for belongings. A planned regional departure may allow a short preparation sequence; urgent escape does not. What if the destination changes? Use a suitable checked alternative and notify the outside contact when safe. At arrival, account for people and verify essential care rather than assuming the original arrangements still apply. Identify why you are leaving and how urgent it is An immediate escape from fire or a visibly unsafe building is different from a regional evacuation with preparation time. Do not delay immediate escape to finish a packing checklist. For a developing hazard, confirm the affected area, applicable deadline, current route instructions, and suitable destination while there is still time to arrange support. Departure priorities People Account for the household and required assistance; leave immediate danger without waiting for belongings. Destination and route For a wider evacuation, use current hazard-specific directions and a checked place to arrive. Essentials and contact Take urgent care items and the manageable bag when time permits; report the destination when safe. Editorial planning aid. Actual hazards, access needs and current instructions control the decision. Sheltering can sometimes be the safer action during an airborne chemical or radiation hazard. Do not assume that movement is always protective. Use the specific incident guidance and the actual condition of the building. If the building itself is burning, flooding, or failing, that immediate danger also matters. Confirm a destination that meets the actual needs A destination is usable only if it is reachable, accepting people, and suitable for their needs. Call or use an appropriate current information channel when available. Check the exact address, opening status, entry requirements, accessibility, essential care, pet arrangements, and what supplies people must bring. A map marker is not evidence of admission or medical support. Destination checks before a non-immediate move Check Useful question Location Is it outside the specific hazard area, and is the route currently usable? Acceptance Can the whole household stay, and is acceptance confirmed? Access Can a person use the entrance, toilet, sleeping space, and available movement routes? Care Can necessary equipment, medicine storage, or caregiving continue? Pets Are the actual animals permitted, with suitable transport and supplies? Alternate What is the next realistic option if this location closes or cannot accept you? If emergency conditions prevent confirmation, keep the uncertainty visible in the plan and prioritize the best available protective information. Do not describe a potential shelter as a guaranteed solution to another household member. Plan transport around people, not only bags Count seats, helpers, pets, mobility equipment, care supplies, and bags together. Confirm who drives or provides transport, where pickup happens, and when the arrangement must be used. Someone who can usually use stairs may be unable to do so while carrying equipment or supporting a child. If using a vehicle, preserve fuel or charge and confirm a suitable route. Do not depend on every station being open. For arranged assistance, verify the actual service, registration, eligibility, and pickup arrangements in advance where possible. If there is no car, identify realistic alternatives early rather than waiting until roads or transit are disrupted. Do not assume walking preserves the original plan. Distance, weather, mobility, safe routes, and carryable supplies change the decision. Keep contact and destination information on paper as well as in a device. The Florida county reference illustrates advance zone and transport planning, not rules for every location. Your own community’s arrangements may differ. A registration or a request for help should not be confused with a confirmed immediate pickup. Evacuation without a car Access and mobility needs Use a departure check that does not slow escape For a planned departure with time available, use a short ordered check: people and care, transport and destination, then manageable essentials. Place daily-use medicine and equipment on a grab list so they are not forgotten. Assign tasks without leaving a dependent person alone while every adult searches for supplies. Account for people and pets and identify who assists each person. Check transport, destination, and current route information. Take necessary care items, identification, keys, a light, contacts, suitable water, and the tested bag as time allows. Tell the outside contact where the group is going and when you expect another check-in, when safe. Leave without returning for optional items. Do not enter danger to complete the checklist. Secure the home only when it is safe and does not delay departure. Utility shutoff is not a universal evacuation task; follow the applicable utility or incident instructions and do not manipulate unfamiliar systems. A property checklist belongs below people and care, not above them. If the route or destination changes Do not force the original route through flooded, closed, or actively dangerous roads. Use current route instructions and a safer checked alternative when available. A navigation app may be unaware of the hazard or a closure. If no safer movement is available, compare the immediate danger of staying with the danger of the route and use hazard-specific guidance. Plan changes to rehearse before departure Change Response to prepare First destination is closed Use the suitable alternate and send a change-of-plan message when safe. Vehicle is unavailable Activate the realistic transport alternative; reassess what can be carried. Group becomes separated Use the agreed safe meeting and contact arrangements; do not improvise a hazardous search. Care requirement changes Prioritize the relevant urgent-care or provider-directed plan. An airborne hazard makes travel unsafe Use the specific shelter instruction and reassess; movement is not automatically safer. A useful change message states who is present, the new destination, immediate needs, and the next expected contact. Sending it must not delay getting clear of danger. Keep necessary records private and share the location with trusted people who need it, rather than posting a detailed household route publicly. Arrival, separation, and safe return At arrival, count everyone, settle essential care, and tell the outside contact the actual location when safe. Check sleeping, hygiene, water, and device power arrangements before assuming the journey solved all needs. Confirm who is responsible for children and pets during the stay and how the group will reconnect if someone leaves briefly. Return is a new decision. Use current access and hazard instructions, and do not enter a damaged building or unsafe utility area simply because a road reopens. Think through care, water, food, and sanitation before a non-urgent return. Take the appropriate safe route and avoid making several unnecessary trips through a disrupted area. Keep receipts and useful records of losses and accommodation when appropriate. Replenish the bag and transport reserve after use. Record which destination, route, contact, or carrying assumption failed. Update the household plan using what was actually available, rather than only the original intended arrangement. A safe practice beforehand can test the departure sequence without simulating a hazardous journey. Discuss one route closure and one unavailable destination. The goal is a flexible household plan that another capable adult can use. Make two destinations and more than one route in advance. Keep a small grab list by the door, especially for medications, pets, and items that cannot be prepacked. If a route is unsafe, do not force it. Follow current local instructions or contact emergency services for help. Some hazards, especially radiation fallout, can make immediate travel more dangerous than sheltering; follow the hazard-specific order. Choose a reachable destination with someone you trust, identify a second route, and agree on a check-in. Do not wait for transport that has not been confirmed. If the route is actively dangerous, compare the specific hazard of staying with the hazard of moving; shelter while reassessing if no safer route is available. Give dependents a written contact card and agree who stays with each person. Keep essential medicine and mobility equipment accessible. A pet carrier or heavy bag must not block a caregiver from helping someone move. Evacuation Identify why you are leaving and how urgent it is Confirm a destination that meets the actual needs Plan transport around people, not only bags Use a departure check that does not slow escape If the route or destination changes Arrival, separation, and safe return Confirm the order Check the official zone, deadline, route, shelter options, and whether the order includes your address. Gather people first Account for everyone and pets. Take required medication and medical supplies, documents, accessible equipment, keys, and a charged phone. Do not spend critical time packing extras. Choose a destination Go to a trusted contact or designated shelter outside the hazard area. Check pet rules, accessibility, and transport needs. Leave and report safely Use current official routes. Share your destination with an out-of-area contact, keep fuel in the vehicle if relevant, and do not return until authorities say it is safe.

title: Evacuation with access or mobility needs
summary: Plan movement around the person who needs the most assistance. Keep mobility aids, medicines, communication tools and essential care supplies together. Confirm accessible transport and a suitable destination directly; do not assume a shelter, lift or public rescue vehicle will be available.
text: Plan movement around the person who needs the most assistance. Keep mobility aids, medicines, communication tools and essential care supplies together. Confirm accessible transport and a suitable destination directly; do not assume a shelter, lift or public rescue vehicle will be available.  Does accessible entry mean the destination meets my needs? No. Check toilets, sleeping, communication, power, essential care, assistance and equipment arrangements separately, then verify actual conditions on arrival. Should we practice carrying someone down stairs? Do not improvise an untrained carry. Develop the building-specific plan with the person and appropriate professionals, and rehearse only safe agreed actions. Describe assistance as tasks, with the person’s input Start with what the individual says they need and what safely works for them. A diagnosis alone does not explain how to leave a building, communicate, travel, use a toilet, or maintain essential care. Plan for a difficult day as well as a good one. Pain, fatigue, noise, loss of power and an unfamiliar setting may change what the person can manage independently. A practical assistance record Task Record the real requirement Movement Usable distance, stairs, transfers, mobility aid and safe assistance. Communication Preferred language or format, aid, interpreter or written prompts. Care Prescribed routine, equipment dependencies and care-provider contacts. Transport Suitable vehicle, boarding requirements and equipment space. Destination Entry, toilet, sleeping, charging and caregiver arrangements. Use consent to decide which helpers receive sensitive details. Keep a concise task note available to trusted people without publishing medical records. Ask the care provider or equipment supplier about technical and clinical questions rather than inventing a generic carrying method or backup power rule. Check the entire route, including the building exit A route is only usable if the person can move from their actual starting place to the destination. Check doors, locks, thresholds, corridors, stairs, outside surfaces, pickup position and vehicle boarding. Do this in normal safe conditions with appropriate support. Do not rely on an elevator as the only exit arrangement, especially in a fire, power failure or damaged building. Every part of the route needs a workable answer Building How does the person reach the appropriate safe exit or planned refuge? Transport Who assists, what vehicle fits, and how are the person and equipment moved safely? Destination Can the site support access, communication and essential care on arrival? Editorial planning aid. Actual hazards, individual needs and current instructions control the response. Discuss the site-specific evacuation plan with building management or the responsible fire-safety professional before an emergency. If a refuge is part of that plan, know how assistance is requested and what the arrangement actually provides. Do not assume an unmarked landing is safe for every hazard. Never practice by blocking exits, disabling alarms, or improvising an untrained carry down stairs. Arrange named helpers and transport backups Make the primary helper’s role explicit: check in, reach the person, assist with specified tasks, and communicate the outcome. Ask whether they can realistically reach the location when roads, lifts or phones fail. A nearby relative may face the same disruption. Identify another viable option and keep current contact information for both. A message requesting help is not confirmation that someone is on the way. Ask helpers to learn the person-approved assistance method through suitable training or professional guidance. Confirm who can unlock the location and how lawful access is arranged. Check whether the transport provider can accommodate the actual mobility equipment and necessary companion. Ask any local registry or assistance program about eligibility, registration deadlines, contact procedures and limits; registration is not a rescue guarantee. Decide how the person reports a failed arrangement and the precise assistance still required. Editorial example: a driver offers a car but the required wheelchair will not fit and the person cannot safely transfer. The offer does not complete transport. Resolve the whole journey in advance rather than counting a phone number as a confirmed capability. Recheck when equipment, mobility, helpers or living arrangements change. Keep essential equipment and a useful handover together Write a portable care and equipment note for the person and trusted helper. Include necessary current instructions, contact details, compatible chargers, required consumables, and where daily-use items are kept. Medicines and equipment must be stored and transported under their specific requirements. Use a provider-directed contingency for electricity-dependent care; an ordinary phone power bank does not establish support for a medical device. Separate what travels from what must be grabbed Layer Useful contents or information Always accessible Communication card, trusted contacts and concise assistance preferences. Prepared carry items Suitable charger, approved consumables, spare aids where appropriate. Daily-use grab list Current medicines or equipment that cannot remain packed. Technical instructions Device model, safe operation, power limits and supplier contact. Keep the person with essential mobility or communication aids and a necessary caregiver whenever feasible. If a separation cannot be avoided, record where equipment went and who is responsible for reuniting it. Do not make children lift equipment or carry medicines beyond their ability.
