Avoid a bag so heavy that it competes with safely supporting the person. Confirm the destination’s specific capabilities An “accessible” label may refer only to an entrance. Ask about the full stay: toilets, washing, sleeping position, turning space, safe electrical supply, medication storage, communications, necessary assistance and service-animal arrangements. A general evacuation center may not provide clinical care or a personal caregiver. State needs clearly and ask what is confirmed, what must be supplied, and what remains unavailable. A destination must match the care plan If essential care cannot be sustained there, investigate another suitable arrangement before travel becomes urgent. Do not assume the presence of staff or a generator means the person’s specific needs will be met. Record the date, contact and limits of a confirmation, then recheck when conditions change. A relative’s home can be a suitable option only if entry, toilet access, equipment and care arrangements actually work. Plan a realistic alternative for a site that fills, loses power, or becomes unreachable. On arrival, verify conditions rather than treating the pre-emergency conversation as permanent assurance. Checking a shelter destination Household evacuation planning Rehearse safely and state what to do if assistance fails Use discussion and a supported normal-condition route check with the individual’s agreement. Keep medical support operating and stop if the exercise causes pain, distress or an unsafe condition. Time useful steps without turning movement into a race. Check whether the backup helper can find the instructions and explain the actual assistance instead of simply saying they will help. Describe the warning and how the person perceives it. Identify the building response appropriate to that hazard. Locate the communication card and essential grab list. Confirm helper, vehicle and destination arrangements. Introduce one failure on paper and identify the next realistic option. Record the unmet need, responsible person and next action. If an emergency occurs and help cannot be reached, use the safest available location appropriate to the hazard and communicate exact location and assistance needed through a safe working channel. Do not treat delayed help as permission for an unsafe transfer. For a developing threat, earlier movement can preserve options; immediate fire or structural danger needs its own building emergency response. Review the plan after any failed step. Practise the plan with the person’s consent and revise it when equipment or care needs change. Keep an alternative plan for power loss and an unavailable caregiver. Do not separate a person from essential equipment or a necessary caregiver if avoidable. An untrained lifting attempt can injure both the person and the helper. Use your confirmed private support network and a destination suited to care needs. If transport cannot be arranged, identify the safest available refuge and communicate the precise assistance required through a safe channel. Ask the individual what assistance is safe and useful. Include named helpers and a backup, and keep essential equipment and a necessary caregiver with the person wherever feasible. wheelchair evacuation disabled evacuation accessible shelter mobility emergency Describe assistance as tasks, with the person’s input Check the entire route, including the building exit Arrange named helpers and transport backups Keep essential equipment and a useful handover together Confirm the destination’s specific capabilities Rehearse safely and state what to do if assistance fails Identify the actual assistance Write down transfer needs, walking distance, stairs, powered devices, communication needs and care routines. Ask the person what help is safe and useful. Check the route Assess exits and stairs before a crisis. Do not use lifts in a fire or damaged building, and do not improvise a dangerous carry. Confirm support Arrange more than one trusted helper and transport option. Make the responsibility specific rather than assuming someone else will come. Keep essential equipment close Include medicines, charger, batteries, mobility aids and a concise care note. Keep a portable backup where possible. Verify the destination Ask about step-free entry, toilets, charging, refrigeration, caregivers and service animals. A general promise of accessibility is not a confirmed arrangement.

title: Evacuation without a car: arrange transport early
summary: Arrange more than one realistic transport option, confirm what each can carry, and leave extra time. Do not wait for a ride that has never been agreed.
text: Can I rely on a local evacuation registry? Use it as one part of the plan. Ask how the service operates, when it stops taking requests and what it actually promises. Keep personal transport alternatives and carry essential information. Write down the handover Editorial pickup note: names and count of passengers, pickup point, alternate point, departure trigger, destination, accessibility needs, pets and essential equipment. Give a copy to the driver and household. Resolve disagreements before a warning arrives, especially if someone wants to bring more than the vehicle can hold. Leave before the last possible moment The plan needs a trigger that allows loading and travel time. Account for congestion, bridge closures, darkness and the helper’s own household. If your only ride depends on someone crossing the threatened area, look for a closer backup. A transport registration can be useful, but it is not a guaranteed dispatch or rescue service. Call the proposed driver today and confirm the exact pickup point and passenger capacity. Record a second arrangement that does not depend on that same driver. Transit, taxis, rideshare and shelters may stop operating or have restrictions. Never present an unconfirmed service as an assured way out. If your confirmed ride fails, contact the backup early where possible. Use a safer nearby waiting place only if reachable without crossing the hazard. Share a concise location and access needs when safe assistance becomes reachable. Include children’s restraints, mobility equipment, communication aids and pet accommodation. Discuss assistance with the person receiving it; do not assume they can use stairs or transfer into an unfamiliar vehicle. no car evacuation transport assistance accessible ride Identify transport dependence Write down who needs a lift, accessible vehicle, car seat, equipment space or help reaching the pickup point. Start with people, not luggage. Confirm a primary ride Ask a trusted person what warning they need, where pickup will happen and what would stop them reaching you. Check that the destination is willing and able to receive the group. Arrange a second option Research accessible public or community transport before an emergency. Record contact details, operating limits and booking requirements; availability during disaster is uncertain. Practice the pickup Test the route to the meeting point and the actual load. Use a compact carry bag and leave bulky replaceable supplies if they prevent people or essential care equipment fitting.

title: Explosions & nearby shelling
summary: Move away from windows and exposed areas into the most protective intact shelter you can reach safely. Stay clear of damaged buildings and unfamiliar debris. Keep family members together and shoes, a light and medicines close. A pause in explosions is not an all-clear; do not go out to film, investigate or collect fragments.
text: Move away from windows and exposed areas into the most protective intact shelter you can reach safely. Stay clear of damaged buildings and unfamiliar debris. Keep family members together and shoes, a light and medicines close. A pause in explosions is not an all-clear; do not go out to film, investigate or collect fragments.    Prepare for loss of water, power and communications. Choose a reunion contact and a second shelter option. Use recently verified humanitarian or local information to judge whether movement is safer than staying. No ordinary room is guaranteed protection against weapons. Do not travel through active fighting or assume a claimed safe corridor has been secured. If broadcasts and emergency numbers fail, keep sheltering while it remains intact and safer than movement. Check essential supplies, agree on short check-ins and use trusted neighbours without sending people into exposed areas. Assign a trusted adult to each person who needs assistance. Keep medicines, essential contacts and a workable reunion plan with the group. Make decisions around the least mobile person, not the fastest; avoid splitting the family without a clear, safe way to reconnect. For this situation, brief every person on the first action: get out of exposed space. Agree who will manage children, pets or mobility needs while that action happens. No ordinary room is guaranteed protection against weapons. Do not travel through active fighting or assume a claimed safe corridor has been secured. shelling bombing explosions nearby air raid missile attack Get out of exposed space Use a designated protective shelter if it is safely reachable. Otherwise choose the most protective intact interior space available, away from glazing. Consider fire, collapse, flooding and escape access; a basement is not safe if these hazards are present. Protect yourself from secondary hazards Keep away from windows, loose masonry and damaged electrical equipment. Keep footwear on when moving. Do not use a lift in a damaged building. Check people without increasing exposure Account for the household from shelter. Provide first aid only where you will not become another casualty. Send a brief private status message if service is available. Reassess the building Smoke, fire, instability or flooding may require movement to a safer reachable place. Do not interpret a quiet period as proof that streets or unexploded objects are safe. Keep debris untouched Never handle suspicious fragments, wires, containers or munitions. Keep children and pets away. Do not approach to take a photograph.

title: Extreme cold
summary: Get into a warm, dry place, replace wet clothing and add dry layers. Confusion, extreme drowsiness or loss of coordination can indicate hypothermia; call emergency services. Use safe heat and never bring grills or generators indoors.
text: Why does wet clothing matter? Wet and wind-exposed clothing can accelerate heat loss. Move to a sheltered warmer place when safe and change wet layers using what is available. Avoid unvented fuel-burning appliances, generators or outdoor cooking equipment for indoor heat. What if someone becomes confused or drowsy? Treat serious cold-related changes as a medical emergency, reduce further heat loss and handle the person gently. Follow reachable clinical guidance rather than making them walk to warm up or giving an unconscious person a drink.  Keep medicines, transport and backup plans ready. Watch for numb, pale or waxy skin that may signal frostbite. Do not rub frostbitten skin or apply direct intense heat. Use one dry room, layered clothing, blankets and insulation beneath you. Keep fuel-burning outdoor equipment outside. If you cannot keep people warm, identify a reachable warm place before they become confused or weak; do not wait for a warming centre to open. Check children, older adults and people with limited movement rather than relying only on their report that they feel fine. Keep dry layers and a reachable warmer location in the plan. Protect medicine and mobility equipment from temperature damage according to their instructions. Winter Get sheltered Limit outdoor exposure and protect hands, feet, head and face. Change wet clothing Use dry layers and blankets; warm the body gently. Find safe heat Use approved heaters as directed, keep them away from combustibles and maintain CO alarms. Arrange help If heat fails, contact local warming shelters and help people with limited mobility relocate safely.

title: Extreme heat
summary: Move to air conditioning or a designated cooling space, reduce exertion and drink water regularly unless your clinician restricts fluids. Confusion, collapse or seizures in heat can mean heat stroke: call emergency services and start rapid cooling.
text: Is confusion just tiredness? Confusion, collapse or other serious neurological changes in heat can indicate heat stroke and require urgent medical help plus immediate cooling. Do not give drinks to someone who is not fully awake or cannot swallow. The cooling center is closed — what now? Check another cooler location and reduce exertion while arranging access. Confirm opening and transport before relying on a listed center. Do not leave a person in a vehicle while trying to solve the next step.  Plan activities for cooler hours and follow heat alerts. Arrange safe transport before the home becomes dangerously hot. Heat stroke can occur with sweating. Do not wait for dry skin. Use the coolest reachable space, wet skin or cloths, reduce activity and check vulnerable people repeatedly. A closed room can become more dangerous than outdoor shade. If indoor heat becomes intolerable, move early to a safer location rather than waiting for power to return. Check infants, older adults and people taking medicines that affect heat tolerance. Share the cooling plan in a form everyone can understand and name a person responsible for check-ins. Do not treat a fan or closed-window plan as suitable at every temperature. Heat & dry conditions Find a cooler place Use air conditioning, a public cooling center or another safe indoor location. Reduce heat load Rest, loosen unnecessary clothing and use cool wet cloths or a cool shower. Check on others Older adults, infants, outdoor workers and people with illness may need help. Never leave anyone or pets in a parked vehicle. Recognize an emergency For altered mental status or collapse, call emergency services and cool the person while waiting; do not give drinks to someone unable to swallow.

title: Family separation & reunification
summary: Stay in a safe place, try the agreed contact and meeting plan, and record the missing person’s last confirmed location and time. Keep children with a trusted caregiver. Use verified Red Cross or humanitarian family-tracing channels if available. Do not publish sensitive personal details or enter danger to search.
text: Stay in a safe place, try the agreed contact and meeting plan, and record the missing person’s last confirmed location and time. Keep children with a trusted caregiver. Use verified Red Cross or humanitarian family-tracing channels if available. Do not publish sensitive personal details or enter danger to search.  Should I post all identity details publicly? No. Limit any appeal to useful appropriate information and seek verified tracing guidance. Keep identity numbers, private medical records, addresses and live movements out of public posts. What closes the search? Confirm identity, location and any assistance needed, tell the coordinator and relevant tracing services, and update obsolete requests. A reported sighting alone is not a verified reunion. Stabilize your own group and record the last confirmed facts Before searching for anyone, protect the people already with you and establish a safe contactable base. A frantic series of moves can create another missing person and erase the location someone expects you to use. If a child is missing or someone may be in immediate danger, contact the appropriate emergency or protection service through a safe available channel. Do not postpone that request while completing a perfect record. A private first record Field What belongs in it Person Name, recent description or photograph, and relevant identifying details. Last confirmed contact Exact place, time, who observed it and how they know. Immediate concern Age, essential care or a specific known hazard; avoid guessing. Attempts made Number or channel, time, outcome and any reference from a service. Your contact A reachable trusted coordinator and safe way to send updates. Separate what you witnessed from a reported sighting and a rumor. “Someone said they were at a shelter” is not a confirmed arrival. Retain the original message if safe, note its time, and check the sender through a known channel. Keep the working record private rather than placing a full identity profile on social media. Use the existing reunion plan before inventing several searches Try the person’s agreed contact channel and the household’s outside coordinator. Send one short factual update with your location, the people with you, and a next check-in time. Ask for confirmation when practical. If a prearranged meeting place is reachable and appropriate to the hazard, use the written plan. Do not treat that plan as permission to cross danger or enter a damaged building. One coordinator keeps the search coherent Record Collect confirmed last-contact details and current concerns. Coordinate Use agreed contacts and a safe meeting plan; assign distinct checks. Update Log each result, keep your own group reachable, and close outdated requests. Editorial planning aid. Actual hazards, individual needs and current instructions control the response. A useful division of work is for one adult to contact the known school or host while another stays with children and maintains the record. Give each task a clear end point and reporting time. Avoid several people independently driving to the same unverified location. If no message gets through, maintain a predictable safe location as far as the incident allows. Use school, childcare and caregiver release procedures A school or care facility may move people to a different site and may restrict collection to authorized adults. Before an incident, ask for its emergency contact, release, relocation and identification procedure. Put the relevant details with the household plan. During an incident, use independently verified facility information rather than an address supplied by an unknown caller claiming to have your child. Name the authorized backup collector and make sure the facility’s records agree. Record what identification or permission the actual facility requires, without assuming one universal rule. Arrange who stays with other children while a collector travels. Use a calm handover: verify the child’s identity, the collecting adult and the confirmed destination. If someone offers to move or reunite a child, verify their role and organization before allowing a handover; seek verified protection help when needed. For an adult requiring assistance, record how they communicate and who is authorized to help. A caregiver’s failure to answer does not prove that the adult was transferred elsewhere. Check the facility or known support contact and ask for a specific confirmed status. Respect privacy limits; an institution may need to verify your identity before disclosing information. Find an appropriate tracing or welfare service and verify it The American Red Cross describes different family and welfare inquiry services for U.S. disaster separations, with eligibility criteria. Use its current contact-and-locate page or an independently verified local chapter to learn which service fits. For international separation, use verified Red Cross or Red Crescent family-links channels appropriate to the situation. Neither an inquiry submission nor a registration guarantees a rapid location or reunion. Before sending sensitive information Check Ask or verify Identity of service Find the organization through an independent known channel. Scope Does it handle this disaster, geographic area and type of separation? Required information Which details are necessary, and where are they stored or shared? Reference and follow-up What case reference and safe update method will be used? Costs or demands Question unexpected payment, pressure or requests for unnecessary identity documents. Keep any case reference with the coordinator’s record. Do not send private documents through a stranger’s link because they claim the person has been found. If official services are unsafe or unavailable in the local situation, use a trusted humanitarian channel and the household’s own safe contacts while protecting sensitive location information. Check reported sightings without exposing the person A report should include when and where the person was seen, what the observer actually knows, and a safe way to verify it. Several reposts of one claim do not create several independent sightings. Use known contacts or the relevant verified service to check the report. Do not send a child, a vulnerable adult, or an untrained volunteer into a hazardous search area. Public appeals need a privacy decision Consider what minimum information could help, who might see it, and whether the person faces a safety threat. Keep full identity numbers, medical records, private addresses and live movements out of public posts. Ask a verified tracing service what publication is appropriate. Editorial example: a stranger says a relative is at a hotel and asks for a fee before giving a room number. Record the claim, independently contact the hotel or verified service through a known number where appropriate, and do not pay merely to unlock the story. A convincing photograph can be old or copied. Avoid promising a reward or sharing more private information before verification. Communications outage Recognizing disaster scams Confirm the reunion and close the information loop When contact is restored, confirm identity through familiar knowledge or a trusted verified handover, establish the person’s actual location and condition, and agree how to reconnect safely. Someone answering a borrowed phone may be reachable but still unable to travel. Do not call the search finished until the coordinator understands what support or onward arrangement is needed. Confirm who was reached, where they are and when the contact happened. Check whether urgent care, an accessible journey or a trusted caregiver is needed. Tell the household coordinator and relevant verified tracing services. Update or remove outdated public requests where you control them. Keep necessary case and care records private, and stop unnecessary circulation. Review what caused separation and improve contact cards or release arrangements. Reunion can be physically and emotionally difficult. Provide calm information, suitable food and water, essential care, and rest where available. Avoid requiring a child to repeatedly recount frightening details to every adult. Once safe, replace assumptions in the plan with what actually worked: a reachable contact, a clear collector, a confirmed destination, and a paper fallback. Keep one person coordinating the information so sightings, contacts and dates are not lost. Update the record when someone is found and tell verified tracing services to stop circulating old requests. Scammers may demand money or identity documents. Do not post full identity numbers, sensitive addresses or real-time movements publicly. If networks fail, follow the written reunion plan only where safe and leave a message with the agreed trusted contact. Keep your own location predictable rather than repeatedly moving between unsafe places. Keep children with a trusted responsible adult and assign one person to coordinate confirmed information. Plan communication, authorized collection and care needs without sending several people into unsafe searches. missing family separated child family lost reunite cant find family Stabilize your own group and record the last confirmed facts Use the existing reunion plan before inventing several searches Use school, childcare and caregiver release procedures Find an appropriate tracing or welfare service and verify it Check reported sightings without exposing the person Confirm the reunion and close the information loop Record facts Write the last confirmed contact, location, time, description and medical needs. Distinguish what you know from rumours. Keep a recent photo privately if available. Try agreed channels Send a short text to the person and the out-of-area contact. Leave your own location and next check-in time. A sent message may not be delivered. Use the safe meeting plan Go to the meeting point only if the route and location are safe. Do not send several people independently into a hazardous area. Verify tracing services Use independently found Red Cross or humanitarian contacts. Check the organisation rather than trusting a forwarded number, and ask how information will be protected. Protect children Never hand a child to an unverified adult promising reunification. Keep a written contact card and involve a trusted caregiver or verified protection service.

title: Financial disaster plan: records, payments and recovery
summary: Gather account contacts and insurance information, keep protected copies accessible, and understand your coverage and deductibles before disruption. Build a practical plan for essential payments and unexpected costs around your budget. Keep private account details out of public forms and shared links.
text: The policy wording is unclear? Ask the insurer and retain the response. An aid message asks for sensitive data? Verify its source before sharing anything. Is there a single correct emergency savings amount? No. Use your actual household costs and constraints. A small achievable reserve and usable records are practical starting points. A worksheet you can build yourself Editorial fields: provider, verified contact, policy or account reference stored privately, regular due date, usual payment method and alternate contact method. Keep a separate expense list for relocation and recovery. Update contact details after changing providers so an old document does not lead you to the wrong service. Practice finding the records Choose one adult to simulate a lost-phone situation. Can they find the insurance contact and housing reference without your phone, email inbox or password reset? Resolve the access problem safely, then return the documents to protected storage. The exercise should not expose passwords or account numbers to the group. Check one policy and one backup-access method this week. Ask the insurer specific coverage questions rather than assuming every storm loss is covered. Anyone promising guaranteed aid or demanding unusual payment may be a scam. Verify through independent official channels before providing identity or account information. If providers cannot be reached, keep dated notes of attempted contact and unavoidable expenses, preserve receipts and try verified channels when service returns. Do not assume a payment pause or assistance approval exists until confirmed. Plan for a person who normally manages the finances becoming unavailable. Give an appropriate trusted person the access they actually need, while keeping sensitive records away from children and public shared folders. financial preparedness disaster money plan emergency finances Build a contact list Record verified contacts for housing, utilities, insurance, banking and essential care. Use numbers from account statements or the provider’s own site. Protect important records Keep identity, policy and account information in protected storage with a separate backup. Decide who can access it if you are unavailable. Understand your insurance Check covered hazards, exclusions, deductibles and claim instructions with your insurer. Standard home insurance generally does not include flood or earthquake damage. Prioritize essential needs Editorial planning: list the costs of safe housing, transport, food, water and care. Choose a realistic saving target after essentials; avoid buying gear with money already needed for bills.

title: Firearm storage: locks, safes and household access
summary: Choose storage for three separate jobs: prevent unauthorized access, resist theft and protect condition. A cable lock, lockbox, cabinet and safe offer different levels of protection. Compare independent ratings, installation, humidity and backup access; a heavy enclosure or “fireproof” label is not a complete storage plan.
text: Four storage options and what each can reasonably do Storage categories are not interchangeable Option Main role Important limitation Cable or trigger lock Restricts operation when appropriate to the model and installed as instructed. Does not enclose the firearm or prevent it being carried away. Lockbox An enclosure useful for controlling access to a limited number of items. Portability can also make theft easier; installation and ratings matter. Locking cabinet Organized enclosure, often lighter and less expensive than substantial safes. Do not assume substantial forced-entry or fire resistance. Security container / safe An enclosure that may carry defined security or fire ratings. The word “safe,” its weight and its appearance do not establish those ratings. Match the storage method to the actual firearm and the household, not a generic photograph. Follow the firearm and locking-device instructions; a lock that fits one model may be unsuitable for another. Secure firearms unloaded and keep ammunition separately secured. A locking device is a useful layer, while an appropriate locked enclosure also limits physical access. A household with one sporting rifle has a different capacity problem from a collection of handguns and long guns. There is no benefit in buying an enclosure that forces equipment together or cannot close properly. Choose usable capacity, including normal cases and fitted accessories, before comparing marketing capacity numbers. Theft resistance: understand the label instead of the showroom weight Security claims should identify the exact product, standard and test level. UL distinguishes residential security containers from other safe categories and evaluates resistance under defined test conditions. A certification for a lock is not automatically certification for the entire enclosure. Likewise, a claim that a product “uses UL components” does not identify an enclosure rating. A useful security comparison Question What to look for What was independently tested? The exact enclosure or component, identified by model. Against which standard? A named standard and classification, not just “tested.” What is the test scope? The stated attack level and conditions; laboratory results are not a promise of indefinite resistance. Does installation matter? The documented mounting or anchoring requirements. Can the product be removed? Consider portability, location and the complete installed system. Anchoring is not a decorative final step. Follow the product’s installation instructions and assess the supporting structure. A heavy enclosure can still present floor-loading and tip-over concerns. Renters should obtain permission for required installation; a mobile home or upstairs room may need structural advice before a large safe is delivered. Think about the whole access path: delivery route, door swing, working clearance and whether a household member can use the storage without leaving it unsecured. A system that is inconvenient is more likely to be bypassed. Plan the installation first, then select an enclosure that fits it. Fire ratings: useful evidence with specific limits “Fireproof” is an overstatement for ordinary consumer storage. A fire rating describes a defined test, time and performance criterion. UL’s safe fire testing includes interior temperature limits and may address different content types. A rating aimed at preserving paper does not establish that electronics, ammunition or a firearm will be unaffected in every real fire. Compare the test temperature profile, time, maximum interior conditions, testing organization and exact rated model. Two “60-minute” claims are not necessarily equivalent when the criteria differ. Burglary resistance, fire endurance and water resistance are separate properties. A product can perform well in one category without carrying meaningful evidence for another. Ask for the exact rating document or label rather than an unexplained badge. Distinguish an independent certification from a manufacturer’s own test. Treat fire and water claims separately; firefighting water creates another exposure. Keep an inventory and appropriate insurance records outside the enclosure in a private backup. After a real fire, obtain qualified assessment rather than relying on the original rating. A safe is property protection, not shelter. During a home fire, evacuate people and follow the emergency plan instead of retrieving equipment. Replacement records can help afterward; risking a delayed exit to save a firearm defeats the household purpose of preparedness. Humidity and corrosion: inspect the inside, not only the room An enclosure can have a moisture problem even in a home that feels comfortable. Local leaks, damp flooring, temperature changes and air exchange affect conditions. Measure inside the storage space and follow the safe and firearm manufacturers’ care recommendations. There is no single humidity number that replaces the instructions for every material and product. Desiccant and powered moisture-control devices work differently. Desiccant has finite capacity and needs replacement or regeneration as directed; a powered product depends on power and approved installation. Neither corrects a leaking building or makes a flood-risk location appropriate. Keep cables, mounting and ventilation consistent with the manufacturer’s instructions. A quick condition review Check What to record Interior conditions Humidity trend and evidence of condensation or a leak. Equipment surfaces New rust, unusual staining, moisture or packaging damage. Moisture control Service date and whether a powered unit still functions. Enclosure condition Door closure, seal condition where fitted and exterior corrosion. Avoid long-term storage in a damp soft case or with unapproved materials that can hold moisture against the firearm. The care routine must suit the actual finish and stock material. Check conditions again after a plumbing leak, prolonged outage or a move; the previous room’s routine may not transfer to the new location. Keys, codes, backup access and changing household risk A secure enclosure with a visible backup key or widely shared code has a weak access policy. Decide which adults are authorized, keep backup access separate and review the list when circumstances change. Children, visitors and a person experiencing an emotional crisis can change the household’s risk even when the storage hardware is unchanged. Electronic, mechanical and biometric locks have different maintenance and usability considerations. Follow the lock manual, including approved battery types, replacement intervals and documented recovery procedures. A biometric feature is not a promise that it will recognize every user in every condition. Confirm what happens after a power or battery problem before relying on it. A suitable accessibility review includes vision, dexterity, reaching the lock and understanding its feedback. Conduct normal access checks with the enclosure empty when appropriate, without turning a household demonstration into firearm handling. The goal is a reliable authorized-access routine while preventing access by everyone else. If household risks escalate, consider a lawful temporary storage arrangement with an appropriate provider. Rules about transfers and custody vary. Plan this option while there is time to verify it rather than leaving equipment with an unprepared friend during a crisis. Evacuation, shared housing and destination storage Normal storage may not be available after a hurricane, fire or displacement. Decide beforehand whether equipment will remain in a secured lawful location or be moved under applicable transport rules. A vehicle is not a substitute for ordinary home storage: heat, theft and unauthorized access are different concerns there. Verify the destination’s rules before travel. Shelters, hotels, other households and jurisdictions can have restrictions or lack suitable storage. Keep firearms apart from shared emergency supplies and children’s belongings. Do not delay an urgent evacuation to solve a storage problem that should have been planned beforehand. For apartment and trailer living, a modest enclosure that can be installed appropriately may be more workable than a large safe chosen only for capacity. Consider landlord permission, structural support, flood exposure and destination options together. Review the plan after a move and once per year; household access, equipment size and building conditions change. Finish with a simple record: storage model, installation completed, authorized access, last moisture check and a verified evacuation arrangement. That record turns a purchase into a functioning system and identifies the remaining work without assuming that owning a safe has solved every risk. Choose storage around the room and household Compare the installed arrangement, not just the advertised box. Measure the usable room, access path, door swing and actual interior space. Consider whether shelves, cases and other stored items reduce usable capacity. Plan an appropriate installation with the manufacturer and a qualified installer when structural attachment is involved; this guide does not supply anchoring or building-load specifications. Storage selection worksheet Constraint Question to resolve Available space Will the unit fit through the access route and open without blocking the household’s exit? Household access Who can use it, who must not have access, and what changes when a visitor or caregiver arrives? Power and keys What does the manufacturer specify for a depleted battery or unavailable key? Environment What care and monitoring does this exact unit require in this room? Serviceability Can the maker provide parts, instructions and support for the model? A large cabinet can become inconvenient if normal household activity obstructs its door. A smaller unit may serve the real collection better when it has a suitable location and documented access controls. Review the plan when the household changes instead of assuming the purchase permanently settles the question. Keep a storage handover and maintenance record Use a private storage sheet to distinguish equipment facts from household arrangements. Record model, official instructions, service contact, required consumables and the review date. Keep recovery information in an appropriately protected place that the authorized owner can reach; do not store the only recovery route inside the locked unit. For shared housing, agree who is responsible for checking access after visits, maintenance or a move. Discuss how necessary information is passed to an authorized helper during an illness or evacuation without casually sharing access with everyone. Document any professional service so a later problem is not guessed at from memory. After a move, reassess the new room and installation with the manufacturer rather than reusing assumptions from the old location. When changing an access arrangement, follow the product instructions and check that the authorized person can still use it. Keep proof of purchase and identifying records separate from public photographs and visible labels. Treat a lost key, unreliable lock or unknown access history as a reason to resolve the storage arrangement promptly. Check one enclosure: actual capacity, closure, permitted anchoring, backup-key security, lock service and interior moisture. Fix the weakest link before purchasing accessories. Keep firearms unloaded and locked with ammunition separately secured. Manufacturer-approved installation, controlled keys and periodic review are essential; neither concealment nor a child’s promise replaces storage. Keep equipment away from shared supplies and unauthorized people. Use a previously verified lawful storage alternative where available. Flood- or fire-exposed equipment needs assessment before reuse; do not assume the enclosure rating proves it is unaffected. Reassess keys, codes and backup access after guests, a move, separation, memory changes or a household crisis. Teach children to leave an unfamiliar firearm alone, while retaining adult responsibility for storage. Secure storage Choose storage around the room and household Keep a storage handover and maintenance record Define the access risks Account for children, visitors, burglary risk, shared housing and changing household circumstances. Compare the enclosure and lock Read the exact model’s security claims, installation instructions, dimensions and backup-access arrangements. Choose the location before purchase Consider flood exposure, floor loading, doorway clearance, usable access and installation permission. Review the complete system Check keys and codes, anchoring, moisture, actual capacity and destination storage during evacuation.

title: Flash flood
summary: Move to higher ground immediately if a flash-flood warning affects you or water is rising. Never cross flowing water on foot or in a vehicle. Leave low areas, canyons and basements without waiting to see how high the water gets.
text: Can I cross a shallow-looking road? Do not enter moving or uncertain floodwater on foot or in a vehicle. Depth, current and road damage are difficult to assess from the surface. Choose another route or a safer higher location before the crossing becomes your only option. A warning arrives while camping — now what? Move out of low channels and drainage paths promptly when safe. Conditions upstream can change your location quickly even without local rain. Keep the group together and carry only essentials that do not delay the move.  Wait for official clearance. Water may rise after rain stops or when storms occur upstream. A small-looking current can sweep away people and vehicles. Move uphill before the route fills; leave belongings behind. If trapped above floodwater, remain in a safe elevated position and signal your location. Do not attempt to swim a current or enter water to rescue property. Plan a route that avoids low crossings and can be used by everyone. Carry children only within the helper’s real ability and do not attempt improvised water rescues. Know where the family will regroup on higher ground. Flooding Get uphill Move away from streams, low roads and drainage channels. Turn around Do not drive across a flooded road; the roadbed may be missing. If trapped Call emergency services and move to a higher open level without becoming trapped in a closed attic. Follow routes Use current evacuation and road-closure instructions.

title: Flood cleanup & mold
summary: Do not enter an unsafe flooded building. Check structural, electrical, gas and contamination hazards before cleanup. Keep children and vulnerable people away, use suitable protection and stop if the work exceeds what can be done safely.
text: Electricity or gas is uncertain Stay out and request qualified assessment. Do not operate a breaker while standing in water. Cleanup causes breathing symptoms Leave exposure, seek appropriate care and reconsider who can safely do the work. Can I mix cleaners to make them stronger? No. Mixing bleach with ammonia or other cleaning products can produce dangerous gases. Follow a single product’s label.  Seek specialist advice for major contamination, sewage, structural damage or persistent mold. Keep disposal rules and insurer documentation in mind without delaying urgent protective action. Do not run a generator indoors or in a garage during cleanup. Avoid working alone in unstable structures. Respirators need correct fit and do not make an unsafe building safe. Keep the area isolated if equipment, clean water or safe entry cannot be obtained. Document damage from a safe location and prioritize drinking water, sanitation and a clean sleeping space. Delaying unsafe cleanup can be safer than entering without protection. People with asthma, lung disease or weakened immunity should avoid mold cleanup when possible. Keep children, pets and food away from contaminated materials. Assign shorter work sessions, rest and clean handwashing; a dust mask cannot resolve every exposure.  Confirm safe entry Do not enter standing water near electrical equipment or a structurally damaged building. Qualified assessment may be needed before work begins. Separate clean and dirty areas Create a clean place for drinking water, first aid and rest outside the work area. Keep flood-contaminated shoes and tools away from household supplies. Use suitable protection Wear protective boots, gloves and eye protection. Mold cleanup may need a properly fitting NIOSH-approved N95 or better respirator; it does not protect against gases. Dry and clean safely When safe, remove contaminated porous materials that cannot be cleaned and dry affected areas promptly. Follow product labels; never mix bleach with ammonia or other cleaners.

title: Flooding
summary: Move away from rising water to safe higher ground without crossing floodwater. Follow evacuation orders. Never walk, swim or drive through a flooded route. If trapped in a building, move to a higher level, avoid a closed attic, and call emergency services with your location.
text: Distance from floodwater is the first safety decision. My street is outside the mapped high-risk zone. Can I ignore a warning? No. A long-term flood-risk classification does not cancel current warnings or local evacuation orders. Water is entering the basement. Should I save appliances or switch off the power? Do not enter water to retrieve items or reach a breaker. Keep clear and ask the utility or an electrician for safe isolation. The rain stopped. Can I drive home? Only when the route is open and safe and any reentry restrictions are lifted. Water and road damage can remain after rain ends. Where can I look up my flood zone? Enter your address in the FEMA Flood Map Service Center linked above. This U.S. planning and insurance tool is separate from evacuation zones and current flooding. Where can I see water levels? Use NOAA’s National Water Prediction Service for U.S. gauge observations and forecasts. Check timestamps and coverage, and read local warnings separately. It cannot certify a safe road crossing. Make the first decision from the water, not the map Flooding can build slowly or arrive with little warning. It can happen while the rain is falling somewhere else. If rising water threatens you, move toward a safe higher location immediately; do not wait for an app to confirm what you can already see. Staying out of the water is the central rule. Choose the safest reachable place LOW GROUND + DRY ESCAPE Move promptly to safe higher ground. Follow evacuation directions and take essentials already at hand. WATER ACROSS THE ROUTE Stop. Do not test the depth, walk through, or follow another vehicle. Turn around if you can do so safely. BUILDING CUT OFF Use the highest accessible safe level if water is rising. Do not enter a closed attic; call for help. ALREADY SAFELY ABOVE THE FLOOD Stay away from the water, keep warnings on and follow instructions. Do not travel into the affected area. Use the condition that applies; these are alternatives, not steps to follow in sequence. This is a protective-action diagram, not a route map. Current warnings, evacuation orders and visible hazards take priority over a saved plan. No safe crossing depth Do not use depth estimates, vehicle size, swimming ability or a map color to justify entering floodwater. Hidden road damage, current and electrical hazards can make appearances misleading. Use flood-risk maps and live forecasts for different jobs FEMA · Flood Map Service Center Find your U.S. flood zone by address. FEMA’s official flood-hazard maps support insurance, planning and floodplain management. They are NOT evacuation zones or a real-time flooding map. FEMA / NFIP · Flood zones and maps FEMA / NFIP explains flood-zone labels. A lower-risk or unmapped-looking location does not establish zero flood risk. National Weather Service · Local forecasts and active alerts Read current U.S. flood and flash-flood warnings and your local forecast. Search your location and open the full warning, not just the map color. NOAA · National Water Prediction Service NOAA’s U.S. river and water portal provides gauge observations, forecasts and available flood-inundation layers. Check the location, units, observation time, forecast time and layer legend. National Weather Service · NWPS product and users guide (PDF) Explains NWPS map layers, hydrographs, observations and forecasts. Some gauges or layers may be unavailable, stale or outside the area you need. For a planning check, search your home, school or workplace in FEMA’s Map Service Center, confirm the map covers the correct location, and save the map date with your notes. Ask the local floodplain administrator if the boundary or coverage is unclear. Then separately identify local evacuation instructions, higher ground and road-closure information. A gauge is not a road inspection A river gauge describes its measurement location; a forecast is a prediction. Neither proves that a particular street, bridge or underpass is safe. Missing data and areas without mapped flooding are not an all-clear. Never enter water because a map appears reassuring. Outside U.S. coverage, find equivalent tools from your national weather or hydrology service and local disaster authority. An overseas map or a nearby river’s graph cannot substitute for information about your location. Read alerts and choose an early departure trigger What the U.S. warning language means Notice Action Flood watch Flooding is possible. Check the forecast, prepare transport and supplies, and be ready to act. Flood warning Flooding is occurring or imminent. Read the location and protective instructions and act. Flash-flood warning Rapid flooding is occurring or imminent. If in a flood-prone area, move immediately to higher ground. Evacuation order Follow the local order and specified route or destination. Do not wait for water to reach the doorstep. Osprey planning worksheet: write down which warning or official instruction starts your departure, who receives it, and what happens if that person is away. Choose the higher-ground destination and a backup before rain begins. Identify the point at which a route is no longer usable; any floodwater or closure means you do not use that route. For river flooding, keep following forecasts even after local rain stops. For sudden flash flooding, use the short response guide below. Storm surge needs a coastal evacuation plan made before the water arrives. Flash flood: the fast-response brief Storm surge: coastal evacuation decisions Prepare before the route is threatened Pack food, safe water, medicines, lights, charging equipment and essential documents before an evacuation becomes urgent. Include children’s and pets’ needs. Identify low spots, underpasses, stream crossings and roads that commonly flood along your usual journeys. Know a safer destination and more than one possible route. Keep documents in a water-resistant container and save copies securely. Charge devices and keep a battery radio available. Move valuables only while it is safe and time allows. Sandbags and property protection must never delay leaving. Osprey practice exercise: starting from a normal evening at home, identify who finds the alert, who calls the pickup driver and who carries essentials. Walk the indoor exit route while conditions are safe. Check whether the plan still works in darkness or if the usual driver is at work. Change any step that depends on a single missing person or device. Prepare buildings before the emergency Ask qualified professionals about drainage, backflow prevention, pumps and building-level risk reduction. During flooding, do not enter a wet basement to save a pump or reach electrical controls. Property protection is not a reason to remain in danger. Make the plan usable for everyone Flood departure plans need to reflect how people actually move and communicate. Include the person who needs assistance in the decisions. Review accessible exits, transport, medication and equipment with caregivers, building management and local emergency services before the threat develops. Plan an alternative if a helper, vehicle or normal route is unavailable. Osprey household check Question Complete answer Who needs help leaving? Name the person’s requested support, the primary helper and a backup. What must travel with them? List essential medicines, access aids, communication aids and medical information. Can everyone use the exit? Check the route with the person who uses it; arrange an accessible alternative in advance. Where can everyone stay? Confirm accessibility, equipment needs and arrangements for pets and service animals. Do not rely on an assistance registry as your only plan; responders may be delayed. If you need help now because a flood is threatening, contact emergency services and explain your location and what assistance is needed. If the danger is not immediate, use local transport or emergency-management contacts to resolve the arrangements early. American Red Cross · Inclusive preparedness resources Red Cross planning prompts for disability-related access, support networks, communication and evacuation. If water cuts you off, change the plan In a building with dangerously rising water, move to the highest accessible level and call emergency services. Do not climb into a closed attic where rising water could trap you. Go onto the roof only if necessary and signal for help. Do not enter floodwater to retrieve a vehicle, equipment or belongings. If a vehicle is trapped in rapidly moving water, Ready.gov advises staying inside; if water is rising inside, seek refuge on the roof. Contact emergency services if possible. This is an emergency fallback, not permission to drive into water or attempt a water rescue. Osprey emergency-call prompt “We are at [address or landmark], on [floor or vehicle location]. There are [number] people. Water is [where it is now] and [rising or unknown]. We need [mobility, medical or other assistance]. My callback number is [number].” Answer the dispatcher’s questions and follow their instructions. If the call cannot connect, keep trying when possible, use a safe visible signal and conserve phone power. Stay with your group in the safest accessible location. Do not send someone into the water to look for a signal or improvise a rescue. No response time can be assumed. Wait for reentry, then check hazards before cleanup Receding water does not clear a building or a road. Wait for authorities to permit return, obey barriers and avoid unnecessary trips through affected areas. Do not enter a flood-damaged building until it has been declared safe. Water can weaken floors, walls and other structures. Reentry is a sequence of separate checks AREA REOPENED? If not, stay out. Follow official notices rather than the absence of visible water. BUILDING SAFE? Structural damage, gas smells or remaining floodwater require stopping and qualified assessment. ELECTRICAL SYSTEM CHECKED? Stay out of water near electricity. Wet circuits and equipment need qualified inspection before use. SAFE TO BEGIN LIMITED CLEANUP? Use health guidance, suitable protective equipment and help; stop if conditions or your health worsen. A positive answer to one question does not answer the next. This checklist cannot certify a building, utility or appliance. Never stand in water to turn power on or off. Have the utility or a qualified electrician deal with inaccessible controls and damaged wiring. An appliance that looks dry may still need inspection. Photograph damage only from safe positions, then ask the insurer what records are needed. Protect health during the recovery days Floodwater can carry sewage, chemicals and sharp debris. Keep children and pets away. If skin contacts it, wash with soap and clean water as soon as possible. Seek medical attention for contaminated puncture wounds, embedded debris or signs of infection such as increasing redness, swelling, pain or fever. Use the local drinking-water advisory for drinking, food preparation and hygiene. Do not assume the tap is safe because service has returned. Discard food contaminated by floodwater and check the separate guidance for food affected by power loss. Never taste food to decide whether it is safe. Keep generators outside and at least 20 feet from windows, doors and vents. Never run fuel-burning equipment in a home, garage or enclosed shelter. Osprey recovery worksheet: list safe accommodation, drinking water, essential care, transport and a working phone contact first. Record damage and expenses separately. Decide what requires a professional and what can safely wait. Arrange someone to check in during cleanup, and stop for exhaustion, illness, new hazards or renewed warnings. Flood cleanup and when to stop Food safety after an outage Downed power lines Keep monitoring warnings, river forecasts and local closures from your safe location. Return only when authorities permit it, and treat building, electrical, water and cleanup safety as separate checks. Floodwater can arrive from upstream rain, and roads may fail beneath it. Never interpret a flood-zone map, gauge reading, navigation route or another driver’s crossing as proof that a road is safe. Move to safer higher ground while you have a dry route. If routes are already flooded, stay out of the water and use the safest accessible elevated location. Try emergency services, give a precise location and signal safely. Do not improvise a crossing because assistance is delayed. Assign an adult to each child or person requesting help. Keep pets secured and access aids with their users. Count everyone at departure and arrival. A helper should not enter floodwater to collect belongings or reach another household. Flooding flood maps higher ground river forecast flood warning evacuation Get out of the water’s path Leave low ground before routes flood. If water is already blocking your route, do not cross it. Read the current warning Check the affected area, issue time, instructions and road closures. A familiar road can become impassable quickly. Keep people away from hazards Keep children and pets out of floodwater and away from drains, culverts, electrical equipment and damaged structures. If trapped, ask for help Give emergency services your exact location, floor, number of people and access or medical needs. Move higher if water threatens.

title: Food safety after power loss
summary: Keep refrigerator and freezer doors closed. Without power, a refrigerator keeps food safe for about 4 hours; a full freezer about 48 hours and a half-full freezer about 24 hours. Never taste food to test safety. Use official discard guidance and a thermometer.
text: Should I open the refrigerator to check? Keep doors closed as much as possible. Use the outage time and a reliable food thermometer rather than repeated inspection. Record the temperature if it can be checked without prolonged opening; smell and taste do not prove safety. What can move to a cooler? Use a clean insulated container and enough ice or cold packs to maintain a safe temperature. Keep raw meat separated from ready-to-eat food. If safe cooling cannot be maintained, switch to shelf-stable food rather than stretching a doubtful supply. Start a time and temperature record The useful evidence is time and temperature, not whether an appliance light works or a carton still smells normal. Write down when power failed. Keep refrigerator and freezer doors closed, and use appliance thermometers. Normal targets are 40°F (4°C) or below in the refrigerator and 0°F (−18°C) or below in the freezer. Outage holding times with doors kept closed Refrigerator About 4 hours without power. Plan a cold-source transfer before this limit if the outage continues. Full freezer About 48 hours. Keep it closed; assess actual food condition when making recovery decisions. Half-full freezer About 24 hours. Less stored cold means a shorter approximate holding period. CDC closed-door guidance. These are planning limits, not a guarantee after opening doors, flooding, or other unsafe conditions. Record what is known and what is uncertain. If you discover the outage only after returning home, do not invent a start time. A restoration message or a working fridge cannot prove the food stayed within safe conditions while you were away. Understand the four-hour and two-hour rules The four-hour refrigerator figure describes food in a closed refrigerator after power loss. It is not permission to leave perishable food on a warm counter for four hours. The item-by-item FoodSafety.gov chart uses exposure above 40°F for more than two hours for many refrigerated perishables. These rules describe different conditions. Use the rule that matches the evidence What you know How to use it Closed fridge, outage time known, no added cold source Use the outage guidance; discard refrigerated perishables after four hours without power. Food is measured above 40°F for more than two hours Use the item-specific FoodSafety.gov chart; many perishables must be discarded. Cooler or fridge has an added cold source Measure and maintain safe temperatures; ice being present is not sufficient evidence on its own. Frozen food still has ice crystals or is 40°F or below Many items can be refrozen or cooked, subject to the item-specific chart. Time or temperature history is uncertain Do not taste-test or guess; use conservative discard decisions for suspect perishables. Cooking is not a rescue plan for unsafe storage Do not plan to save questionable perishable food by cooking it after an unsafe time or temperature history. Make the storage decision first, then cook only food that is still safe to use. Prepare the cooler before the deadline If a continuing outage makes a transfer necessary and you have a suitable cooler and cold source, organize the move before the refrigerator’s holding time is exhausted. Get the cooler, ice or frozen packs, thermometer, and meal plan ready first so the door need not remain open while you search for supplies. Choose the food that can still be safely kept and that the household will realistically use. Place it in the cooler with enough ice or another suitable cold source to maintain 40°F or below. Keep raw foods contained so they cannot leak onto ready-to-eat food. Use the thermometer to check conditions, and note the transfer time. Open the cooler only as needed. Recheck temperature and replace the cold source as necessary. Do not assume an insulated shopping bag will perform like a properly managed cooler. A large purchase of ice may be wasted if the household has no suitable container, no thermometer, or no safe place to collect it. Plan around what you can maintain rather than around a one-time cold feeling. Assess foods by type, not one blanket rule Selected examples from the official refrigerated-food chart Food type After more than two hours above 40°F Raw or cooked meat, poultry, fish; leftovers Discard. Milk, yogurt, eggs, soft or shredded cheeses Discard. Cooked rice or pasta; cut produce Discard. Uncut fresh fruit or vegetables Generally keep under the chart, if otherwise uncontaminated and suitable. Bread, tortillas, peanut butter Generally keep under the chart, if otherwise uncontaminated and suitable. This short selection is a navigation aid, not the complete official chart. Use the full reference for the particular food, including cheese, sauces, produce, frozen meals, and ice cream. Follow product labels as well. “Shelf-stable” before opening does not mean the opened product can be kept without refrigeration. Avoid mixing discard food back into the normal pantry or freezer. Keep it separate, document losses if useful for insurance, and dispose of it appropriately. Make the safe meal plan from what remains instead of repeatedly reconsidering the same questionable items. Plan meals that do not create another cold-storage problem Choose familiar foods that meet the household’s needs and can be eaten in one sitting or safely stored after opening. A single-portion package can be more practical than a large container when you cannot keep leftovers cold. Check allergies, chewing or swallowing needs, infant feeding, and any prescribed dietary requirements. Keep a manual opener with the pantry food that needs it. Write a short sequence of meals rather than repeatedly opening the fridge to browse. Include foods needing little preparation water, and confirm drinking water is suitable for any food preparation. Use outdoor cooking equipment only in an appropriate outdoor setup according to its instructions. Do not bring it indoors because the kitchen has no power. Handle cold food only when the next action is ready: serve, transfer to a maintained cooler, or discard. Example planning exercise: build one day of no-cook meals from your ordinary pantry and check the labels for storage after opening. Note the water, utensils, opener, and cleanup each meal requires. Replace any meal that leaves a large unmanageable refrigerated remainder. This is an editorial planning exercise, not a universal diet or nutrition prescription. Floodwater and contamination change the decision The power-outage clock is irrelevant if food has been contaminated by floodwater. CDC advises throwing away food that may have contacted flood or storm water and food in packaging that is not waterproof. Also reject damaged, bulging, or open containers as directed in the official guidance. Keep potentially contaminated packaging away from clean meal-preparation areas. Do not open a questionable container just to investigate its smell, and do not give rejected food to pets. Children and dependent adults need the same separation from uncertain food as other household members. Cleaning has its own instructions CDC provides specific procedures for food-contact surfaces and certain commercially packaged foods after flooding. Follow those procedures exactly where applicable; this guide does not turn a quick wipe or a rinsed package into evidence of safety. If the kitchen itself was flooded or affected by sewage, restore safe preparation conditions before using it. A working refrigerator does not make a contaminated counter, utensil, or water supply suitable for food preparation. Restart, replenish, and reduce the next loss After power returns, assess food using the recorded time, measured temperature, and the official item-specific chart. Clean affected appliance surfaces following appropriate instructions and remove rejected food. Check that the refrigerator and freezer actually return to their normal temperatures before relying on them. Restock gradually, prioritizing food the household will use and emergency meals that are simple to prepare. Replace used ice packs and review the thermometer, cooler, and meal arrangements. Keep a brief record of the outage: start time, transfers, temperatures, and the biggest difficulty. If the problem was not having an opener or not knowing what to eat without cooking, fix that before buying a larger appliance. If the same fridge was opened by several people, agree a household rule and post the next planned meal. Medicines, infant feeding, and powered medical equipment require their own guidance. Do not apply the food chart to medicine stability or decide that a medically important supply is unusable without appropriate advice. Use the care provider, pharmacist, and product instructions as applicable. Power outage checklist Water outage Long-duration blackout Clean appliances and replace spoiled supplies. Keep thermometers available before the next outage. Do not serve questionable food to people or pets. Track the time power stopped and use a fridge thermometer if available. If time or temperature is unknown, discard suspect perishable food and use shelf-stable food. Spend scarce fuel on safe water and essential cooking rather than trying to rescue unsafe food. Plan a safe meal for each person before using the most vulnerable refrigerated food. Include infant feeding and food allergies. Keep the food decision separate from medicine storage: a clinician or pharmacist must advise on a specific medicine. Food & water Start a time and temperature record Understand the four-hour and two-hour rules Prepare the cooler before the deadline Assess foods by type, not one blanket rule Plan meals that do not create another cold-storage problem Floodwater and contamination change the decision Restart, replenish, and reduce the next loss Note the time Record when power failed and avoid opening cold storage. Use temperatures Check appliance and food temperatures when safe; appearance and smell do not prove safety. Discard risky food After 4 hours without power or another cold source, discard refrigerated perishables such as meat, eggs and leftovers. Check frozen food Food with ice crystals or at 40°F or below can generally be refrozen or cooked; use official food-specific charts.

title: Food when cooking is unavailable
summary: Use safe ready-to-eat food, protect drinking water and keep hands and utensils clean. Do not run a camping stove, grill or charcoal indoors. Check food-storage times and temperatures after power loss; never taste suspect food to decide whether it is safe. Plan around dietary and medical needs.
text: Use safe ready-to-eat food, protect drinking water and keep hands and utensils clean. Do not run a camping stove, grill or charcoal indoors. Check food-storage times and temperatures after power loss; never taste suspect food to decide whether it is safe. Plan around dietary and medical needs.  Can everyone eat the stored food? Check allergies, chewing or swallowing limitations, infant feeding and the need for safe water. Prefer foods the household already eats. A no-cook food still needs safe storage and handling after opening. What if there is no safe refrigeration? Choose shelf-stable portions that can be used without keeping unsafe leftovers. Keep opened food away from heat, insects and contamination. Do not make a meal plan depend on a working refrigerator when power is uncertain.  Replenish through a verified reachable source before supplies become critical. Set aside easy-to-carry food for movement and avoid creating a plan that depends entirely on fuel or refrigeration. Food that looks and smells normal can still be unsafe. Do not salvage leaking, swollen or flood-contaminated packaging. Use known safe shelf-stable food already present and a written meal inventory. If no safe cooking position exists, choose food that does not need cooking rather than improvising an indoor flame. Assign portions around actual dietary needs and available safe drinking water. A manual opener should be usable by the person preparing food. Keep pet food and special feeding supplies included rather than assuming a generic emergency meal works for everyone. no stove no cooking food blackout cold emergency meals Inventory safe food Count shelf-stable items that can be eaten without heating and identify a manual opener. Separate suspect refrigerated food from safe supplies. Plan small portions Open only what can be eaten safely when refrigeration is unavailable. Read the label for storage after opening. Protect water and hygiene Use safe water for food and essential washing. Keep preparation surfaces separate from toilet waste and dirty containers. Keep combustion outside Use cooking equipment only in the location and manner its instructions allow. Never burn charcoal or use a camp stove inside a room, garage or enclosed balcony. Include special needs Plan for infants, allergies, diabetes, swallowing difficulty and pets. Do not change prescribed diets or infant formula preparation without qualified advice.

title: Frozen and burst pipes
summary: A frozen pipe may have little or no flow; a burst pipe is a leak emergency. Keep people away from water near electricity. Stop a leak at a known, permitted household shutoff only if you can reach it safely, then contact the building manager or a qualified plumber. Never use a flame to thaw plumbing.
text: Active leak and a known permitted valve is safely reachable Isolate the water and call for repair. Active leak but unsafe or uncertain access Stay clear and request isolation help. No flow but no visible leak Check for a wider outage; use only limited, safe warming of an accessible intact pipe. Frozen area is hidden or warming is unsuccessful Stop and use a qualified plumber. Water returns after a wider service interruption Check the utility’s water-quality and restart instructions. Should every tap drip? No. Ask the local utility which fixture, if any, should drip. Follow restrictions and do not leave running water in an empty building. Can a leak appear after thawing? Yes. Check accessible areas after flow returns and report fresh wetness. Can tape repair a break? Do not rely on a makeshift patch to restore pressurized service. Use a qualified plumber. Work out which problem you have Cold weather and low flow are clues, not a diagnosis. A single affected tap can indicate a local problem; several affected homes can suggest a utility interruption. Ask a neighbor or building manager and check official outage information, without delaying action on a visible leak. Briefly check other accessible taps, then close those you are not monitoring. Choose the safe pipe response Danger present? Water near electricity or a sagging ceiling: stay clear and seek emergency help. Water escaping? Use a known, permitted household shutoff only if safely reachable; call for repair. No visible leak? Check utility and building outages before assuming freezing. Frozen section uncertain? Hidden, inaccessible, damaged, or hard to assess: use a qualified plumber. Choose the condition that applies; these cards are alternatives, not steps to perform in sequence. This is a decision aid, not permission to operate shared or utility valves. Tell the responder where the problem is, when it began, and whether water is near electricity. You do not need to locate the exact break first. An active leak: isolate it without entering danger Keep people and pets away from the wet area. Warn nearby occupants if water may reach their space. Close the correct household shutoff only when you know its operation, have permission, and can reach it safely. Do not force it. If access is unsafe or uncertain, or isolation fails, request help from the building contact, utility, or plumber. Leave the supply off pending repair advice. Tell the household, and ask the professional about affected heating or hot-water equipment. Shared buildings and utility valves Renters should use only a valve they have been shown and may operate. Do not operate shared mains, fire-sprinkler valves, street valves, or unfamiliar meter fittings. Utility rules about customer-operated valves are location-specific. Never enter standing water to reach an electrical panel. Do not touch wet electrical equipment or use a mains-powered appliance in the wet area. If power must be isolated but the route or panel is unsafe, have the electricity provider or an electrician handle it. Wet equipment needs assessment before reuse. Suspected freezing with no visible leak Consider gentle warming only when the suspected section is visible, safely accessible, apparently intact, and local or building instructions allow it. Know who can isolate the water and stay present: an unseen crack may appear during thawing. Otherwise, use a qualified plumber. For an intact suspected frozen line, keep the affected faucet open while it is being thawed, as advised by the utility or plumber. This is different from leaving multiple taps running unattended. Gently warm the surrounding room with the normal heating system. Warm towels around an accessible pipe may help. Avoid scalding water and surfaces. Never use a torch, open flame, fuel-burning heater, or improvised electrical thawing equipment. Do not use electric thawing devices in standing water or a wet area. Do not cut into walls, dismantle joints, strike the pipe, or attempt to thaw underground or concealed plumbing. If water starts escaping, stop warming and switch to the leak response. If access is uncertain or flow does not return, use a licensed or otherwise locally qualified plumber. Do not leave a warming attempt unattended or treat restored flow as proof that nothing cracked. Before the next freeze Make vulnerable plumbing a maintenance job before severe weather. Exterior-wall pipes and unheated spaces deserve attention. Have insulation and any pipe-heating product selected for the actual pipe and location and installed according to the manufacturer’s directions. Disconnect outdoor hoses and arrange proper winterization of exterior taps and irrigation. The correct draining steps depend on the installation. Keep normal indoor heat steady. If away during cold weather, the Red Cross recommends leaving heat on at no less than 55°F / 13°C; that is a minimum precaution, not a guarantee for every building. Open under-sink cabinet doors to let room heat circulate where appropriate. Move cleaners and other hazards out of children’s and pets’ reach. Keep a garage containing water pipes closed. Arrange repairs to drafts near plumbing without blocking required ventilation. Ask the local utility whether a controlled drip is appropriate and allowed during the particular freeze. Do not override water restrictions or leave running water unattended in an empty building. If heat fails A thermostat setting cannot protect pipes when the heating system is not working. Contact the building manager or heating service and make a safe place-to-stay plan; plumbing winterization may require a professional. Manage the wait and essential needs Use this planning checklist for a repair delay; it does not predict a response time. Choose one household contact. Record the job number, responder, update time, and isolation instructions. Tell the responder if there is no functioning toilet, no safe drinking water, or a water-dependent care need. Ask what temporary arrangements are available. Use small, manageable stored-water containers. Decide who can collect water and who can carry it; do not assume everyone can lift a large container or use stairs. Arrange another place to stay if cold, water damage, or access makes the home unsafe. In an apartment, ask which facilities remain usable and whether a leak affects other units. Do not test communal valves yourself. A returning supply can still be subject to a boil-water, do-not-drink, or do-not-use notice. Follow the exact local advisory. Boiling does not solve chemical contamination. The water-outage and emergency-hygiene guides cover the separate problem of living without usable tap water. Recovery starts after the leak is controlled Have damaged plumbing repaired and ask how the supply should be restored and checked. Observe accessible repaired areas when service returns; report renewed wetness or unexplained flow promptly. Do not repeatedly reopen the supply to see whether a broken line has improved. Once safe, act promptly on moisture. EPA advises drying wet materials within 24–48 hours to reduce mold growth. A surface wipe cannot establish that hidden spaces or soaked materials are dry; arrange restoration help when needed. Photograph damage from safe locations, record when it was discovered, and keep repair and temporary-living receipts. Contact the insurer or landlord about documentation.
