Do not switch on wet appliances, sockets, or heating equipment to speed drying. Obtain electrical advice first. Ask for restoration help for widespread or concealed wetting, contaminated water, persistent dampness, or mold. Do not cover damp surfaces with paint or new finishes. Record the repair and the cause the professional identified. Schedule the prevention work rather than assuming warmer weather fixed the underlying problem. Make a five-minute household pipe card This Osprey Zero worksheet is a planning aid, not a plumbing procedure. Fill it in with the landlord, utility, or plumber and keep it accessible. Suggested pipe-card fields Record Include Permitted shutoff Exact location, a photo or label, who may operate it, and any access barrier. Emergency contacts Building manager, water utility, plumber, and electricity provider. Known vulnerable areas Previously frozen taps or pipes and any maintenance already recommended. Household backup Where safe water is stored, an accessible toilet option, and a warm place to stay. Away-from-home plan Who can check the property and how they can reach the person responsible for repairs. Arrange safer valve access before winter if operation requires unusual force or entry into a cramped space. Red Cross pipe-freeze checklist National preparation and thawing guidance; local utility directions take priority. Seattle utility shutoff example Seattle-specific valve permissions, illustrating why rules must be checked locally. EPA moisture recovery guide Drying, moisture control, and when professional help may be needed. Update the pipe card after repair and arrange recommended prevention work. Watch for fresh wetness, renewed leaks during thawing, and rooms losing heat. If help is delayed, prioritize safe water and somewhere warm to stay. Keep a safely isolated leaking supply off and avoid improvised repairs. Agree who calls for help, assists anyone with limited mobility, and keeps children and pets away. Share temporary toilet and care arrangements. frozen pipes burst pipe water shutoff winter plumbing leaking pipe renter thawing water damage Check for danger Stay out of water near electricity and away from sagging ceilings. Call emergency services for an immediate threat to people. Look for a leak Escaping water needs isolation and repair. Reduced flow without a visible leak needs outage checks and assessment for freezing. Call the right responder Contact the building manager if you rent; otherwise a qualified plumber for household plumbing or the utility for supply problems. Use safe water Use stored safe water and check for water-quality advisories.

title: FRS, GMRS and amateur radio: choosing a household system
summary: Choose radios around who needs to use them, the legal service, certification and actual tested coverage. More advertised power or a longer feature list does not guarantee better household communication.
text: A household choice checklist Can every intended user operate the device lawfully? Is the hardware certified for the service? Does it work inside your building, at your meeting point and along the planned route? Can it be recharged during an outage? Are controls readable and usable with gloves or limited dexterity? Answer these before selecting a product. Licensing is not the only constraint A license does not authorize any radio on any service. Check equipment, channels and operating conditions separately. In U.S. GMRS, the rules specify which family members can operate under an individual’s license; do not assume unrelated friends are covered. Verify the current rule before sharing equipment. Borrow or buy a suitable basic system and perform a lawful coverage test at three actual locations before buying additional radios. Radio laws and equipment approvals vary by country. Marketing range figures are not a safety guarantee. Use phone texts, agreed meeting points and written check-in times if a lawful radio system is not available. If radio contact fails, follow the missed-contact plan rather than repeatedly draining batteries. Plan accessible controls and earpieces where useful. Do not put the entire household’s communications plan behind one person’s technical knowledge or license. Two-way radios FRS GMRS amateur radio Define the task Decide whether you need short local check-ins, a vehicle-to-house link or a trained amateur-radio activity. Note buildings, terrain and who must operate independently. Check service rules For U.S. FRS use certified equipment. For GMRS verify equipment certification and license coverage. Amateur operation has separate requirements; do not confuse services because channel numbers look similar. Test compatibility Match channel or frequency and relevant receiving settings on lawful compatible devices. Different manufacturers’ numbering or preset lists may differ. Budget for complete use Include batteries, chargers, labels, training and a backup method. Spend on demonstrated coverage and usability rather than an untested range claim.

title: Generator safety
summary: Operate a portable generator outdoors at least 20 feet from doors, windows and vents, with exhaust directed away from buildings. Never run it in a home, garage or enclosed space. Use working CO alarms and never connect a generator to a wall outlet.
text: Where is the exhaust going? Check the generator’s position relative to every nearby opening, not just your own back door. Outdoor exhaust can enter neighboring buildings. Keep the required separation and point exhaust away; a garage with its door open is still an unsafe location. Can I connect it to a household outlet? Never feed power into a wall outlet. Backfeeding can endanger utility workers and others. Household circuit connections need appropriate installed transfer equipment and qualified electrical work. Use equipment and cords according to the actual manufacturer’s instructions. First decide whether a generator fits your home A portable fuel-burning generator is an outdoor engine, not an indoor power bank. Before considering wattage, determine whether your property has a genuinely suitable operating position, a safe connection method, permitted fuel storage, and someone capable of following the instructions. If any of these are missing, the household needs a different backup plan. Four gates before starting Position An outdoor location with the required separation from all nearby doors, windows, and vents. Connection Suitable intact cords or professionally installed transfer equipment; no connection through a wall outlet. Operation Manufacturer-approved setup, dry conditions, working CO alarms, and an adult who understands shutdown. Fuel Correct fuel, approved storage, and a safe cool-down and refueling routine. This is a planning checklist, not an installation diagram or a substitute for the equipment manual. A balcony, garage, shared corridor, or partly enclosed courtyard may not provide a safe or permitted location. In dense housing, consider neighbors’ openings and shared spaces. Rental rules and local fire restrictions can matter as well. If the space is unsuitable, do not try to solve the problem with an improvised exhaust hose or an open door. Plan the location before the weather turns bad CDC advises outdoor operation at least 20 feet from doors, windows, and vents. Check every occupied building nearby, including neighbors. Direct exhaust away from buildings and follow any greater manufacturer separation requirement. The minimum distance is not a guarantee that exhaust can never re-enter a building. Check the whole route from generator to appliance. A safe generator position is not useful if the available cord is too short or cannot be routed safely. Keep entrances and escape routes clear. Prevent children and pets from reaching hot parts, fuel, or cords. Keep the unit dry using only an appropriate setup that preserves open airflow and follows its instructions. Do not move it into a garage when rain starts. Recheck placement when wind, nearby openings, parked vehicles, or household activity changes. No smell does not mean no carbon monoxide Carbon monoxide cannot be seen or smelled. A running fan or an open garage door does not make an enclosed location safe. If a CO alarm sounds or symptoms suggest exposure, get to fresh air immediately and seek emergency help. Know the difference between appliance and building power Two connection approaches, with important boundaries Approach What it requires What to avoid Direct appliance supply Compatible appliance, suitable outdoor cord, ratings and instructions checked Damaged plugs, overloaded cords, pinch points, wet connections, or improvised adapters. Household circuit supply Appropriate installed transfer equipment and qualified electrical work Plugging the generator into a wall outlet, male-to-male cords, or an improvised panel connection. Backfeeding means energizing building wiring through an unsafe connection such as a wall outlet. It can expose utility workers and other people to electrical danger. Switching a breaker off yourself is not a substitute for appropriate transfer equipment. This guide intentionally does not provide wiring or installation instructions. For direct appliance use, inspect the entire cord and its plugs before connecting. Match the cord and equipment ratings to the actual setup, including the total attached load and the manufacturer’s requirements. Do not assume an indoor power strip or a household extension lead is suitable simply because it fits the socket. Stop using damaged equipment rather than patching it during an outage. Choose a limited load plan List the appliances you intend to support, then use their actual labels and manuals to record running power and any starting demand. Motors and compressors can require additional power to start. Use the generator’s continuous and starting ratings correctly; a large advertised peak number is not a continuous operating allowance. A load sheet to prepare before an outage Record Example of the information needed Appliance and purpose Refrigerator: keeping food cold, rather than general household convenience. Running demand The appliance’s documented operating watts or current and voltage. Starting requirement Manufacturer information for a compressor or motor, where applicable. Connection requirements Suitable plug, cord, protection, and any equipment-specific restriction. Operating priority Which load stays connected and which can wait. Start with a smaller, verified group of loads rather than trying to reproduce normal household electricity. Follow the equipment instructions for starting, connecting, disconnecting, and shutting down. For powered medical care, compatibility and reliability must come from the care provider and device manufacturer; an informal load estimate is not enough. A battery may meet modest communications and lighting needs with less operational work. It still has output, capacity, charging, and storage limits. Choose equipment around the need you have verified, not around the largest number on a product listing. Fuel, heat, and the refueling routine Treat refueling as a separate task that requires time and attention. Turn the generator off and allow it to cool before adding fuel. Use the specified fuel and approved, properly labelled storage containers. Store fuel outside living areas and away from ignition sources; check the rules that apply to your property and fuel type. Before a planned session, check fuel and other maintenance items exactly as the manual specifies. Keep the manual and shutdown instructions accessible to the adult operating the unit. End the session using the prescribed shutdown sequence, then allow cool-down before refueling. Inspect for leaks or damage from a safe position. Do not restart suspect equipment. Record maintenance and replenishment needs instead of relying on memory. Do not store fuel beside a water heater or bring a fuel container into the household base. Keep food, drinking water, children’s supplies, and fuel clearly separated. Avoid buying more fuel than you can store legally and safely. Fuel availability during an outage is uncertain, so the plan also needs a non-generator fallback. Recognize a stop condition Stop using the setup when these conditions appear Condition Response CO alarm or possible exposure symptoms Move people to fresh air immediately; seek emergency help. Do not re-enter until cleared as safe. Wet or flooded setup Do not touch or operate unsafe electrical equipment; use a different backup and qualified assistance. Fuel leak, smoke, or damaged components Keep clear and follow emergency or manufacturer guidance; do not troubleshoot a running hazardous unit. No suitable outdoor position Leave the generator off; use batteries and the relocation plan for essential needs. Required load cannot be supported reliably Reduce nonessential demand or use a confirmed alternative for the essential need. A second capable adult should know where the instructions are and how to recognize a stop condition. Do not assign children to manage the generator. Alarms and automatic shutdown features supplement safe use; they do not make unsafe placement acceptable. Build a backup plan that works without the generator Write down what the household will do if the unit will not start, fuel is unavailable, rain makes the setup unusable, or a neighbor’s open window makes the position unsuitable. Include battery lighting, a modest charging plan, no-cook meals, and a confirmed alternative location for essential medical or temperature needs. Practice the manufacturer’s setup with a qualified person where necessary, in appropriate conditions and without disconnecting essential household systems. The useful result is an operator who can explain placement, connections, ratings, alarms, refueling, and shutdown. Buying equipment without that knowledge leaves the most important part of the backup incomplete. Power outage household plan Long-duration blackout Read the manufacturer instructions before a crisis. Plan weather protection that does not enclose the generator or obstruct exhaust. An open garage door does not make indoor generator operation safe. If there is no safe outdoor position, do not run the generator. Use battery lights and ration stored electrical power for medical needs and communications. Do not improvise a connection to household wiring or operate it indoors because the weather is bad. Keep children and pets away from the running equipment and fuel. Check working carbon-monoxide alarms near sleeping areas. One adult should control refueling and keep fuel storage separate from occupied rooms and escape routes. Backup power First decide whether a generator fits your home Plan the location before the weather turns bad Know the difference between appliance and building power Choose a limited load plan Fuel, heat, and the refueling routine Recognize a stop condition Build a backup plan that works without the generator Choose outdoor placement Keep the generator away from occupied buildings and openings, including neighbors. Connect safely Use rated cords as instructed; a building connection requires a professionally installed transfer switch. Refuel safely Shut down and let it cool before refueling. Store fuel safely outside living areas. Check CO alarms If an alarm sounds or symptoms occur, leave for fresh air and call emergency services.

title: Get-home planning: when the usual journey fails
summary: Choose a safe waiting place, a backup way home and a check-in plan before your commute fails. Getting home is a decision, not an instruction to walk through danger.
text: Your usual service stops? Check current conditions and the agreed waiting place before deciding to travel. The pedestrian route is unverified? Use the waiting or overnight alternative; a road route does not establish a walking route. You change destination? Send the new destination and next check-in privately to the agreed contact. Should a get-home plan always end at home? No. A confirmed safe waiting place or overnight destination may be more workable while travel conditions are unsafe. How much should the everyday bag hold? Enough for your realistic delay and care needs at a manageable mass. Measure it and keep larger reserves separately; do not assume a heavy pack makes an unsafe journey viable. Start with the journey you actually make Pick one recurring journey: work, school, a clinic or a family visit. Write the start, normal destination, transport method and likely times. List the places where the route depends on one service: a bridge, ferry, train line, lift, interchange or person providing a ride. This is a dependency map, not an instruction to replace every failed service with walking. For each dependency, name a reachable place to wait and an alternative destination. Confirm permission and accessibility with the relevant person or organization. A shop, station or public building may close; record an outside-opening-hours alternative. For a person using medication or assistive equipment, include the effect of a delay on essential care before estimating how far they could travel. A private route card Field Write down Regular journey Start, destination, normal service and usual times. Waiting place Address, permission, opening/access arrangements and alternate. Pickup Named helper, confirmed meeting point and limits on the arrangement. Overnight fallback A destination that has agreed to receive the person. Care handover Who covers dependents if the usual adult is delayed. Decide whether movement improves the situation Getting home is one option. Staying at a suitable waiting place, reaching a confirmed nearby host or delaying the journey can be more practical. Compare the conditions at your current place with those along the complete route and at the destination. Uncertainty about family does not make an unverified journey safer. Conditional travel decision Immediate danger here Move to a nearby safer position if the current place is hazardous; seek urgent assistance where available. Place suitable, route uncertain Use the agreed waiting arrangement, protect essential needs and gather current information. Route and destination confirmed Choose the transport that the person can actually use and tell the contact what has changed. Osprey Zero planning aid. These are conditional choices; current conditions and individual needs control the decision. The branches are alternatives, not a fixed sequence. Check weather, daylight, closures, legal access, physical ability and whether the intended destination can receive you. Do not ask a helper to cross the same hazard merely to collect you. If a route requires a bridge, check whether pedestrian access actually exists and remains usable. A navigation app’s vehicle estimate is not a walking assessment. Build a small delay kit around real needs The everyday bag supports a realistic delay rather than an imagined expedition. Start with daily care, communication, weather protection, a light and manageable drinking water. Carry suitable footwear when ordinary work shoes would make a verified pedestrian journey uncomfortable. Include food you can eat as packed and information you can read without a charged phone. Ordinary delay-kit trade-offs Need Useful decision Phone power Test the cable and battery with the actual device; record where they are kept. Weather layer Match season and waiting conditions, including a cool indoor space. Water Measure the filled container; water adds about one kilogram per litre. Care Follow individual storage needs and arrange a workable backup with the relevant provider. Information Keep addresses and numbers privately accessible without exposing unnecessary identifiers. Weigh the complete bag and test it during a normal, safe journey. If it conflicts with a mobility aid, childcare or manual work, change the carry method or load. Larger vehicle supplies can supplement it but should not contain the only essential contact or care information. Review the bag when work location, phone connector, season or household responsibilities change. Make check-ins specific enough to use Agree who receives the first update and who informs the rest of the household. A useful message gives your actual location, condition, intended action and next check-in. For example: “At the agreed office waiting room, okay, train service stopped, staying here while we check the alternate, next message at our agreed time.” Use your own arrangement; the example is not a universal timetable. Decide what a missed check-in means before a disruption. A delayed message might reflect battery or network failure. The contact should know which steps to take, whom to ask and when the circumstances justify seeking help. Avoid repeated speculative messages that change destinations without confirming them. If you leave the waiting place, update the contact with the new destination and arrival/check-in expectation. Keep routine updates private. Do not publish an empty-home announcement or a dependent person’s care details to a public feed. If communications fail, use the previously agreed plan and reassess conditions. There is no need to keep moving merely because a message has not been delivered. Plan the dependent-care handover A commute failure affects more than the traveler. List school pickup, an adult needing assistance, pets, time-sensitive care and any household member who cannot be left alone. Agree the permitted helper and confirm how the relevant organization verifies pickup or access. Record the helper’s limits: availability, transport capacity and whether they can provide the necessary care. Give the helper the minimum information required for the role and keep it current. Avoid making a child responsible for deciding whether to leave a school or meeting an unfamiliar driver. For an adult needing assistance, include their preferences and the equipment actually required. If the backup helper is unavailable, identify who can reassess the care arrangement without starting another unsafe journey. Rehearse the handover as a conversation while everyone is available. Ask the backup person to explain their role in their own words and locate the written information. Resolve gaps now rather than assuming a trusted relationship automatically supplies practical knowledge. Treat a stranded vehicle as its own decision A vehicle provides a different waiting environment from a transit stop. Use the applicable roadside and weather guidance for the actual situation. NHTSA’s winter guidance recommends staying with a stranded car, making it visible and managing carbon-monoxide risks. An active roadway, fire, rising water or another immediate hazard changes the assessment; the decision must account for the specific site. Keep the phone, essential medicines, suitable layers and useful light accessible rather than buried under luggage. Tell the contact the location and whether assistance is arranged. Do not use a planned urban walk as a blanket answer to rural roadside stranding. The vehicle’s position, traffic, weather, people and available help determine what is feasible. Vehicle breakdown Vehicle emergency kit Rehearse one failure and keep a dated card Choose a normal journey and imagine one dependency failing. Keep real services available while testing the plan. Find the written card, identify the waiting place and explain the care handover. Check the alternate destination’s agreement and accessibility rather than relying only on its address. Choose one journey and one failure, such as a stopped train or unavailable pickup. Name the first suitable waiting place and the reason it is suitable. Check the realistic carry load and daily care requirements. Draft a private update with location, intention and next check-in. Ask the contact what they would do after a missed update. Record one correction, an owner and a review date. Repeat after a work move, change in dependent care or transport schedule. Keep a short card with confirmed facts and a longer private plan if needed. The useful result is an arrangement another adult can understand, not a thick collection of untested routes. NHTSA · Winter driving Read the weather and stranded-vehicle guidance when a failed journey involves a car. Red Cross · Make a plan Use the household communication and meeting-place framework to coordinate the people affected by a disrupted journey. Choose one regular journey and identify the first safe waiting place, one backup destination and a person who knows the plan. Do not cross floodwater or enter restricted routes to shorten a journey. Avoid meeting arrangements that force someone else to travel into the same hazard. If transit and communications fail, use the previously agreed waiting place or backup destination if accessible and safe. Reassess conditions rather than setting off simply because messages are not arriving. Plan school pickup authority, care handover, mobility limits and pets left at home. Make sure your backup helper knows what they can realistically do and where their responsibility ends. get home bag commute disruption stranded at work Start with the journey you actually make Decide whether movement improves the situation Build a small delay kit around real needs Make check-ins specific enough to use Plan the dependent-care handover Treat a stranded vehicle as its own decision Rehearse one failure and keep a dated card Map the usual journey Identify where you depend on a bridge, transit line, lift, ferry or single road. List safe places you could wait near work, school and regular destinations. Choose alternatives Write down an alternate route, a pickup location and a place to stay if travel becomes unsafe. Confirm arrangements with the person who would help; an assumed ride is not a plan. Carry everyday essentials Keep comfortable shoes, weather protection, water, a small snack, a light, charging supplies and necessary personal items within realistic carrying limits. Agree on a check-in Set an out-of-area contact, a time to check in and what the household should do if a message does not arrive. Use plain location descriptions and avoid broadcasting sensitive details.

title: Go bag
summary: Pack a portable bag with the essentials you need to leave quickly: medicines, documents, contact information, water, food, light, phone power and weather-appropriate clothing. Keep it light enough to carry and a separate grab list for items used every day.
text: What is the right bag weight? The right load is one the actual person and helpers can manage with their mobility, care and transport needs. Test it safely; no universal percentage makes every bag suitable. Should I pack all household water in it? A home reserve and a carryable portion are different. Maintain adequate safe water planning while choosing a load that can actually move, and verify the next supply rather than pretending a small bottle covers every need. Pack for a destination, not an imagined wilderness A go-bag supports leaving an unsafe location and reaching a suitable place. Start by asking where you are likely to go, how you will travel, and what support is available there. A bag for a short vehicle trip to family differs from one that must be carried through stairs or on public transport. Neither should depend on sleeping outdoors in an unverified location. List the tasks the bag must help with: essential care, identification, communication, hydration, a suitable meal, weather protection, and basic hygiene. Add what the destination does not provide. Keep the bag’s role separate from the larger home reserve. No bag can compensate for an unsafe route or a destination that cannot accept the household. A useful packing order Protect essential needs Care items, mobility or communication aids, and the information needed to continue support. Support the journey Contacts, destination details, keys, carryable safe water, appropriate food, light, and phone power. Add manageable comfort Suitable clothing, hygiene and limited personal items after carrying needs are tested. Editorial planning aid. Actual hazards, access needs and current instructions control the decision. Use a core list, then personalize it A practical go-bag checklist Group Items to consider Check before packing Identity and information Suitable document copies, contact card, destination and route notes Keep sensitive information protected but accessible when needed. Care Medicines and care information, glasses, hearing or mobility supplies Storage conditions, refills, and equipment compatibility are individual. Journey Keys, charged phone, correct cable, light, manageable drinking water and food The person can use and carry them; food matches dietary needs. Weather and hygiene Suitable clothing, compact hygiene supplies, required personal care items Match the season, privacy needs, and the expected destination. Children and pets Necessary feeding, care, identification and transport items A caregiver can still assist the person while carrying the load. These are planning categories rather than a mandatory shopping list. Check what you own and remove items that do not support the journey or stay. For documents, consider what is actually needed to access care or accommodation. Do not put all irreplaceable originals into a bag that is routinely left unattended. Separate prepacked items from the last-minute grab list Some items are needed every day and cannot sit permanently in a bag. Write a short grab list for them: current medicines, glasses, the phone, keys, essential care equipment, and a pet carrier if not already positioned. Record where each is normally kept. A grab list must be short enough to use without searching every room. Attach the list to a place the responsible person actually looks, and keep a copy with the bag. Use clear labels for each person’s equipment and avoid transferring a shared item between several bags without recording its location. Check items with temperature or storage requirements against their instructions; a sealed backpack is not automatically suitable. Agree who collects each dependent person’s daily-use items and who checks the transport. Treat immediate escape differently: leave a fire or other urgent hazard without completing the list. Example: an adult uses glasses and a medicine stored in a specific location. The bag may hold the written care information and a suitable spare item, while the grab list names the glasses and current medicine. Test that another trusted adult can locate them without needing a vague explanation such as “in the usual place.” Test weight, access, and the actual carry method There is no universal bag weight that is suitable for every person. Pack the proposed contents, then test a safe walk and the normal exit route according to the person’s abilities. Keep essential care available and stop if the exercise causes discomfort or unsafe movement. A wheeled bag may help on smooth ground but may be awkward on stairs; a backpack may conflict with caregiving or a mobility aid. Problems a carry test should reveal Problem Possible adjustment Cannot lift or carry the bag Reduce nonessential items, distribute suitable loads, or arrange realistic assistance. Need both hands for care or movement Choose a compatible carry arrangement and reduce loose items. Cannot find care items quickly Use a clearly labelled accessible pouch and a location list. Water makes the bag unmanageable Keep a carryable portion and plan a verified supply at the destination; do not pretend a smaller amount meets every need. Transport space is limited Check seats, equipment, pets, and bags together before departure. Do not solve a heavy-bag problem by leaving necessary care equipment behind without an appropriate alternative. Change the transport or destination plan if that is what the need requires. The practical test is whether the complete household can move, not whether one strong adult can lift all the bags. Keep pets and children in the movement plan Prepare care and comfort items suitable for the actual child or animal, and identify what the destination allows. A pet-friendly listing does not guarantee acceptance during an emergency. Keep the carrier, leash, identification, and required medicines usable. A child should have age-appropriate contact information without being made responsible for finding adults or deciding the route. Assign a responsible adult to each person needing assistance. Count people at departure and arrival, and agree where to meet if separated. Include a simple familiar comfort item when it fits, especially if it helps a child manage an unfamiliar setting. Keep that comfort item easy to reach without unpacking essential supplies. Do not overload the helper The person supporting a child, pet, or dependent adult may need a lighter personal load. Test that their hands, movement, and attention remain available for the assistance they must provide. If the preferred destination cannot accommodate a need, resolve it before relying on that destination. Keep an alternate and the relevant contact details. The bag is one part of this arrangement, not the entire evacuation plan. Maintain, rehearse, and use it at the right moment Review the bag when seasons, medicines, clothing sizes, phones, pets, or household members change. Rotate consumables appropriately and check equipment function. Put the review date on the inventory so another adult can tell whether it is current. Keep the bag accessible without obstructing an exit or exposing it to inappropriate storage conditions. Find the bag and explain its purpose to another household member. Use the grab list in a safe practice and note any item that was hard to find. Check that the destination notes, contact numbers, and transport arrangements still work. Open and use a light, charging cable, and food package during practice. Remove unnecessary items and replenish anything used. Make one alternate plan for a closed destination or unavailable vehicle. In an actual evacuation, prioritize the people and urgent care needs. If time allows, take the tested bag and daily-use items; if immediate danger is present, do not remain or return for belongings. Replenish the bag after use so a successful departure does not leave the next one unsupported. Evacuation actions Evacuation without a car Work through an illustrative carried load Use a scale and one unit of mass to make the packing decision visible. The example below is an invented adult load for a journey to a confirmed indoor destination. It is not a prescribed kit, a complete three-day water supply or a suitable load for every person. Actual medicines, assistive equipment, clothing, containers and food may change it substantially. Illustrative load; replace every entry with your measured mass Group Example mass Empty bag 0.80 kg 2 litres drinking water Approximately 2.00 kg Water containers 0.20 kg Ready-to-eat food 0.50 kg Weather layers 0.80 kg Light, charging equipment and cables 0.45 kg Personal care essentials 0.35 kg Hygiene supplies 0.25 kg Contact/document pouch 0.10 kg Example total 5.45 kg The water arithmetic is the main lesson: about one kilogram per litre before the container. An additional litre adds about one kilogram. A U.S. gallon is approximately 3.785 litres, so three gallons are about 11.36 kilograms of water alone. CDC’s household reserve guidance therefore cannot simply be squeezed into every personal bag. Keep the reserve goal visible while planning transport and a verified next water source; reducing the carried portion does not reduce the person’s need. Weigh the packed bag, not merely the inventory. Include the bag itself, filled containers, daily-use additions and anything clipped outside. Test the actual stairs and carry method in calm conditions with a helper where needed. Record the result and choose the load around the person who must use it. Stage personal, vehicle and destination supplies separately Three different places for different loads Stage What belongs there Failure question On the person / personal bag Care essentials, contact card, light, weather layer, manageable water and phone power. If separated from the vehicle, can this person still manage the next immediate needs? Vehicle reserve Additional water, clothing and shared supplies secured appropriately for the trip. If the vehicle becomes unavailable, which essentials remain personally accessible? Confirmed destination Host-agreed spare supplies or known services. What changes if the destination cannot be reached or accepted? Avoid the two extremes: putting every reserve into a backpack, or putting every useful item into the vehicle. Pack the personal core first, then document what the vehicle adds. A shared pouch should have a named carrier; otherwise everyone may assume another bag contains it. Keep materials subject to temperature limits in suitable storage rather than assuming a parked vehicle is a permanent cache. Before departure, count people, care equipment, bags and seats together. Take the accessible personal core even for a short drive. For a planned move to family, agree what the host can actually supply, such as bedding or a suitable meal, and keep a fallback for a changed arrangement. Reassess at each transfer: vehicle to waiting room, waiting room to transport, transport to destination. Red Cross · Kit supplies Use the source checklist to identify needs, then measure and distribute the actual household load. Keep bags accessible and plan for pets, infants and mobility equipment. Never delay an urgent evacuation to finish packing. If you have minutes rather than days, grab essential medicines, documents, shoes, water and a phone charger first. Divide necessary supplies among people who can carry them, without giving children or a person with limited mobility an unmanageable load. Pack for actual infants, pets, access needs and the likely transport mode. Agree which adult carries shared items and who stays with each dependent. Include a destination plan; a bag does not establish that a shelter will admit or support the household. Kits & supplies Pack for a destination, not an imagined wilderness Use a core list, then personalize it Separate prepacked items from the last-minute grab list Test weight, access, and the actual carry method Keep pets and children in the movement plan Maintain, rehearse, and use it at the right moment Work through an illustrative carried load Stage personal, vehicle and destination supplies separately Plan the destination Know where you can go and how you will get there. Pack personal essentials Include medication arrangements, identification copies, keys and accessible supplies. Add basic support Pack water, snacks, light, charger, hygiene supplies and appropriate clothing. Test and maintain Carry the bag briefly, reduce excess weight and refresh dated items.

title: Grey man basics: ordinary discretion, privacy and de-escalation
summary: Reduce avoidable attention in everyday travel and disruption: dress for the setting and weather, keep possessions organized, share information selectively, and leave escalating arguments when it is safe to do so. Stay reachable to trusted contacts and make yourself visible when you need rescue.
text: An argument is becoming volatile? Prioritize distance and a safe departure; seek appropriate assistance rather than proving a point. Someone needs your location? Use the agreed private contact method and precise current information. You are lost or need rescue? Make yourself findable; ordinary discretion no longer serves the immediate need. Does grey man mean dressing in one special color? No. Practical fit with the setting, weather and your needs matters more than a costume. Should I avoid asking for help? No. Requesting appropriate help and being findable during an emergency take priority over reducing ordinary attention. Define discretion as an ordinary household skill The useful version of low-profile behavior is mundane: a person can travel, wait and communicate without advertising possessions or unnecessary personal details. The goal is a manageable routine, not becoming untraceable. A recognizable contact arrangement and accessible identity or care information can be important when something goes wrong. Start with your actual settings: work, school, a station, a clinic, a shared building or a destination during disruption. Ask what makes the routine easier and what disclosure has no purpose. The answer may be putting documents away, reducing loose gear or sending an update privately. It does not require changing your identity, inventing a story or treating every stranger as a threat. Useful discretion versus an unmet need Situation Practical choice Crowded commute A manageable bag that closes and does not block movement. Clinic visit Necessary care information available to the appropriate person. Household departure Private check-in to the agreed contact rather than a public empty-home post. Outdoor emergency Visible clothing and clear location information when seeking rescue. Choose clothing and bags for the real setting Prioritize weather protection, comfort, movement and access to essential items. Ordinary clothing appropriate to the journey often draws less unnecessary attention than conspicuous equipment, but no clothing choice guarantees how others react. Do not sacrifice visibility around traffic or during a search-and-rescue emergency for an aesthetic. A useful bag closes, keeps documents and care items accessible and leaves the person able to use handrails, assist dependents or operate a mobility aid. Avoid loosely attached valuables or labels that reveal more than a legitimate return arrangement needs. Test the load during normal travel and remove items with no defined task. For a shared household, let people choose workable clothing within their own needs and culture. A medical aid, service animal or accessibility requirement is not an embarrassment to hide. Plan how the group moves together and how someone requests help if overwhelmed. Discretion should reduce friction rather than creating a costume that makes the day harder. Share information by audience and purpose Before a public post, consider what it reveals about time, location, dependents, documents or an empty home. FTC’s privacy guidance emphasizes that posts can reach a larger audience and persist through screenshots even when privacy settings or deletion features are used. Ask permission before sharing another person’s photo or information. An editorial disclosure worksheet Information Who needs it Useful method Current location and destination Agreed household contact or appropriate responder. Private message or direct conversation. Care detail The helper or clinician who requires it. An accessible private care card or suitable direct exchange. Travel photo People pictured and the audience you choose. Review what appears in the background before posting. Identification copy A legitimate service when actually required. Provide only the required information through a verified channel. Keep a private contact card distinct from a public bag label. Review photographs for addresses, identifying documents and visible possessions before sharing them. Location sharing can help a trusted contact when deliberately arranged; decide its audience and purpose rather than treating all sharing as either essential or forbidden. Keep a simple interaction plan Most everyday disagreements do not require a complex script. Use a short, courteous statement, avoid crowding another person and keep the exchange focused on the immediate practical issue. CISA’s de-escalation guide stresses calm communication, respect for personal space, limits on intervention and seeking safety when a hostile act is imminent. Its context is organizational violence prevention; this page adapts only ordinary civilian communication principles. Prepare phrases that fit your routine: “I need a moment to check that,” “Please show me the written information,” or “I’m going to leave this conversation.” Do not insist on finishing an argument when the situation becomes volatile. If leaving is safe, prioritize the departure and the people with you. Appropriate staff, security or emergency assistance may be needed; there is no promise that calm words can stop violence. For a person who has difficulty processing speech under stress, agree a simple cue with a trusted companion. The companion can help ask for space or clarify the practical request. Avoid diagnosing another person’s intent from appearance or identity. Assess observable behavior and the actual situation. Plan waiting and meeting without unnecessary exposure Choose a suitable waiting place for a disrupted journey and agree how the contact learns where you are. Confirm access, opening arrangements and any care needs. A place that was open yesterday may not be available during the disruption, so keep a separately checked alternative. An ordinary disruption plan Wait Use a suitable confirmed place if travel is uncertain and the current location is safe. Update Privately state location, condition, intended action and next check-in. Reassess Check route, destination and household needs before moving. Seek help Use appropriate assistance when the situation exceeds the household’s workable plan. Osprey Zero planning aid. These are conditional choices; current conditions and individual needs control the decision. The diagram describes an editorial communication routine, not a covert movement plan. Avoid public meeting instructions containing a child’s location or sensitive care information. Make the meeting point unambiguous to the people using it: the actual entrance, accessible path and fallback if the building closes. If the plan changes, update it explicitly rather than expecting others to infer your new destination. Make the trade-offs visible to the household Privacy can conflict with convenience, and discretion can conflict with necessary visibility. Discuss those trade-offs explicitly. A trusted helper may need an address or care card; a public post does not. A person on a dark roadside needs to be seen; blending into the surroundings would undermine the immediate task. During a search, responders need accurate location and useful identifying information. Give each person an age-appropriate role. A child can know the trusted contact and meeting arrangement without carrying a complete collection of adult documents. An adult using assistive technology should retain the settings and support they need. Respect consent when sharing location, and avoid quietly imposing monitoring arrangements on another person. If a threatening or coercive situation affects the household, obtain appropriate specialist support and make decisions around the real circumstances. General discretion tips are not a substitute for an individualized protection plan. Avoid escalating confrontation to test whether the household can stay calm. Get-home planning Civilian distress signaling Practice a small review rather than a disguise exercise Choose one routine and inspect it calmly. Look at the packed bag, a recent draft post and the household’s current check-in arrangement. Identify what serves a useful need and what simply reveals extra information or creates a carrying problem. Name the ordinary setting and the weather/access needs. Close and carry the actual bag; check necessary items remain reachable. Review one photo or message for unnecessary identifying details. Write a short private check-in with location, intention and next update. Rehearse one polite way to end an unproductive exchange. Keep one correction and review it after the next real journey. Judge the result by practical questions: can the person move comfortably, receive help, contact the right people and manage their needs? No exercise can certify invisibility or prevent every bad interaction. Keep the useful routines simple enough to use when tired, and preserve clear rescue signaling for actual emergencies. FTC · Share with care Review online sharing, audience and location-setting considerations. CISA · De-escalation action guide Read the concise official communication and intervention-limit guidance; this external PDF is not an Osprey download. Review one everyday journey, one public post and one household check-in arrangement. Remove unnecessary disclosure while preserving useful contact and assistance. Ordinary discretion does not guarantee invisibility or safety. This guide provides no impersonation, surveillance evasion, escape-from-capture or avoidance-of-lawful-authority instructions. Use a confirmed suitable waiting place, maintain private check-ins when possible and keep essential care accessible. If communication fails, follow the previously agreed household plan rather than improvising concealment or risky travel. Explain what information is shared with whom. Include children, sensory needs, service animals and mobility aids without expecting anyone to disguise their identity or suppress necessary assistance. Define discretion as an ordinary household skill Choose clothing and bags for the real setting Share information by audience and purpose Keep a simple interaction plan Plan waiting and meeting without unnecessary exposure Make the trade-offs visible to the household Practice a small review rather than a disguise exercise Match the ordinary setting Choose practical clothing and a manageable bag for the weather, journey and access needs. Limit unnecessary disclosure Share location and care information privately with the people who need it; avoid public empty-home announcements. Keep interactions calm Use short, courteous statements and respect personal space. Do not intervene in a volatile situation beyond your ability. Retain a help plan Keep a trusted contact, meeting place and accessible written information; discretion must not prevent help or rescue.

title: Hail
summary: Get indoors and stay away from windows during hail. If driving, stop in a safe place out of traffic when you can; stay inside the vehicle and protect yourself from broken glass. Do not stop beneath a highway overpass.
text: Check for injuries and roof or window damage only when conditions are safe. Photograph damage from ground level. Do not climb a wet or damaged roof to inspect it. Remain under substantial shelter while hail continues. Keep shoes on and avoid glazing. Afterward, assess damage from the ground; loose roofing and hidden electrical damage can be more dangerous than the hail itself. Account for children, older people, pets and anyone who needs assistance before moving. Keep shoes, medicines and a torch in the shelter area. Decide who helps whom and who carries the essential supplies; do not send a lone child to retrieve items. For this situation, brief every person on the first action: leave the open. Agree who will manage children, pets or mobility needs while that action happens. Do not climb a wet or damaged roof to inspect it. Severe storms Leave the open Move into a sturdy building before collecting possessions. Stay away from glass Use an interior room and keep pets inside. If in a car Pull over safely out of traffic, avoid flood-prone areas and remain in the vehicle. Follow other warnings Hail can accompany tornadoes, lightning and strong wind; act on those warnings as well.

title: Heating failure in cold weather
summary: Use dry layers, blankets and a smaller dry room while you identify safe heat or a warmer reachable place. Never use a gas oven, barbecue or generator to heat indoors. Confusion, slurred speech, unusual drowsiness or poor coordination can mean hypothermia: seek urgent care and begin safe warming.
text: Use dry layers, blankets and a smaller dry room while you identify safe heat or a warmer reachable place. Never use a gas oven, barbecue or generator to heat indoors. Confusion, slurred speech, unusual drowsiness or poor coordination can mean hypothermia: seek urgent care and begin safe warming.    Contact a qualified repair provider when reachable and safe. Plan for medication storage, food, water and sanitation during a longer outage; a portable heater alone does not solve all needs. Do not give alcohol as a warming method or rub frostbitten skin. Fuel-burning devices can create lethal CO even when you cannot smell anything. Use the safest dry shelter and insulation available while confirming a warmer private or community destination. Leave early if you cannot keep vulnerable people warm rather than waiting for official shelter. Assign a trusted adult to each person who needs assistance. Keep medicines, essential contacts and a workable reunion plan with the group. Make decisions around the least mobile person, not the fastest; avoid splitting the family without a clear, safe way to reconnect. For this situation, brief every person on the first action: get dry and insulated. Agree who will manage children, pets or mobility needs while that action happens. Do not give alcohol as a warming method or rub frostbitten skin. Fuel-burning devices can create lethal CO even when you cannot smell anything. no heat heater broken freezing house heating outage Get dry and insulated Replace wet clothes, layer loose dry clothing and insulate beneath the body as well as above it. Keep vulnerable people away from draughts. Use one workable space Choose a dry room that remains safe and has a usable exit. Close unnecessary interior doors without blocking ventilation needed by approved heating appliances. Avoid combustion shortcuts Use only heating equipment approved for indoor use according to its instructions, with working CO alarms. A grill, oven or indoor generator is not a backup heater. Check people regularly Cold can impair judgement. Pay particular attention to infants, older people and anyone with illness or limited mobility. Do not rely on a person saying they feel fine. Move before severe exposure Confirm a warmer destination and safe route while people can still travel. Do not cross dangerous ice or an active hazard merely to reach a public warming centre.

title: Home fire
aliases: there is a fire in my kitchen
summary: Get out, stay out and call emergency services from outside. Use the nearest safe exit, stay low beneath smoke, and close doors behind you if possible. Do not stop for belongings or go back inside for people or pets; tell firefighters where they may be.
text: Can I retrieve a phone or a pet? Do not delay escape or reenter for belongings or animals. Once outside, tell responders where anyone may remain. Keep the household assembly point clear so missing people can be identified without people searching inside. The exit is blocked — what then? Do not force a hot door or a route filling with smoke. Close doors between you and the fire, call and signal your exact location. A high-rise needs its building-specific plan; use the Apartment & high-rise fire guide rather than guessing at an elevator or window escape. An active fire: protect people before property A fire response begins with getting away from danger. Do not use a household checklist as a reason to collect documents, photograph damage or investigate the source. Once outside, stay outside. Contact the appropriate emergency service from a safe place and tell responders if someone or a pet may still be inside. If a route is unsafe or blocked, use the trapped-person action in the immediate checklist rather than forcing your way into smoke. Keep the decision clear Situation Protective priority Smoke or fire inside Use the nearest safe escape route and stay out. A route is blocked Separate yourself from smoke with closed doors and signal your location. Someone is unaccounted for Report their possible location; do not reenter to search. The building becomes quiet Remain outside until the fire department permits reentry. This is a general home-fire guide. An apartment or high-rise also needs its building-specific plan; follow the companion guide and obtain that plan before an emergency. Do not improvise an elevator or window escape. Make an escape plan that fits the actual home Before an emergency, draw a simple floor plan and identify the available exits from each room. USFA recommends two ways out where possible, an outside meeting place and practising the plan. Include anyone who needs assistance. A route that works for one adult may not work for a child, a wheelchair user or someone waking from sleep. Use the planning exercise to record unresolved practical questions. Does a visitor know where the exit is? Does a door require a key that is not accessible? Has furniture narrowed the route? Is an assumed exit unavailable after a renovation? Put each problem on a short action list with a responsible adult and a review date. For a rental or shared building, request the actual safety arrangements from the responsible provider. Write the meeting place in plain language everyone understands. Include visitors and overnight guests in the explanation. Keep supplies and furniture out of the route. Revisit the plan after a move, renovation or change in mobility. Alarms need a maintenance system, not a one-time purchase USFA recommends smoke alarms in every sleeping room, outside each separate sleeping area and on every level of the home. It advises monthly testing and replacement of alarms at ten years. Follow the product’s instructions for power, maintenance and replacement; choose suitable accessible alerting equipment for anyone who may not hear a conventional alarm. Make maintenance visible Record Household action Location and model List each alarm so none is forgotten. Installation or replacement date Keep the date with the household maintenance record. Test responsibility Choose an adult and a repeatable reminder. Fault or missing equipment Record it as an action requiring prompt resolution. Accessibility need Ask the appropriate provider about a suitable alerting arrangement. If a landlord or another provider is responsible for equipment, make the question explicit and follow up on unresolved faults. Keep the record separate from a shopping list so a purchased but uninstalled alarm does not appear as a completed protection. An alarm notification is a prompt to act, not an invitation to ignore danger until everyone agrees on its cause. An extinguisher has strict limits USFA’s extinguisher guidance makes escape the overriding priority. It describes extinguisher use only when everyone has left or is leaving, the fire department has been called, the fire is small and contained, smoke does not put the user at risk, and a clear escape route remains. If those conditions are not all satisfied, leave. Owning an extinguisher does not establish the skill or conditions to use it. For preparation, ask a qualified local provider about appropriate equipment, hands-on instruction and inspection. Read the exact product label and identify who is responsible for its condition. Do not make an internet summary your only training. Keep the distinction between having equipment and having a usable plan visible in the household record. Prioritise evacuation over an attempt to save property. Arrange appropriate instruction before relying on unfamiliar equipment. Keep inspection and service information with the product record. Treat uncertainty about the fire, smoke or escape route as a reason to leave. Practise roles without creating a hazard Use a calm household walkthrough in ordinary safe conditions. Explain that a real fire does not wait for the practice routine. Walk the intended route, describe the alternate and identify the meeting place. Discuss who helps a dependent and who stays with children once outside. Do not create smoke, darken stairs dangerously, block an exit or stage a frightening surprise to make the exercise seem realistic. A short household review Question What to resolve beforehand Who needs assistance? An arrangement that fits the person, building and available support. Who may be absent? A backup responsibility when the usual adult is away. Where do visitors go? A clear route explanation and meeting place. What about pets? A preparation plan that never asks someone to reenter a fire. How is the plan maintained? A review after changes and a visible list of outstanding tasks. Keep the review specific. “Everyone knows what to do” is difficult to verify; “we walked the route and found an obstructed door” gives the household an actionable improvement. Record the problem, resolve it and then check the corrected arrangement. Use a qualified provider when the building or a person’s needs create a question the household cannot answer. After the fire: separate reentry, support and recovery Once everyone is outside, keep the meeting place organised and tell responders who is missing. Do not go back for a medicine, wallet or phone. Reentry depends on the fire department’s permission and the building’s condition, not on whether flames are visible. The Red Cross provides preparation and recovery resources and a route to local support; assistance and capacity depend on location and circumstances. For household recovery planning, identify temporary accommodation options, a way to contact an insurer or landlord, and private backups of essential records before an incident. These are advance planning tasks, not things to retrieve during a fire. Keep the contact record somewhere separate from the home when practical. Ask relevant providers how essential prescriptions or access equipment could be replaced if belongings cannot be recovered. Prepare a private list of insurance, landlord and care-provider contacts. Identify an accommodation option suitable for the actual household. Keep replacement questions separate from dangerous retrieval attempts. Follow the building assessment and relevant provider instructions before cleanup. Recovery can involve several decisions at once. Keep a simple dated record of instructions, outstanding questions and the next safe action rather than trying to solve everything immediately. Install and test smoke alarms and practice two ways out with the household. Plan assistance for children and people with mobility needs. An extinguisher attempt must never delay escape or block your exit. Escape immediately, gather outside and keep the exit area clear. If trapped, close the door between you and smoke, signal from a window and send your exact location if possible. Do not reenter because the fire seems quiet or because firefighters have not arrived. Practice the route with children and anyone needing movement assistance. Agree on a nearby meeting point and who will supervise dependents once outside. Include a second safe way out when the building permits it; never block an exit with stored supplies. Fire Leave immediately Follow the escape route and use stairs, not elevators. Check doors for heat before opening; use another exit if unsafe. If the exit is blocked Close doors between you and fire, call emergency services with your location and signal from a window. Meet outside Account for everyone at the meeting point and report missing people to firefighters. Stay outside Do not reenter until the fire department permits it.

title: Home preparedness and practical hardening
summary: Start with working alarms, usable exits, secure doors and windows, and maintenance against local hazards. Hardening should reduce risk while keeping everyone able to escape.
text: A sensible order of spending Fix a broken exit, alarm or lock before buying specialized equipment. Then address the highest local hazard and the household’s greatest access need. Photograph the baseline, record repairs and keep contractor and insurance information accessible. Cosmetic reinforcement does not establish structural safety. Security without entrapment Do not use traps, electrified barriers or improvised defensive devices. Window bars and additional locks can delay escape or responders; choose lawful systems that occupants can operate in an emergency. Clear sightlines, ordinary lighting and working hardware support everyday security without turning evacuation into a puzzle. Complete a room-by-room audit: one exit issue, one alarm issue, one maintenance issue and one practical security improvement. No home improvement guarantees safety against violent entry or severe weather. Do not remain in a building that has become unsafe because it has been “hardened.” Use the safest usable parts of the home and avoid damaged electrical or structural systems. Where a repair needs a professional, restrict access and relocate if the hazard cannot be controlled; do not improvise structural work during an event. Test locks and exits with the people who actually use them, including those with limited grip, vision or mobility. Store critical equipment at reachable heights. Homes & security home hardening house hardening Audit basic safety Check alarms according to their instructions, keep escape paths clear and identify damaged locks, unsafe wiring, water leaks or blocked drainage. Match improvements to hazards Use local wind, flood, wildfire and heat risks to set priorities. Consult qualified professionals for structural, electrical, roofing or flood-resistant work. Improve access control Repair suitable locks, latch hardware and exterior lighting. Secure outdoor tools and avoid hiding spare keys in obvious places. Preserve safe emergency exit operation. Plan safe occupancy Choose appropriate interior shelter locations for the relevant warning. Keep lights and essential supplies accessible without turning rooms into trip hazards.

title: Household drought and water-saving plan
summary: Follow your water provider’s current restrictions, cut avoidable use, and repair leaks. Protect drinking, food preparation, medical needs, and essential hygiene. A drought restriction is not automatically a contamination warning or a water outage; each needs its own response. Plan now for accessible safe water if service becomes unreliable.
text: Restriction only; water remains available and safe Follow the listed limits and reduce avoidable use. New contamination advisory Follow its specific instructions; use the water-disruption guide. No usable water Use stored safe water and the water-outage plan; report the problem. Essential care or hygiene cannot be maintained Contact the provider and care team immediately for a safe alternative. Private-well supply or quality changes Seek a well professional and local health-department advice. Rain arrives but no official change is announced Keep following the current restrictions. Does drought make tap water unsafe? Not automatically. Follow water-quality notices separately. Should we store enough water for the whole drought? Keep a practical emergency reserve and replenishment plan. A drought may outlast household storage. Does meter movement prove a leak? It is a clue; automatic equipment or shared connections can also cause use. Investigate unexpected demand. Can we reuse washing water? Follow local health and plumbing rules and obtain qualified advice; this guide supplies no greywater recipe. Know what the notice actually means Drought is prolonged dry weather. A household shortage depends on the system supplying you, which may draw water from far away. Rain in your street does not establish that its supply recovered. Use your provider’s notice to decide what restrictions apply. Match the water problem to the response Restriction only If supply and quality remain normal, reduce the specified uses; check quality notices separately. Quality advisory Follow the exact boil-water, do-not-drink, or do-not-use instructions. No usable supply Report the interruption and switch to your water-outage plan. Essential needs at risk Contact the provider and care team promptly for a safe alternative. Choose the condition that applies; these cards are alternatives, not steps to perform in sequence. Drought-map categories do not determine your household’s restrictions or prove tap-water safety. Save the notice, date, and official contact number for offline use, but check for updates. Ask the provider about unclear instructions. Make a baseline you can actually use Use a recent bill or usage portal. Record its period and unit; longer billing periods and more occupants can increase totals without new waste. Compare like periods. If permitted meter access is safe, EPA suggests comparing readings over two hours with no water use. A change suggests a leak or another demand to investigate; automatic equipment can also use water. Never interrupt essential medical equipment or open a locked utility enclosure for this check. Osprey Zero example log: fictional values, not a usage target Day Reading in gallons Household notes Monday, 8 a.m. 12,000 Four people home; usual routine Tuesday, 8 a.m. 12,240 Difference: 240 gallons; two laundry loads Wednesday, 8 a.m. 12,430 Difference: 190 gallons; laundry postponed This fictional example teaches subtraction, not a household allowance. One quiet day does not prove savings. Note visitors, irrigation, laundry, and repairs. With shared bills or no meter access, track activities and report faults instead of estimating individual use. Reduce indoor waste while keeping healthy routines Turn off taps while brushing teeth or shaving. Shorten showers when doing so is compatible with care and accessibility needs. Run laundry and dishwashers with full, appropriate loads and the manufacturer’s recommended settings. Do not overload machines or skip cleaning that is needed for health. Keep an eye on toilets that keep refilling, dripping taps, and wet areas under appliances. Report leaks to the landlord or arrange an appropriate repair. Thaw frozen food in the refrigerator rather than under a running tap. Follow safe food-handling directions for the food. When fixtures need replacement, compare efficient models, including WaterSense-labeled products, and check for local rebates before buying. Conserve water, not essential care Do not ration necessary drinking water or stop handwashing to meet an arbitrary household target. Continue prescribed fluid limits or other medical instructions; ask the care team how to prepare if safe water becomes scarce. Choose a few sustainable changes. If use remains unusually high, investigate a leak or equipment problem rather than assuming someone is careless. Make the largest outdoor changes first Outdoor demand is often the easiest place to reduce nonessential use. Local watering limits override generic advice to water early or use drip irrigation. Pause optional lawn watering, vehicle washing, or topping up decorative water features when restricted or unnecessary. Check that irrigation is not leaking, watering pavement, or running on an old schedule. Arrange help for an underground or complex fault. If watering is permitted, follow local guidance for the particular landscape and conditions. Avoid inventing a universal lawn schedule. For future landscaping, ask local horticultural or extension services about suitable drought-tolerant plants and establishment needs. Even suitable new plants may need watering. Do not improvise a second water system Rainwater and used household water are not automatically safe drinking water. Greywater reuse depends on local rules, plumbing design, and the intended use. Do not cross-connect it to drinking-water plumbing or create a homemade drinking-water supply. If irrigation is shared, ask whoever controls it to confirm the required changes. Prepare for supply problems, including a private well Private-well owners are responsible for water safety; public utility results do not describe their well. Keep maintenance and testing records. If supply or quality changes, contact a qualified well professional and the health department rather than altering the pump or deepening the well. Use bottled or another known safe source if contamination is suspected. Clear appearance, a new filter, or returning flow does not establish water safety. For a short interruption, CDC recommends storing at least one U.S. gallon, about 3.8 litres, per person per day for at least three days; a two-week supply is preferable when practical. Needs can be higher in heat, illness, pregnancy, and for pets. This is a preparedness baseline, not a drinking-water limit. Keep supplies in suitable containers and use the water-storage guide for details. Confirm local emergency-water reporting, delivery, container, and assistance arrangements before depending on them. Build access and health needs into the plan Drought can overlap with heat, smoke, dust, and wildfire risk. Follow those warnings alongside water restrictions; seek care promptly if someone becomes unwell. This Osprey Zero planning exercise identifies access gaps; it does not set a medical water allowance. Write one workable answer for each need Need Planning question Water-dependent treatment or equipment Who in the care team can specify the required water quality, quantity, and backup location? Limited strength or mobility Who can collect or deliver small containers, and can they reach the home? Children or other dependants Who will supervise safe drinking water and keep non-drinking water clearly separate? Pets Where is their drinking supply, and who can bring more? Low income or limited storage Which local assistance or distribution option can be used without a large up-front purchase? Communication needs Who can obtain notices in a usable language or accessible format? Choose who checks notices and a backup helper or transport option. Report access barriers early; registration does not guarantee delivery or uninterrupted service. Review the plan as conditions change Keep following restrictions until the responsible authority changes them. Local rain may not replenish your supply. Keep useful conservation habits when restrictions ease. Weekly during restrictions, check the official stage, essential-water access, and unresolved leaks. Check sooner when notices change. If service becomes unreliable, move from the conservation plan to the water-outage plan. Check separately for water-quality advice. After a notice ends, follow any provider instructions about flushing or restarting equipment. Do not perform a large, unnecessary flush simply because drought conditions improved. Compare usage over similar periods, accounting for repairs, occupancy, and season before claiming savings. The weekly review is an Osprey Zero suggestion, not an official requirement. Update the plan after moving or changing care arrangements. Drought.gov current conditions U.S. regional drought maps and outlooks; check your utility for actual restrictions. EPA household leak checklist Practical leak-detection guidance and an official downloadable checklist. CDC drinking-water advisories Explains boil-water, do-not-drink, and do-not-use notices. Read a bill, resolve the most obvious leak, and agree on a safe-water fallback. Monitor official restrictions, quality advisories, unexpected use, well-supply changes, heat, smoke, and fire warnings. If collection is impossible or safe water is running short, contact the provider, emergency management office, or community assistance service before essential needs go unmet. Keep tasks practical for age, disability, tenancy, and who controls shared equipment. Protect essential hygiene and prescribed care. drought water restrictions water conservation water meter private well safe drinking water leaks heat Read your current notice Check the official restriction stage for your address, its start date, affected uses, and update channel. Cut avoidable use Pause unnecessary or prohibited outdoor demand and report leaks. Protect essential needs Maintain drinking, food safety, hygiene, and prescribed care. Seek help if water limits threaten these needs. Check your fallback Plan accessible safe-water collection or delivery before service becomes unreliable.

title: Household emergency plan
summary: Agree on how to receive warnings, where to shelter, when and where to evacuate, and how to reconnect if separated. Write the plan down and include people who need medication, mobility assistance or caregiver support.
text: How long should the written plan be? Keep the first-action, contact, role and destination information concise. Put equipment manuals and more detailed care information where they can be found separately. Test whether another person can use the plan without the organizer explaining it. What if a helper is unavailable? Name another realistic option and mark any unconfirmed arrangement. Review the person’s essential needs directly; do not make the entire plan depend on a single neighbor or a reply to one message. Start with the household you actually have A useful plan describes who does what when normal arrangements stop working. Begin with the people, pets, places, and services your household relies on. Include anyone who stays part time, someone away at school or work, and a person who may need help communicating or moving. A plan for four fit adults will not work unchanged for a family with a toddler and an adult who cannot use stairs. Build a dependency list before buying equipment Need Write down Fallback to investigate Care Medicines, powered equipment, caregivers, and storage requirements Provider-approved backup and an accessible alternative location. Movement Stairs, transport, keys, mobility aids A second helper or transport arrangement that can actually be reached. Communication Usable devices, languages, hearing or vision needs A written contact card and an agreed accessible contact method. Daily essentials Drinking water, food, toilet arrangements, pets Supplies everyone can use and the point at which home stops working. Make the list short enough to update. Write facts you have checked and mark assumptions that still need work. An advertised shelter, a neighbor’s vehicle, and an electric door are not reliable fallbacks until their limits and availability are understood. Separate immediate escape from planned relocation Choose a nearby meeting point for escaping a home fire and a separate destination for being unable to return to the neighborhood. These serve different purposes. The fire meeting point is where people can be counted after leaving; it is not necessarily somewhere to sleep. A relocation destination needs a safe route, acceptance, and suitable care and access. Three parts of a complete movement plan Get clear Leave immediate danger without collecting belongings. Use the appropriate building escape plan. Account for people Meet at the agreed safe place, count everyone, and communicate any missing person to responders. Continue safely For a wider evacuation, use a checked destination and route, with an alternate if they fail. Editorial planning aid. Actual hazards, access needs and current instructions control the decision. Do not send someone back into a dangerous building to retrieve a bag, pet, or missing person. Tell responders what is known. For a developing regional emergency, preparations can happen before departure becomes urgent: transport, medicines, pets, destination, and an alternate. Keep that longer checklist distinct from immediate escape. Write the contact and reunion rules Choose an out-of-area contact who agrees to the role. Give everyone the same contact information on paper as well as in their devices. Decide what to report: who is with you, your condition, where you are, and when you expect to make contact again. A missed message should trigger an agreed, realistic response rather than an improvised search into danger. Record school or daycare pickup rules, authorized collectors, and where children may be taken if the normal site closes. Agree what a person should do if unable to reach the primary meeting point.
