The alternative must also be safe for the actual incident. Include helpers who can support access or care needs, with permission to share only the information necessary for the task. Keep address and destination information readable without an internet connection. Protect sensitive records; do not post a household plan publicly. Example: two adults are at work when a neighborhood is evacuated. The plan should explain who can collect the child, where the child will go, and how the other adult learns the new destination. Both adults independently driving to the school can waste time and leave the next decision unclear. Assign tasks and backups without making one person indispensable Distribute tasks by ability and location. One adult can manage a dependent person while another checks transport and communicates. Someone living alone can still assign an outside check-in contact and keep the essentials organized for self-use. Avoid a plan that requires the only person away at work to come home before any action can begin. A compact task sheet Task Primary person Backup or limit Support each dependent Name the adult and the specific assistance Identify an alternative; do not assume neighbors are available. Transport and destination Name the driver or transport contact Record another realistic option and when to switch. Contacts and updates Name the information person Keep the paper list accessible to another adult. Essentials Name who keeps bags and daily-use grab list ready Never let packing delay immediate escape. Give tasks clear end points. “Handle the pets” is less useful than “put each pet in its labelled carrier and bring its medicine.” Keep a paper location list for daily-use items that cannot live in a bag. Do not give children responsibility for fuel, electrical work, or decisions about whether a building is safe. Set decision triggers before an emergency A trigger states the condition that changes the plan and the action that follows. Use conditions you can recognize: an applicable evacuation order, an unsafe building, an essential device losing backup, or the inability to maintain safe water and sanitation. A vague promise to “leave if things get bad” gives a tired household too much to debate. List the local hazards that could require leaving and those that may require sheltering. The correct response depends on the hazard. For care and equipment, use provider and manufacturer limits. Do not invent a general battery percentage that applies to every person. Choose a time to review stable conditions, but act immediately if an urgent danger develops. Record what information would change a decision, where it comes from, and what you can do if that channel fails. For an editorial example, a household may decide to relocate while transport remains available if it cannot sustain a particular care need at home. That threshold belongs to the individual care plan. A restoration estimate or social-media rumor should not silently replace it. Staying home with exit limits Evacuation planning Test the plan with a realistic tabletop exercise Gather the people who use the plan and choose one scenario: power fails while one adult is away and phones are unreliable. Ask each person to explain the next action, not simply agree that the plan looks sensible. Keep essential equipment operating; this exercise is discussion and safe practice, not a deliberate loss of medical support. Locate the contact card, light, medicines grab list, keys, and relevant bag without turning the exercise into a race. Describe the first check-in and the response if it cannot be delivered. Check the destination and route assumptions, including pets and access. Introduce one change: the driver is unavailable, a road is closed, or the destination cannot accept everyone. Write down the first three problems and fix the most consequential one before adding more equipment. Review after moving, a new medical need, a change of school, a new pet, or a different caregiver. Put the review date on the plan and retire confusing old copies. Success means another household member can explain and carry out the plan, not that the folder is impressive. Keep copies offline and in go bags. Share relevant details with caregivers and trusted contacts. A plan that depends on one vehicle or one working phone network needs alternatives. Give each household member a written copy with two meeting places, two contacts and essential medical details. Practise the plan with phones off. Include a destination you can actually reach without an official shelter or rescue transport. Write the plan in formats everyone can use: plain text, large print, translated wording or another needed communication format. Ask each person which assistance they want. Store private identity and health details securely rather than in public shared links. Planning Start with the household you actually have Separate immediate escape from planned relocation Write the contact and reunion rules Assign tasks and backups without making one person indispensable Set decision triggers before an emergency Test the plan with a realistic tabletop exercise Identify local risks Use local emergency management information and plan for likely hazards. Choose meeting places Pick a nearby safe place and an out-of-area destination plus backup routes. Assign contact arrangements Name an out-of-area contact, write phone numbers and agree on check-in times. Practice and update Run a simple drill and revise for changes in health, school, work or pets.

title: Household inventory: what you own, what works and what is missing
summary: A useful inventory records usable supplies, condition, location and next action. Count what works for your actual household instead of turning preparedness into an endless shopping list.
text: Quantity is not duration Duration depends on people, pets, climate, actual use and safe storage. Calculate water and meal requirements separately and avoid a single readiness percentage that hides a failing essential. Record consumables alongside any equipment that needs them. Location is part of inventory Write where supplies are stored and how they can be accessed in low light or without lifts. Keep exits and equipment ventilation clear. Split portable items from home reserves and keep urgent medicines or support information readily reachable. Inventory one shelf and one essential device today, then complete the highest-priority missing action. Do not count expired, damaged or incompatible supplies as usable. Avoid heavy storage that creates injury or blocked exits. Use a notebook or a simple spreadsheet if an app is unavailable. Update quantities when supplies are used. A basic accurate record is more useful than an elaborate dashboard full of old data. Include allergies, mobility aids, pets, infants and the needs of people who visit or provide care. Do not expose sensitive records on a shared device without discussing access. Planning inventory stockpile supplies Start with essentials Record water, food, medication arrangements, lighting, communications, hygiene, care equipment and portable departure supplies. Test usability Check dates, batteries, cable compatibility, labels, container condition and who knows how to operate equipment. A broken or inaccessible item is not a reliable reserve. Record a clear next action Give each gap a practical action, owner, cost estimate and due date. Prioritize essential needs and access issues. Review at a manageable interval Check after use, a household change or an approaching local hazard season. Keep a routine simple enough to maintain.

title: Household preparedness drills that reveal real gaps
summary: Use short, safe rehearsals to test actual people, equipment and decisions. Improve one weak step at a time rather than staging dangerous surprise emergencies.
text: A simple monthly rotation Rotate a short contact check, supply-date review, departure rehearsal and safe equipment familiarization session. Keep the schedule manageable so it survives normal life. Record an action completed, not just a readiness score. A checklist full of untested assumptions does not establish capability. Include failure deliberately Try a unavailable driver, a phone with no signal or a forgotten charger in a controlled setting. Ask which alternative is usable without help. Do not simulate hazards by actually disabling safety systems or blocking exits. A drill should make the household calmer and more capable, not frightened or exhausted. Choose one ten-minute drill this week and complete its single highest-value improvement before scheduling the next. Never stage surprise armed scenarios, real smoke exposure, dangerous driving or deprivation exercises. Practice the protective steps you can complete independently. Keep a short paper plan so the exercise does not require internet, a paid app or a responding service to succeed. Adapt drills to age, disability, language and anxiety. Use predictable steps, consent and breaks. Record where help is needed rather than labeling someone as the problem. Practice & maintenance Pick one scenario Choose departure, a communications failure or locating equipment in low light. State the objective and stop conditions before starting. Protect essential care Do not disconnect necessary medical equipment, withhold medicines or create hazardous heat, cold, smoke or fire. Tell participants it is a drill. Use real equipment Try the actual bags, chargers, contacts and accessible routes. Note missing adapters, forgotten keys, unclear roles and uncomfortable carrying loads. Review and fix Ask what worked, what failed and one concrete change. Assign an owner and a date, then repeat only the affected part.

title: Hurricane
summary: Check local evacuation instructions for your address. If told to leave, evacuate before wind or water makes travel unsafe. Otherwise, use a sturdy shelter away from windows and above flood risk. The forecast cone and wind category do not show every dangerous impact.
text: My evacuation zone has been ordered out. Should I wait for the next forecast? No. Follow the current local order while travel remains safe. Forecast updates do not cancel an order. The home is outside the evacuation zone. Is staying automatically safe? No. Consider building strength, local flood risk, access needs and the ability to cope with outages. Arrange a safer destination early if the home is unsuitable. My planned road is flooded. Should I follow navigation anyway? No. Turn around without entering the water, obey closures and use current official route guidance. Where is the flood-zone map? Use the FEMA Flood Map Service Center linked above for U.S. flood-risk planning. Get evacuation-zone maps and actual orders separately from local emergency management. Can an inland location be affected? Yes. Tropical cyclones can bring damaging wind and rainfall flooding far inland. Check your local forecast and warnings, not only the coastal forecast. Choose the right action before conditions deteriorate A hurricane brings several hazards that need separate decisions: wind, storm surge, rainfall flooding and sometimes tornadoes. A hurricane watch means hurricane conditions are possible; a warning means they are expected. Preparations must finish before dangerous winds arrive. Read the full local notice, including its location, issue time and instructions. Evacuate early, or shelter according to the hazard ORDER TO LEAVE? Yes: use the directed evacuation route while travel is safe. Do not wait for water to appear. NO ORDER, BUT UNSAFE HOME? Arrange a safer building before the storm. Mobile homes and RVs are not safe shelters for tropical-storm or hurricane-force winds. STAYING IN A SUITABLE BUILDING? Choose an interior wind shelter above the expected flood risk; keep warnings on. ALREADY CUT OFF? Do not cross floodwater. Move to the safest accessible higher space if water threatens and call for help. Read these as decision branches, not a countdown. An evacuation order overrides a plan to stay. This diagram cannot assess a building or a route. The category is only about wind A lower wind category, a weakening storm, or a forecast track farther away does not make storm surge or rainfall flooding safe. Open the right map for the question Use your exact address and the correct jurisdiction. An evacuation zone is a locally defined area; an evacuation order tells you whether to leave now. Check both on your city, county, parish, tribal or territorial emergency-management website. Zone letters are local labels and cannot be transferred between jurisdictions. FEMA · Flood Map Service Center U.S. flood-zone lookup for insurance and long-term planning. Enter an address or coordinates. This is NOT an evacuation-zone map and does not show current flooding. NOAA National Hurricane Center · Current tropical cyclones Current Atlantic and eastern North Pacific tropical-cyclone advisories, with Central Pacific information linked. Open the named storm and read its latest Key Messages, warnings and hazards. NOAA NHC · Forecast graphics explained Explains NHC cone, wind-arrival and storm-surge products. The cone concerns the storm center; hazardous weather extends outside it. Check each graphic’s issue time. NOAA NHC · National Storm Surge Risk Maps Community-level storm-surge planning for the coasts and territories listed on the site. Coverage is not worldwide, and this map must not replace local evacuation-zone maps. National Weather Service · Local forecasts and active alerts U.S. local forecasts, warnings and Hurricane Local Statements. Search your location for expected local wind, flood and other impacts. FEMA · State and territory resources FEMA’s U.S. state and territory resource finder is a starting point for reaching your emergency-management authority. Then use the local authority’s website for its evacuation map and current orders. Map colors are not a departure instruction FEMA flood zones, NHC surge forecasts and local evacuation zones answer different questions. A blank map area is not proof of safety. For places outside U.S. coverage, use the national weather service and local disaster authority. Write a short departure plan Before a storm is close, decide where you will go, how you will get there and who needs assistance. Confirm the destination is outside the relevant flood and evacuation area and suitable for wind protection. A nearby safe destination may be more practical than a long trip. Keep a second option in case the first is unavailable. Osprey planning worksheet: fill this in before departure Decision Write down Destination Address, contact, whether they expect you, and a backup location. Route Official route, an alternative permitted by officials, and where closures are reported. Transport Driver or pickup provider, seats, mobility-device space and agreed pickup time. Household Who collects each person, who carries medicines, and who handles pets. Communication One contact outside the affected area, a check-in time, and paper phone numbers. Treat unknown answers as work to finish now. “We will find somewhere” is not a usable destination. If you need public evacuation transport, contact local officials before services stop; ask where to wait and what equipment can travel with you. Recheck departure instructions when the storm changes. Prepare supplies without delaying departure Gather medicines, medical information, identification, keys, cash, charging cables, a power bank, a flashlight and a battery-powered radio. Include essentials for children and pets. Fuel or charge your vehicle while conditions are safe. Download or print the route and essential contacts before internet service becomes unreliable. Complete shutters and other planned home protection early. Do not climb, board windows or retrieve outdoor objects once wind or flooding makes the work unsafe. For stored water, CDC recommends at least one U.S. gallon per person per day for three days, and a two-week supply where feasible. Allow more for heat, illness and pets. Use suitable clean food-grade containers; do not reuse chemical containers. Store drinking water separately from water intended only for washing. Osprey packing check Place the bag by the exit and have the person who will carry it lift it. Keep essential medicine and communication aids immediately accessible. A large supply pile that cannot fit in your transport is not a departure plan. CDC · Create an emergency water supply Practical U.S. guidance on safe water containers, quantities and storage. Build supplies before the emergency; packing must not delay an evacuation. If staying, resolve wind shelter and flood risk together For wind, use a small windowless interior space in a sturdy building, on the lowest level that is not likely to flood. Stay away from windows and glass doors. A basement that could fill with water is not a suitable hurricane refuge. In an apartment or multistory building, ask management for the building’s designated shelter and evacuation arrangements beforehand. Keep your shoes, light, radio, phone and essential supplies together in the shelter space. Continue listening for separate flood and tornado warnings. Follow the warning for the hazard affecting your location. Stay inside during the calm eye. Strong winds can return suddenly from a different direction. If water rises dangerously and you cannot leave safely, move to a higher level and call emergency services. Do not climb into a closed attic. Higher-floor shelter is a last-resort response to rising water, not a substitute for leaving a storm-surge evacuation area when directed. Storm surge: the immediate coastal-water response Flash flood: act on rapidly rising water Plan around access, medical and caregiving needs Ask each person what assistance works for them. Confirm accessible transport and shelter arrangements early with local services, rather than assuming a ride or a space will appear. Tell shelter staff about access and health needs on arrival. Keep a concise care summary, medicines and assistive equipment with the person who uses them. An assistance registry is not a rescue guarantee. CDC warns that responders and medical services may be unable to reach people promptly. Build a personal backup plan with caregivers or trusted contacts. Osprey planning prompt: if your usual caregiver cannot come, who knows the essential routine and can help? Osprey planning prompt: if the lift or medical-device power fails, what destination and transport have you already arranged? Osprey planning prompt: does everyone receive the warning in an accessible language or format, and can they repeat the first action? CDC · Sheltering and evacuating CDC guidance on accessible evacuation, communicating needs at shelters, and service animals. American Red Cross · Find an open shelter U.S. Red Cross open-shelter information. Check the current listing and local announcements before traveling; locations can change. Handle outages without creating a second emergency Use battery-powered lighting. Never operate a portable generator indoors, in a garage or in another enclosed space, even with doors open. Keep it outdoors at least 20 feet from doors, windows and vents, with a working battery-powered or battery-backup carbon-monoxide alarm inside. Never run a grill or camp stove indoors. If a carbon-monoxide alarm sounds, get everyone into fresh air and call emergency services. Avoid all fallen wires and wet electrical equipment. Do not enter water to reach a breaker or attempt to restart flood-damaged equipment. Osprey outage log Write down when power was lost, which medical or communication devices remain powered, and the next action if backup power is running low. Keep a separate note of the water utility’s current advisory. Do not assume a restored light means the water supply or every appliance is safe. Generator placement and operation Food after a power outage Return only when the route and building are cleared An improving forecast does not mean you can return. Wait for official reentry instructions and continue checking flood warnings and road closures. Do not enter damaged buildings, buildings surrounded by floodwater, or places where you smell gas. Keep away from fallen wires and weakened trees or structures. Use official updates to establish which roads and neighborhoods have reopened. Avoid unnecessary travel through damaged areas. Follow the local water advisory exactly. Do not eat food contaminated by floodwater; check outage guidance for refrigerated food. If safe, record damage from a safe position and contact your insurer. Leave electrical, structural and other hazardous repairs to qualified people. Osprey recovery checklist: record your temporary address, who still needs a check-in, urgent medication or equipment needs, and the next official update time. Keep receipts and a dated damage record. Separate today’s essentials from repairs that can wait, and stop any task if the building, weather or your health becomes unsafe. Flood cleanup: safe reentry and limits Record damage and claim documents Check the latest local instructions, confirm a safe destination and transport, then complete preparations before travel becomes dangerous. Keep monitoring separate flood warnings after the strongest winds pass. The calm eye is not an all-clear. Wind category, the cone, and FEMA flood-zone shading cannot tell you whether a route is safe or whether your local evacuation order applies. If communications fail, use battery radio and the departure plan you prepared. Do not wait for an online map to load before following an evacuation order. If already trapped, stay clear of floodwater, move higher when water threatens and signal for help from a safe position; rescue may be delayed. Count everyone before leaving and at the destination. Keep children with a designated adult, pets secured for travel, and medicines and access aids with their users. Give each helper one clear task and a backup contact. Tropical weather evacuation zone storm surge flood zone map hurricane preparation Check your location Read the current local order and identify your evacuation zone. Visitors should check their present address, not their home address. Leave when directed Use official routes to a safer destination. Bring people, pets, medicines, identification and phone power; do not delay for belongings. Shelter from wind If evacuation is not required and the building is suitable, use a small interior room on the lowest level that is not likely to flood. Respond to rising water Never enter floodwater. If trapped in a building, move higher and contact emergency services; stay out of a closed attic.

title: Hygiene with limited water
summary: Reserve safe water for drinking, food, medicines and essential hygiene. Wash hands with safe water and soap before food preparation and after toilet or waste handling. Keep clean and dirty tasks separate. Sanitiser with at least 60% alcohol helps when hands are not visibly dirty; it does not remove chemicals or replace washing dirty hands.
text: Reserve safe water for drinking, food, medicines and essential hygiene. Wash hands with safe water and soap before food preparation and after toilet or waste handling. Keep clean and dirty tasks separate. Sanitiser with at least 60% alcohol helps when hands are not visibly dirty; it does not remove chemicals or replace washing dirty hands.  Can sanitizer replace every wash? No. CDC notes that sanitizer has limits, including visibly dirty or greasy hands and harmful chemicals. Plan suitable water and soap, especially around toilet, waste and meal tasks. Can I use water that is unsafe to drink for bathing? Sometimes an advisory allows certain non-drinking uses, but it depends on the contaminant and notice. Follow the specific permission; do not infer it from a different incident. Build a clean-to-dirty workflow When water, drainage, and rubbish collection fail, hygiene is a household system rather than a bottle of sanitizer. Decide where clean drinking water and food stay, where people wash hands, where personal care happens, and how waste is contained. Keep these activities separate enough that a dirty container, glove, or cloth cannot routinely pass through the meal area. A simple hygiene workflow Clean supplies Keep safe water, food, clean care items, and utensils protected. Handwashing Use an accessible dispensing point with appropriate water and soap, and a suitable way to handle runoff. Waste and used items Keep contained waste and soiled materials separate; wash hands before returning to clean tasks. Editorial layout concept. It is not a plumbing or waste-disposal design; local water and sanitation restrictions still apply. In a small dwelling, separation may mean labelled containers, a dedicated changing surface, and a sequence that is easy to follow rather than different rooms. Choose a stable setup the least mobile person can use. Keep walking routes clear, particularly at night. Waste should not be placed where children or pets can access it. Handwashing is the priority CDC advises washing hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds. Important times include after toilet use or handling waste and before preparing or eating food. Check the actual water advisory to determine whether tap water is acceptable for handwashing; a drinking restriction and a do-not-use restriction are different. Match the method to the conditions Condition Practical response Suitable water and soap available Use proper handwashing and a clean drying method. No normal running tap Set up a stable jug dispenser with appropriate water; avoid shared dipping into the supply. Soap and water unavailable CDC identifies sanitizer containing at least 60% alcohol as an alternative in some situations. Visibly dirty or greasy hands Sanitizer is less effective; obtain soap and appropriate water. Possible chemical contamination Sanitizer may not remove harmful chemicals; follow exposure guidance rather than assuming it decontaminates. Keep soap and a light beside the station rather than in a separate cupboard. Plan where runoff goes; do not use drains affected by sewage failure. Teach the setup to children with suitable supervision and arrange assistance for anyone who cannot operate the dispenser. Empty or unstable equipment creates a station that exists on paper but not in practice. Use limited water for essential personal care Choose suitable water for brushing teeth and follow the local notice for bathing. Do not bathe in water potentially contaminated with sewage or toxic chemicals. Reduced bathing can be a practical temporary adjustment, but necessary handwashing, oral care, and provider-directed care still need a plan. Keep each person’s toothbrush, hygiene items, and drying materials identifiable; do not make several people share a dirty cloth. Plan menstrual supplies, continence care, skin care, and privacy explicitly rather than calling all of these “toiletries.” Record special water or cleaning requirements from an individual care plan. A general household routine does not replace those instructions. Keep wounds protected from contaminated water, and seek medical help for signs of infection or other concerning change. Separate pet cleanup from human meal and personal-care surfaces. Estimate water used by an actual routine rather than making an arbitrary ration. Try a safe practice while normal water remains available: locate supplies, operate the dispenser, and complete the usual essential tasks. Use the observed amount to improve the reserve. Never withhold necessary drinking water or prescribed care to make a target last longer. Diapering and assisted care need their own setup Prepare a dedicated, cleanable changing area away from food. Bring the required items before starting so the child is not left unattended while a caregiver searches. Follow CDC’s diaper-changing sequence, including separating soiled items, washing the child’s hands, cleaning and disinfecting the surface as directed, and washing the caregiver’s hands. Use an appropriate product for the surface and follow its label, including any contact time. Disposable gloves, when used, do not replace handwashing. Keep clean diapers, wipes, spare clothes, and bagging materials within reach, while putting the closed used-item container where children cannot reach it. Adult continence care also needs dignity, a stable position, privacy, and any individual skin-care instructions. Plan the whole care cycle A stack of clean diapers is only one part of the plan. Include the changing space, handwashing water, cleaning supplies, soiled-clothing containment, waste route, and a backup caregiver if needed. If a caregiver must also prepare meals, make the transition explicit: finish the dirty task, contain used items, clean as directed, wash hands, then return to clean supplies. Do not put a changing mat on the only meal-preparation surface just because it is convenient. Cleaning is different from disinfecting Cleaning removes visible soil; disinfecting uses a suitable product as directed to address germs. Product type, surface, and instructions matter. Do not mix cleaning chemicals or improvise concentrated recipes. A chemical label must be readable and the product kept out of drinking-water containers. An editorial cleaning checklist Step What to verify Identify the surface and contamination Ordinary household dirt, a changing surface, and sewage contamination need different responses. Choose a suitable product Read the label for permitted surfaces, dilution, precautions, and contact time. Prepare the work area Keep food, people needing care, and pets away from the dirty task. Handle used materials Keep soiled cloths and waste separate from clean supplies. Finish safely Wash hands and restore clean supplies without recontaminating them. Significant sewage contamination may require qualified cleanup and an alternative living space. Do not treat a quick wipe or a splash of bleach as proof that a contaminated room is safe. Keep electrical and structural hazards in view, and avoid entering unsafe water to begin cleaning. Sewer failure and temporary toilets Maintain the routine and know its limits Record suitable water, soap, personal-care consumables, liners, and the functioning waste route. Review actual use and replenish before the routine fails. A supply of waste bags does not establish that collection exists or that every type of waste can go into ordinary rubbish. Follow the relevant local disposal arrangements. Check the station at the start of the day: water, soap, light, stability, and runoff arrangements. Check each person’s essential personal-care needs and the supplies they can actually use. Keep clean and used materials separated, and supervise children appropriately. Record any service or advisory change and adjust the routine. If safe water, care, or waste containment cannot be sustained, arrange a suitable alternative location early. After normal service returns, confirm the appropriate water and drainage instructions, clean affected equipment as directed, and replenish the hygiene kit. Note one preventable difficulty: a missing soap dispenser, an inaccessible container, inadequate privacy, or an unconfirmed waste route. Fixing that difficulty can provide more value than buying another generic emergency pouch. Replenish safe water when a verified source becomes available. Keep a routine that the household can sustain; a simple clean station is more useful than occasional improvised deep cleaning. Surface disinfectant is not drinking-water treatment. Do not apply household bleach to skin or mix bleach with ammonia or other cleaners. Use the smallest workable clean-water station and protect it from contamination. Reduce nonessential washing before cutting drinking water or essential handwashing. Make the hygiene plan usable for children, mobility needs and caregivers changing diapers or handling wounds. Keep gloves, cleaning tools and drinking-water supplies distinct. Tell everyone where the clean handwashing area is and who manages waste. no running water hygiene wash hands outage limited water sanitation Build a clean-to-dirty workflow Handwashing is the priority Use limited water for essential personal care Diapering and assisted care need their own setup Cleaning is different from disinfecting Maintain the routine and know its limits Set up a clean station Put safe water, soap and a clean towel or air-drying arrangement near food and care tasks. Use a container that does not require everyone to dip dirty hands into the supply. Prioritise key washing times Wash after toilet and waste handling, before eating or preparing food and before wound or infant care. Do not use suspected chemically contaminated water on skin. Use sanitiser appropriately Use at least 60% alcohol sanitiser when soap and safe water are unavailable and hands are not visibly dirty. Keep it away from flames and children. Separate waste and food Store rubbish and toilet waste away from water, food and sleeping areas. Clean high-contact surfaces using product instructions without mixing chemicals. Plan personal care Include menstrual supplies, nappies, necessary skin care and clean clothing. Keep wounds clean and covered; worsening redness, pain or fever needs medical assessment.

title: Ice storm
summary: Avoid travel on icy roads and keep away from ice-laden trees and power lines. Prepare for a long outage using safe heat and battery lights. Stay indoors until conditions improve unless your shelter is unsafe.
text: Use footwear with traction for necessary movement and do not enter areas beneath damaged trees. Never touch or approach a fallen wire, even if it appears inactive. Preserve heat in a dry room, keep lights battery powered and avoid unnecessary travel. If you must move because of dangerous cold, do it before people become weak and use a route you know is passable; a car is not reliable shelter if exhaust or roads are blocked. Account for children, older people, pets and anyone who needs assistance before moving. Keep shoes, medicines and a torch in the shelter area. Decide who helps whom and who carries the essential supplies; do not send a lone child to retrieve items. For this situation, brief every person on the first action: postpone travel. Agree who will manage children, pets or mobility needs while that action happens. Never touch or approach a fallen wire, even if it appears inactive. Winter Postpone travel Even thin ice can make roads and sidewalks unsafe. Avoid falling hazards Stay clear of branches, wires and roofs shedding ice. Use safe backup heat Keep combustion equipment outdoors and maintain working CO alarms. Check vulnerable people Plan safe transport to a warm location if heat or essential medical power fails.

title: Infant choking
summary: For a baby under one year who cannot cry, cough effectively or breathe, request emergency help and alternate 5 back blows with 5 chest thrusts. Support the head and neck; never give abdominal thrusts to an infant. If unresponsive, begin infant CPR.
text: Blockage clears Stop thrusts when effective coughing, crying or breathing returns. Continue observing and obtain assessment after serious symptoms. An infant is unresponsive Use Child & infant CPR. Responsive choking thrusts are not the CPR technique. Can I put a finger in the mouth? Only remove an object that is clearly visible. A blind sweep can push it further in.  Seek medical assessment after thrusts, persistent cough, breathing changes or any loss of responsiveness. Review what caused the blockage and safe feeding practices. An infant is under one year. AHA’s 2025 heel-of-hand update differs from older two-finger choking materials; use current training. Do not hang a baby upside down or shake them. Begin the sequence immediately while a helper calls. If alone, use speakerphone if reachable without delay. If the infant becomes unresponsive, change to CPR rather than continuing responsive choking care. A delayed responder is not a reason to pause. Have a second caregiver locate help and open access while the first provides care. Teach every regular caregiver the infant sequence using hands-on training; older-child abdominal thrusts are not appropriate for babies. Keep small objects and age-inappropriate food out of reach.  Check for an effective cough A baby who can cough or cry should be watched closely. Do not begin thrusts while the cough remains effective. Give 5 back blows Support the baby face-down on your forearm, braced on your thigh, with the head lower than the chest. Give 5 firm blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand. Give 5 chest thrusts Turn face-up while supporting the head and neck, keeping the head lower. The 2025 AHA update uses the heel of one hand for infant chest thrusts. Alternate with back blows until relieved or unresponsive. Change to CPR if unresponsive Place on a firm flat surface and begin infant CPR. Before breaths, remove an object only if clearly visible. Never sweep the mouth blindly.

title: Infants & children during disruption
summary: Keep children with a trusted caregiver and plan safe feeding, water, hygiene, medicines and warmth around their age and needs. Put written contacts with each child and agree a reunion plan. Use age-appropriate feeding guidance; do not dilute formula or use unsafe water to stretch supplies.
text: Keep children with a trusted caregiver and plan safe feeding, water, hygiene, medicines and warmth around their age and needs. Put written contacts with each child and agree a reunion plan. Use age-appropriate feeding guidance; do not dilute formula or use unsafe water to stretch supplies.  Can I dilute formula to make it last longer? No. Follow the product and qualified care instructions. If safe supplies or preparation are unavailable, seek verified feeding support; do not improvise dilution or homemade replacements. Is a well-stocked adult kit enough for an infant? No. Feeding, cleaning, storage, hygiene, transport, sleep and caregiver arrangements need their own child-specific plan and usable supplies. Build around one ordinary day of care List what each child uses in an ordinary day: feeding, drinking, hygiene, medicines, communication, sleep and safe transport. Then identify which tasks depend on clean water, electricity, refrigeration, a particular adult or a school. Infants, toddlers and teenagers need different plans. Do not apply an adult pantry or water calculation as a complete infant-care plan. A child-specific planning sheet Need Record Check before relying on it Feeding Usual product or method and relevant care instructions. Safe preparation, cleaning and storage during disruption. Care Prescribed medicines, aids and individual requirements. Current instructions, suitable storage and backup support. Supervision Named caregiver and trusted backup. Pickup permission and how the handover is confirmed. Comfort and communication Useful routine, language and familiar items. What the child understands and can safely do. Movement Appropriate transport or carrier arrangement. Fit, use instructions and actual space with the family’s bags. Write the information so the backup adult can use it. Keep product names and care instructions specific where needed, and separate private records from a simple contact card. Review quantities as the child grows rather than leaving an old diaper bag labelled emergency-ready indefinitely. Protect the feeding method instead of improvising substitutes CDC identifies ready-to-feed infant formula as the safest formula option during emergencies because it does not need mixing water. If formula is used, check suitable products, supply and storage with the child’s needs in mind. Follow label instructions after opening and feeding; unopened shelf stability does not make an opened container safe indefinitely. Do not dilute formula, make homemade replacements or change prescribed feeding without qualified advice. Powdered formula needs a separate safe plan It requires appropriate safe water, correct preparation and clean feeding equipment. If it is the only available option, use CDC’s specific guidance and seek qualified feeding support. A general camping water treatment instruction is not an infant-feeding protocol. If breastfeeding or expressing milk, plan access to appropriate support and any necessary equipment, cleaning and storage. A powered pump introduces dependencies that direct feeding may not have; discuss a workable backup with a qualified lactation provider. Do not assume stress automatically stops milk production or that an unfamiliar feeding technique can safely be learned from a hurried improvisation. Separate feeding, diapering and clean storage Organize care supplies by clean and soiled tasks. Keep the feeding area and equipment separate from diaper waste, cleaning chemicals and contaminated belongings. Use safe water and appropriate cleaning instructions for reusable feeding items. A packet of wipes does not replace every cleaning step required by a bottle or pump. If the required cleaning cannot be done, seek a suitable supported alternative rather than repeatedly reusing contaminated equipment. Keep age-appropriate feeding supplies and their instructions together, with a plan for opened items. Place diapers, suitable personal-care items, clean clothing and waste containment in a separate clearly marked group. Use a dedicated clean storage arrangement for prepared feeding equipment. Record where suitable handwashing water and soap are available. Keep product instructions and clinician-directed medicine information readable; do not estimate doses from an adult product. Editorial example: a family packs enough formula but forgets the equipment and water needed to clean its reusable bottles. The food quantity alone does not support feeding. Walk through one complete feed and one change in normal conditions to identify the missing task. Keep normal care available throughout this exercise. Keep a trusted caregiver and a clear handover Assign who stays with each child during sheltering, departure and arrival. A child should not be left alone while an adult searches for supplies or signal. Keep a trusted backup and current school or childcare pickup permissions. Record the expected destination and how another household adult learns it. Avoid two collectors arriving independently while nobody maintains the contact plan. A simple caregiver handover Confirm Identify the trusted responsible adult and authorized collection arrangement. Equip Provide essential care items, current instructions and a minimal contact card. Report Confirm the child’s location, caregiver and next check-in to the household contact. Editorial planning aid. Actual hazards, individual needs and current instructions control the response. Teach an older child the agreed trusted contacts and an age-appropriate separation response without placing adult responsibility on them. Keep sensitive identity and medical details off visible public labels. A child with communication or sensory needs may need a particular format, familiar aid, or calm explanation. Tell the backup caregiver what actually works instead of describing the child only by a diagnosis. Plan safe arrival, rest and a manageable routine Before relocation, ask what the destination can support for the child: safe feeding, suitable sleeping arrangements, essential care, hygiene, temperature and a caregiver. Do not assume an evacuation site has infant supplies merely because families can enter. Keep an appropriate transport arrangement and follow the child-restraint or carrier instructions; emergency travel is not a reason to improvise unsafe restraint. Arrival check before settling Area Question to answer Caregiver Who has direct responsibility right now? Feeding Can the usual safe plan continue with available supplies and equipment? Rest Is there a safe age-appropriate sleeping arrangement? Hygiene Where are clean care tasks done and waste contained? Communication Does the household contact know the confirmed location? Use simple truthful explanations: what is happening now, where the trusted adult is, and the next step. A familiar story, quiet activity or comfort object may help preserve routine. Avoid promises about when danger ends or repeated exposure to frightening media. Ask qualified child-health support about concerning illness or changes rather than treating this planning guide as a diagnostic checklist. Test quantities and identify the first care gap Inventory supplies against actual use and review them when needs change. For a child using a particular formula or prescribed item, count only suitable usable stock. Keep a daily-use grab list for items that cannot remain in the bag. Check expiration, storage and preparation instructions, and replace supplies used during normal life. A large bag with the wrong sizes or products is not an adequate reserve. Walk through a normal care period with the backup adult. Identify water, power, refrigeration and cleaning dependencies. Check the carry load while accounting for who holds or assists the child. Confirm the destination’s care arrangements and pickup permissions. Write the first essential gap and the safe action to resolve it. Recheck the plan after growth, a care change, travel or supply use. If disruption already prevents safe feeding or necessary care, seek verified qualified assistance promptly while keeping the child with a trusted caregiver. Do not stretch supplies through unsafe dilution or borrow someone else’s treatment instructions. Use a suitable alternative location if available and confirmed. The purpose of the reserve is to preserve care and time to act, not to justify waiting through a worsening situation. Family reunification Emergency hygiene Plan quantities for the actual feeding and care routine, and ask a qualified clinician for special dietary or medical needs. Include medications and transport or sleeping arrangements. Infants can deteriorate quickly with dehydration, temperature exposure or illness. Seek qualified care for concerning symptoms; do not rely on adult treatment advice. Use the caregiver plan and safe supplies already available while seeking verified medical or feeding support. Do not stretch formula with extra water or leave a child alone to find supplies. Name the caregiver and trusted backup for each child. Preserve safe feeding and care, keep children supervised during supply searches, and make communication and handovers appropriate to age and individual needs. baby emergency children war infant supplies formula outage Build around one ordinary day of care Protect the feeding method instead of improvising substitutes Separate feeding, diapering and clean storage Keep a trusted caregiver and a clear handover Plan safe arrival, rest and a manageable routine Test quantities and identify the first care gap Name the caregiver Decide who stays with each child during sheltering and travel. Use a familiar trusted backup; do not hand children to unverified helpers. Protect feeding Maintain breastfeeding where applicable. Ready-to-feed formula can avoid preparation water needs when available; follow product and age-specific guidance. Do not improvise formula or change dilution. Keep hygiene supplies Pack nappies, wipes, soap, clean clothing and safe water for essential care. Keep feeding equipment clean and separate from waste. Keep a contact card Use necessary caregiver contact details and medical information without displaying sensitive identity details publicly. Teach older children the agreed safe contacts. Use simple explanations Explain the next action calmly and specifically. Familiar routines and a comfort item can help; avoid promising that you know when danger will end.

title: Knives, saws and hand tools: selection, care and practical use
summary: Choose a tool for a specific ordinary task, compare grip and maintenance burden, and carry it in a suitable guard or case. Build a small repair kit around work you know how to do; use supervised practice for unfamiliar cutting tasks.
text: The job is unclear? Describe the material and task before choosing a tool. You need unusual force or cannot control the work? Stop and reassess the tool and workholding with qualified instruction. A tool is damaged or its mechanism is unreliable? Use a sound alternative and follow manufacturer service advice. Is a multitool enough for every repair? No. It can cover selected small tasks, but access, grip and tool size may make a dedicated tool more workable. Should the largest knife be the main field tool? Choose around the actual tasks and user. Size adds carrying burden and does not establish suitability or skill. Build the kit from a task list List the work you actually expect: opening packaging, repairing a loose non-critical fastener, cutting cord or maintaining a permitted campsite item. Name the material, location and user. A home kit, a vehicle pouch and a day-hike kit need different tools. Start with familiar tasks rather than the largest blade or most elaborate multitool. Task-first selection examples Task Question before packing Packaging and cord Would suitable scissors or a guarded cutter serve the task more conveniently? Small ordinary fastener Does the correct dedicated driver fit and reach the actual fastener? Permitted wood work Is cutting permitted, is it needed and have you learned the specific tool? Field repair Can the repair restore an ordinary non-critical item, or does it require proper service? Keep specialist work outside the small kit’s promise. An electrical, vehicle-control, load-bearing or medical problem may require qualified assessment. Tape and a multitool do not establish that a critical repair is sound. Choose an existing workable alternative when a repair would introduce uncertainty. Compare form, grip and work setting A tool should fit the task and the hand using it. CCOHS’s ergonomics guidance links tool shape, weight, handle fit and workstation layout with the effort required. It recommends selecting tools that allow an appropriate neutral wrist position. The lesson for a small kit is to evaluate the actual working arrangement rather than choosing a handle from a photograph. Compare the grip while wearing any gloves normally required for the task. Check whether the tool can be controlled comfortably and whether another user can use it without excessive reach or force. Consider access to the work: a compact multitool may pack neatly while a dedicated driver fits an awkward fastener better. A practical comparison record Feature What to inspect Handle Comfort, grip with expected gloves and access for the intended user. Mass and balance How it feels during the actual ordinary task rather than only when lifted. Guard or sheath Fit, retention, access and protection of other packed items. Instructions Clear task limits, care directions and the maker’s service route. Separate carrying convenience from usefulness A folding tool can occupy less space, while a purpose-made dedicated tool may offer a better grip or easier access for a repeated job. Compare those properties at the task level. Do not assume a locking mechanism makes every cutting use appropriate, or that one format is universally superior. For a saw, compare the manufacturer’s stated material and task suitability, guard arrangement, carry dimensions and replaceable consumables. For a knife or cutter, check the intended task, grip and protection in storage. Ask the maker about care for the particular materials and finish rather than applying a universal corrosion or sharpening recipe. Keep edge-care procedures with the product instructions and obtain practical instruction if unfamiliar. An unsuitable edge or damaged mechanism can change the effort needed, but trying an unlearned maintenance process during a disruption can create another problem. Choose equipment you can inspect and maintain under ordinary conditions. Prepare the whole work session The tool is only one part of the job. Arrange stable support, adequate light, a manageable material and enough space to keep other people outside the working area. Plan how the material stays controlled without placing a hand in the tool’s path. Use task-specific instruction for the actual cutting or sawing technique; this guide does not substitute a universal motion for every tool. A controlled ordinary task Define Name the material, desired result and appropriate tool. Arrange Provide light, stable support, suitable protection and a clear work area. Work within instruction Use the task-specific method you have learned and stop if control or conditions deteriorate. Finish Guard the tool, account for parts and scraps, and record any care or service need. Osprey Zero planning aid. These are conditional choices; current conditions and individual needs control the decision. Keep fatigue and distraction visible in the decision. If the job can wait, move it to a better-lit or more suitable place. In a household, agree who supervises children and pets while the work occurs. Do not give the tool user a simultaneous caregiving role that prevents attention to the task. Choose a modest repair pouch A small repair pouch is useful when it supports known non-critical tasks. Build it from your equipment’s likely needs and test it during ordinary maintenance. Keep each consumable’s purpose clear rather than packing several unidentified scraps. Editorial repair-pouch worksheet Item group Useful role Boundary Correct small drivers Known ordinary fasteners on suitable non-critical equipment. No forced fit or improvised repair of safety-critical systems. Manufacturer-compatible repair material A permitted patch or repair for the specific bag or shelter. Follow curing and surface instructions; temporary repair is not a structural certification. Spare ordinary fittings Known replacement for a lost compatible non-critical part. Label it so the intended equipment is clear. Guarded cutting tool A defined packaging, cord or repair task. Use only the method and material you understand. Test the kit by finding the needed item and explaining its purpose to another adult. If the repair requires a missing specialized tool, decide whether to carry it, obtain proper service before departure or use an alternative item. The pouch should reduce the need to improvise, not encourage attempts beyond the equipment or user’s limits. Store and maintain the tools as a set Put guards, sheaths or cases on before packing, and keep the tools from moving loose among food, care items or clothing. Store the set so the authorized adult can find it without exposing a child to unguarded edges. Clean and dry as the manufacturer directs; product labels control any oil or solvent use. Inspect the handle, guard, moving mechanisms and visible condition before a trip. Record a damaged item as unavailable rather than leaving it in the kit with a vague promise to fix it later. Keep service or replacement information with the inventory. If a tool was borrowed, check its condition and return the complete guarded item. Review ordinary access rules for the actual destination and carrier. A tool useful at home may be restricted in a venue or transport setting. Resolve that before departure and choose an allowed task alternative if needed. This page does not make a universal legality claim for knives or tools. Practice one useful skill in ordinary conditions Choose a small task with a clear result and a suitable instructor when needed. Use permitted material in a controlled setting, keep help available and stop if the work becomes awkward. Practice is most useful when it clarifies the tool’s limits and the arrangement required for the task. Name one task and its material. Locate the manufacturer instructions and needed protection. Set up the work area and supervision. Perform only the method you have learned. Check the result against the ordinary task, then guard and pack the tool. Record what needs changing before carrying it on a trip. Repeat with the intended user and expected gloves if that is relevant. Avoid making the exercise a test of endurance or speed. A short successful session followed by a clear inventory note gives more usable information than a bag filled with unfamiliar equipment. CCOHS · Hand tool ergonomics Use the official ergonomic design discussion to compare task, handle fit, mass and working position. Bushcraft foundations Working without a fire Inspect a small tool kit, identify one damaged item and arrange a supervised lesson for one useful task. Pause work when the tool, material, light, footing or user condition is unsuitable. A large tool does not compensate for lack of task-specific instruction. Stop the job if adequate light, footing or competent instruction is unavailable. Use a simpler existing solution or arrange qualified help; finishing a repair is not worth an avoidable serious injury. Keep tools away from shared food and children’s bags. Choose accessible handles and suitable task roles rather than assuming everyone can safely use the same tool. Tools & training knife weapons safety tools Build the kit from a task list Compare form, grip and work setting Separate carrying convenience from usefulness Prepare the whole work session Choose a modest repair pouch Store and maintain the tools as a set Practice one useful skill in ordinary conditions Choose the task and tool Use a purpose-made tool of manageable size. Check handles, guards, locking mechanisms and condition; retire damaged equipment rather than relying on tape to restore safety. Set a controlled work area Use stable footing, adequate light and a secure work surface. Keep other people away from the working area and stop when distracted or fatigued. Carry and store safely Use the correct sheath or guard. Secure tools during transport and keep them inaccessible to children. Do not leave blades loose in bags. Learn with supervision Get practical instruction for the actual task. Practice on suitable material in safe conditions before taking a tool on a trip.

title: Landslide & debris flow
summary: Move away from a slide area if you can do so safely, and obey evacuation warnings. Avoid steep slopes, channels and places downhill from recent burns during heavy rain. Do not cross moving debris or enter a fresh slide to inspect it.
text: Return only after local authorities assess stability. Contact a qualified professional about slope or structural damage. Another slide can follow the first, especially during continued rain. Stay away from channels, fresh debris and unstable slopes after the first movement. Do not cross the slide to check a house or search for belongings. Choose a destination outside the runout area rather than simply a higher point on the same unstable slope. Account for children, older people, pets and anyone who needs assistance before moving. Keep shoes, medicines and a torch in the shelter area. Decide who helps whom and who carries the essential supplies; do not send a lone child to retrieve items. For this situation, brief every person on the first action: notice warning signs. Agree who will manage children, pets or mobility needs while that action happens. Another slide can follow the first, especially during continued rain. Geological Notice warning signs New ground cracks, tilting trees, unusual runoff or rumbling warrant immediate caution and a call to local authorities. Leave the affected area Use an official safe route rather than following a drainage channel. Avoid crossings Mud and debris can sweep away vehicles and hide damaged road surfaces. Report from safety Give the location and visible hazards to emergency services; keep others out.

title: Lightning
summary: When you hear thunder, move into a substantial building or enclosed hard-top vehicle immediately. There is no safe place outdoors during a thunderstorm. Wait at least 30 minutes after the last thunder before going back out.
text: Thunder is audible? Move into a substantial building or enclosed hard-top vehicle immediately. Only a tent or open shelter is nearby? It is not safe lightning shelter. Reduce exposure while heading to a suitable shelter; no outdoor posture removes the risk. The storm seems to have passed? Remain in safe shelter for at least 30 minutes after the last thunder.  Plan the shelter before the activity Editorial planning: identify the nearest substantial building or enclosed hard-top vehicle before heading onto a beach, field or trail. Include the time needed for children or anyone with mobility needs to reach it. Choose an earlier cancellation point when the route to shelter is long; do not wait for the group to become trapped far from cover. Check forecasts before outdoor activity and identify shelter before leaving it. Lightning can strike beyond rainfall. Do not wait for rain to seek shelter. Choose a substantial building or enclosed hard-top vehicle now. A tent, tree or open-sided shelter is not protective. If no shelter is available, reduce exposure while moving toward one; there is no outdoor posture that makes lightning safe. Account for children, older people, pets and anyone who needs assistance before moving. Keep shoes, medicines and a torch in the shelter area. Decide who helps whom and who carries the essential supplies; do not send a lone child to retrieve items. For this situation, brief every person on the first action: leave exposed areas. Agree who will manage children, pets or mobility needs while that action happens. Lightning can strike beyond rainfall. Do not wait for rain to seek shelter. Severe storms Leave exposed areas Get out of water and off ridges, fields and beaches. Do not shelter beneath a lone tree. Choose real shelter Use a building or enclosed hard-top vehicle; picnic shelters and tents are not adequate. Avoid indoor pathways Stay away from showers, sinks, corded phones and plugged-in equipment. Help a struck person Call emergency services. A lightning victim carries no electrical charge; give CPR if needed and follow dispatcher instructions.

title: Lithium battery safety: power banks, tools and e-bikes
summary: Follow the device and charger instructions. Stop using a battery with swelling, leakage, unusual heat, odor or noises. If it is smoking or burning, leave the area and call emergency services from a safe place; do not carry it through the home. Keep charging areas away from your escape route.
text: Ordinary inspection finds damage? Stop use and arrange qualified advice. Smoke or fire? Leave, stay out and alert emergency services from a safe location. Can I fix a swollen battery? Do not puncture, compress or open it. Stop using it and seek appropriate handling instructions. Make a household charging map Editorial exercise: list where phones, power banks, tools and mobility batteries are normally charged. Mark any location that blocks a doorway or stair. Move routine charging to a suitable clear area according to the manufacturer; agree who checks that the right charger is used. Buying backup power Compare the jobs you actually need a battery to do, cable compatibility, storage instructions and reputable certification information. Record the model and support contact. A larger battery adds cost and storage needs; test the smallest suitable option before expanding. Review charging locations, remove incompatible chargers from routine use and ask your local collection service about disposal arrangements. A battery exposed to flooding may need specialist handling. Do not test it by charging. Smoke and fire can make the surrounding air unsafe. If a damaged battery cannot be assessed promptly, keep people away and avoid using or charging it. Smoke, fire or escalating heat calls for evacuation rather than waiting for a repair appointment. Keep children away from chargers and damaged packs. Include e-bikes and mobility equipment in the escape plan; a battery or vehicle must not block the only exit. swollen power bank battery swelling e bike battery lithium battery Check your equipment Use the specified compatible charger and reputable, certified equipment. Do not improvise repairs to a damaged pack. Choose a charging place Keep batteries away from combustible materials, direct sun and hot vehicles. Follow the product temperature limits. Notice changes early Stop using a device with unusual heat, changed shape, leaks, smells or sounds. Seek manufacturer or qualified repair advice rather than opening the pack. Dispose through the right service Do not put lithium batteries in household trash. Ask the local battery collection service how it handles damaged batteries before transporting one.

title: Long-duration blackout
summary: Plan around water, essential medical power, safe temperature, food and communications rather than a restoration estimate. Reserve battery power for necessities and use shelf-stable food when refrigeration fails. Keep all generators outdoors at least 20 feet from openings. Move early if essential care or safe shelter cannot be maintained.
text: Plan around water, essential medical power, safe temperature, food and communications rather than a restoration estimate. Reserve battery power for necessities and use shelf-stable food when refrigeration fails. Keep all generators outdoors at least 20 feet from openings. Move early if essential care or safe shelter cannot be maintained.  What runs out first? List the current water, food, medicine and battery supply in usable quantities. Compare these with actual household consumption. Check the next refill or relocation option while reserves still exist; counting unopened items is not enough when they need power or water to use. Which room should the household use? Choose the safest available room for temperature and accessible movement. Do not use a garage, fuel-burning appliance or a vehicle in an enclosed area for warmth or charging. Keep the exit and sanitation route clear. Shift from waiting to running a daily plan A long blackout becomes a problem of repeated decisions: drinking water, meals, sanitation, care, communication, rest, and movement. Treat the restoration estimate as uncertain. Build a plan that you can operate today, then review it as supplies and conditions change. This guide begins after the immediate hazards in the power-outage checklist have been addressed. A daily operating cycle Measure Count usable supplies and check people’s condition. Use actual quantities rather than how full a cupboard looks. Choose Decide the day’s meals, essential charging, check-ins, and whether home still meets important needs. Review Record what was used, what changed, and the trigger for the next action. Editorial planning cycle; urgent changes require action immediately, not at the next scheduled check. Use one notebook rather than scattered phone notes. Give each day a date and record the latest reliable information with its time. A handwritten log remains readable when batteries run out and helps a different adult take over without rebuilding the whole plan. Measure your runway with usable quantities Runway means the time a resource can support the household at the rate it is actually being used. Keep this as a planning estimate, not a promise. Do not count water of uncertain quality, food that cannot be safely prepared, or backup energy that cannot power the required device. A household status board you can copy into a notebook Need Write down Decision trigger Drinking water Safe amount available; actual daily use; next confirmed source Arrange supply or move before safe water is exhausted. Food Ready-to-eat meals suitable for everyone Change the meal plan before only unusable ingredients remain. Essential care Backup status; medicine storage; reachable support Act on the person-specific care deadline. Sanitation Handwashing water; waste route; toilet status Change arrangements if waste cannot be contained safely. Communication Working devices; charging opportunities; next check-in Use an agreed fallback if a channel fails. Transport Fuel or charge; driver; passable route; destination Preserve the ability to leave before options shrink. Example: 18 gallons of confirmed drinking-quality water divided by measured household use of 6 gallons a day suggests about three days of supply. It does not include uncounted guests, pets, spillage, or extra heat-related needs. Update the calculation after a day of real use. The goal is early decisions, never withholding necessary drinking water to make a number look better. Build a routine that reduces mistakes An example daily rhythm, adapted to your household When Useful tasks Morning Check people, water, food, sanitation, and current information. Decide whether to stay. Daylight Handle safe resupply, prepare the next meal, charge essentials when available, and check agreed contacts. Before dark Clear walking routes, place lights, organize night care, and confirm the next check-in. Evening Record use and problems. Protect a rest period for the adults responsible for care. Keep tasks small enough to complete. If one adult is caring for a child or dependent person, a complicated fuel schedule and multiple trips may be unrealistic. Build around the available help and physical ability. Use daylight for organizing, reading labels, and checking supplies, but avoid travel or exertion when weather or local conditions make those tasks unsafe. Give each recurring task an owner and an alternative person where possible. Use a check mark after a task is done; a discussion about doing it is not the same as completion. Keep children involved in age-appropriate tasks without giving them responsibility for fuel, hot equipment, electrical connections, or safety decisions. Preserve routines such as meals, medication schedules, and sleep as far as the individual care plan allows. Meals and hygiene without normal utilities Create a meal sequence from food that is already safe, familiar, and usable. Prefer portions the household can finish so you do not create leftovers that need refrigeration. Before opening a large container, work out how the remainder would be kept safe. A pantry of dry grains is not a complete plan if you lack safe cooking water or a permitted place to cook. Keep a manual opener with the meals that need it. Check soft-food needs, allergies, and food for pets. Separate safe drinking water from water reserved for an allowed non-drinking use. Clearly label containers so a tired person cannot confuse them. Choose a handwashing arrangement that can dispense safe water without repeated hand contact inside the supply container. If drainage or sewage may be affected, use the sanitation and sewer-failure guides rather than assuming that a toilet will keep working indefinitely. Waste management is part of the plan, not the last item to remember. Keep food waste away from meal preparation and sleeping areas, use appropriate containers, and check what collection or disposal route is actually available. Avoid instructions that depend on a nonexistent collection service or permit unsafe dumping. Emergency hygiene Sewer failure Food safety after power loss Protect care, communication, and rest Map the dependencies for each essential need. A powered device may also need a certain cable, clean water, consumables, an accessible outlet, or a trained caregiver. Write these together. A spare battery without the right adapter is not a working backup; a destination without accessibility may not meet the person’s actual needs. Make check-ins concise. State condition, location, immediate need, and next planned contact. Agree what a missed check-in means and what a supporter can safely do. Do not give every person a different schedule that becomes impossible to maintain. Preserve enough phone power for changes in condition and necessary movement. Use a real care threshold The point to seek another care setting comes from the person’s provider-approved plan and actual circumstances. Do not substitute a general household water or battery calculation for a clinical decision. Fatigue makes ordinary errors more likely: leaving a tap running, confusing containers, missing a care task, or stumbling over clutter. Arrange adult relief when available, keep the work area simple, and write down the important tasks. Someone living alone can ask a trusted contact for scheduled check-ins while still keeping a workable plan if contact fails. Resupply and relocation: make one complete decision Before a trip, decide what you need, where it is confirmed available, how to get there safely, and how to return. An unverified rumor about free ice can cost fuel, time, and phone charge. Combine necessary errands when appropriate, but do not turn a simple water trip into a long search while a vulnerable person is left unsupported. Questions to answer before leaving Question Why it matters Is the source open and the supply suitable? Avoid travelling to closed sites or accepting water of unclear quality. Can we carry the actual amount? Water, fuel, and equipment may exceed physical or vehicle capacity. Who stays with the household? Care, access, and essential monitoring still need to continue. What is the fallback? A failed trip should not leave no safe water or route to another location. Should this be a move rather than an errand? Repeated small trips may conceal that home no longer meets essential needs. If relocating, confirm the destination’s suitability, arrange transport, and take care information and essential equipment. Plan for pets and building access. If immediate danger develops, leave the hazard without delaying for a perfect inventory. Recovery and a useful after-action review After restoration, assess systems separately: electricity, drinking water, drainage, food storage, and communications. Do not assume one working service proves the others are ready. Use the relevant utility or public-health instructions, and qualified assessment for damaged equipment. Recharge and replenish the essentials that made the biggest difference. List the first shortage, the first equipment failure, and the hardest daily task. Identify a low-cost fix for each: a clearer label, a spare cable, a smaller water container, or a simpler meal. Update contact arrangements and relocation choices based on what was actually reachable. Review the plan with everyone who will use it, including a substitute caregiver. A useful review ends with a short list of changes you can make, not a wish list of expensive equipment. Keep the plan modest enough that you will maintain it between emergencies. Share safe tasks and checked information with trusted neighbours. Charge essential devices when safe power is available and use brief scheduled check-ins. Do not rely on an internet-only plan. An announced restoration time is an estimate. Carbon monoxide, unsafe improvised wiring, dehydration and dangerous temperatures can be more urgent than the outage itself. Build a daily plan from current supplies and reachable shelter options. Do not wait for a food distribution, public generator or rescue transport that has not been confirmed. Plan shifts for checking vulnerable people and essential equipment so one caregiver is not awake continuously. Keep infant feeding, safe sleep, medicine storage and pet water on the same written daily inventory. extended blackout days without power grid down prolonged power outage Shift from waiting to running a daily plan Measure your runway with usable quantities Build a routine that reduces mistakes Meals and hygiene without normal utilities Protect care, communication, and rest Resupply and relocation: make one complete decision Recovery and a useful after-action review List critical needs Identify power-dependent care, temperature-sensitive medicines, water access and who cannot manage stairs or heat. Set priorities before using scarce batteries or fuel. Measure what remains Write down safe water, ready-to-eat meals, usable batteries and medicine quantities. Review the inventory daily rather than guessing. Keep fuel use safe Never run generators, charcoal or camping stoves indoors, in a garage or on an enclosed balcony. Do not backfeed house wiring. Protect food and hygiene Keep cold appliances closed and use food-safety time and temperature guidance. Separate drinking water from washing and waste arrangements. Set a relocation trigger Choose the point when medical support, water or temperature can no longer be maintained. Confirm a reachable destination before those needs become urgent.

title: Lost outdoors
summary: Stop moving, stay together and assess your last known position. If there is no immediate threat, stay put, protect yourself from weather and signal for help. Share your location if communication works; do not wander in search of a shortcut.
text: Immediate hazard where you stopped? Reach a nearby safer position with the group, record it and update contact if possible. Suitable site but position uncertain? Remain findable, organize protection and send the best factual location information. No phone service? Use the prepared equipment and trip-contact plan; do not roam solely for reception. Another person is missing? Keep the remaining group coordinated and use the appropriate reporting plan; avoid an unplanned off-trail search. Should I follow a stream downhill? No universal rule makes that a suitable route. Watercourses can introduce cliffs, flooding or difficult access. Use the known facts and the lost-person plan rather than a shortcut guess. Can staying put still require moving? Yes, if the current site has an immediate threat. Make the protective purpose clear, keep the group together and record/update the new position. Does sending a message mean rescue is on the way? No. Distinguish attempted, delivered and acknowledged messages, follow received instructions and continue practical protection. Avoid making the search area larger When you realize the route or position is uncertain, stop unnecessary movement and keep the group together. NPS recommends staying put when lost unless there is an immediate threat to life. Establish the safest workable waiting position and the best location information available. Keep the last confirmed fact distinct from a guess. Write the last reliable landmark, approximate time and what happened afterward. Do not turn “we think that was the junction” into a certain starting point for a new journey. Use the map, signs and available device information without discarding a clear mismatch on the ground. A quick factual assessment Question Record People Who is present and any urgent condition or care need. Place Current confirmed/estimated location and the last reliable landmark. Conditions Immediate hazards, weather and remaining daylight. Supplies Accessible weather system, water, food, light, signal and communication power. Contact Who has the trip plan and what messages have actually been sent. Avoid unplanned downhill travel, river following or a guessed shortcut to a road. The desire to take action is understandable, but action should have a clear protective purpose rather than merely create distance from the known itinerary. Make a precise help message Give current coordinates with their format if available, or the last confirmed landmark and time. State whether the position is known or estimated, the number of people, urgent needs, immediate hazards and the intended action. Keep a reply method available. For example, use the structure “Location [known fact and uncertainty]; people [number and relevant needs]; event [what changed]; hazards [current conditions]; intention [remain or necessary protective move]; contact [available channel].” Fill it with real facts.
